statement: In the two-workspace experiment, the whole-arm model predicted neural activity better than the hand-only model for 238 of 288 neurons, with no significant difference for the other 50.
A whole-arm model trained on both workspaces explained as much neural variance as models trained within a single workspace.
The whole-arm model predicted the shape of directional tuning curves in the two workspaces better than the hand-only model for 138 of 288 neurons, and worse for 2.
The whole-arm model predicted the shifts of preferred direction between workspaces better than the hand-only model, with a circular variance accounted for of 0.75 against 0.57.
In the 120 ms after movement onset, average hand speed was similar in active reaches and passive bumps.
A linear discriminant classifier predicted whether a movement was active or passive 89% of the time from whole-arm kinematics in the analysis window.
Many neurons had an above-chance separability index, the accuracy of a linear discriminant predicting the trial type from that neuron's firing.

In the active/passive experiment the whole-arm model again tended to out-perform the hand-only model, but for many more neurons than in the two-workspace experiment the difference was not significant.

Unlike in the two-workspace experiment, many neurons had no consistent relationship with arm kinematics across active and passive movements, shown by negative pseudo-R2 for the model trained on both conditions.
The consistency of the whole-arm model, its pseudo-R2 when trained on both conditions, correlated negatively with a neuron's separability index.
Over 10 sessions the recordings yielded 95.8 (SD 6.7) sorted neurons and 408 (SD 40.8) trials of the main finger task per session.

Online BCI classification of the cued finger was 86% accurate (SD 4% across sessions, weighted by trials) over 4016 trials in 10 sessions, against a chance level of 17%. No-Go trials of the first session are excluded because the classifier could not output No-Go that day.
Most (70%) of the online classification errors were middle-ring or ring-pinky confusions.

Offline classification of the cued finger from sorted firing rates in the window 0.5 to 1.5 s after the cue, with diagonal LDA and leave-one-out cross-validation within each session, was 92% accurate (SD 2% across sessions) over 4080 trials.
In the calibration task, offline cross-validated finger classification was 96% accurate (SD 3%) over 530 trials in nine sessions.

Most (89%) neurons were significantly tuned to at least one finger movement, by a two-tailed t-test of each finger's firing rate in the 0.5 to 1.5 s window against No-Go trials, p < 0.05 after FDR correction, with neurons below 0.1 Hz excluded and neurons pooled across sessions.
Linear regression could not decode the cue's screen coordinates from neural activity in the attempted-movement window; cross-validated r2 was close to 0 in every session.
A diagonal LDA classifier could not classify the cue location from neural activity in the attempted-movement window.
Fingers could not be classified from neural activity during the control task, in which the participant viewed the cues without attempting movements.

In the session-averaged representational dissimilarity matrix (cross-validated Mahalanobis distance, window 0.5 to 1.5 s, No-Go excluded), the thumb is distinct, while the middle, ring and pinky fingers are close.
The finger RDMs were consistent across sessions, with an average pairwise correlation between session RDMs of r = 0.90 (SD 0.04, min 0.83, max 0.99).
The distances between the most confused finger pairs (middle-ring and ring-pinky) did not increase across sessions (one-tailed p > 0.99) or across runs within sessions (one-tailed p = 0.67).

Across all finger pairs the inter-finger distances did not increase; they decreased slightly across sessions (t(8) = -4.0, two-tailed p = 0.004) and across runs within sessions (t(82) = -2.4, p = 0.019), with very small effect sizes (Cohen's f2 of 0.008 and 0.005).
The able-bodied match and the representational dynamics hold when only well-isolated units (lowest third of L-ratio) are used.

In the time discrimination task, subjects chose the frame that was shown first in 73% of trials when the two frames were separated by no boundary or by a soft boundary, and in 53% of trials, significantly fewer, when they were separated by a hard boundary.
Reaction times in the time discrimination task were longer when the two frames were separated by a hard boundary (2.10 s) than by no boundary (1.62 s) or a soft boundary (1.59 s).
Confidence ratings in the time discrimination task were lower when the two frames were separated by a hard boundary (1.95 on a scale of 1 to 3) than by no boundary (2.52) or a soft boundary (2.59).
Scene recognition accuracy did not differ between frames from clips with no boundary (76%), a soft boundary (75%) and a hard boundary (75%).

Recognition accuracy for a target frame fell with the time between the frame and the boundary before it, for soft boundaries (r = -0.61) and hard boundaries (r = -0.44), but not for clips with no boundary (r = 0.085).

42 of 580 medial temporal lobe neurons (7.24%) were boundary cells, which changed their firing in the second after soft and hard boundaries but not in the middle of clips with no boundary; 2.11% were expected by chance.

36 of 580 medial temporal lobe neurons (6.20%) were event cells, which changed their firing in the second after hard boundaries but not after soft boundaries or in the middle of clips with no boundary; 2.26% were expected by chance.

Boundary cells were most common in the parahippocampal gyrus (18 of 68 neurons, 26%, against 7% in the amygdala and 3.5% in the hippocampus), and event cells in the hippocampus (27 of 343, 7.9%, against 4.3% in the amygdala and 2.9% in the parahippocampal gyrus).
Boundary cells and event cells did not change their firing at clip onsets or offsets during encoding, nor at image onsets or offsets in the two memory tests.
76 of 580 medial temporal lobe neurons (13.1%) changed their firing at clip onsets and 4 of 580 (0.7%) at clip offsets, and none of them was a boundary cell or an event cell.
Boundary cells responded to hard boundaries about 100 ms earlier than event cells; their firing peaked 197 ms after the boundary, against 301 ms for event cells.
Of 405 neurons recorded outside the medial temporal lobe, 8 were boundary cells and 9 were event cells, so boundary responses are largely confined to the medial temporal lobe.

Boundary cells fired more after soft and hard boundaries during encoding when the frame that followed the boundary was later recognised than when it was forgotten; there was no such difference for clips with no boundary, for the time discrimination task, or for event cells.

Event cells' spikes were locked more strongly to the phase of the theta-band local field potential after soft and hard boundaries when the temporal order of the clip was later remembered than when it was not; boundary cells showed no such effect.

The state of the population of all medial temporal lobe neurons changed abruptly in the first 300 ms after soft and hard boundaries, and only slowly in clips with no boundary, measured as the distance in principal-component space from the state at the boundary.

The distance the population state travelled in the second after a boundary correlated positively with later recognition accuracy for soft (r = 0.65) and hard (r = 0.57) boundaries, and negatively with time discrimination accuracy for hard boundaries (r = -0.68).

During scene recognition, population activity correlated with the activity during encoding shortly after the soft or hard boundary of the tested clip, for correctly recognised targets and for foils wrongly called old, but not for forgotten targets or correctly rejected foils.
The reinstated state was most similar to the state about 1.2 s after the boundary that preceded the tested frame, and 1.5 to 1.7 s before the tested frame itself was shown.
Reinstatement after soft and hard boundaries was stronger for old decisions made with high confidence than with low confidence.
For foils wrongly called old, reinstatement was stronger when the foil was highly similar to its target; for correctly rejected foils it did not vary with similarity.
After quality control, 1,227 Patch-seq neurons from mouse primary motor cortex were assigned to transcriptomic types, covering 77 of the 90 neuronal t-types of the reference taxonomy.

A sparse reduced-rank regression of 17 electrophysiological features on gene expression, using 25 genes and a rank-5 latent space, reached a cross-validated R2 of 0.38, with cross-validated correlations of 0.90, 0.74 and 0.67 between the first three pairs of projections.
A reduced-rank regression restricted to ion channel genes did not perform much worse than the full model, with a cross-validated R2 of 0.33 and correlations of 0.86, 0.71 and 0.56.

In a k-nearest-neighbour classification of cells into seven transcriptomic families from electrophysiological features, the confusion matrix was mostly diagonal, with only the ET and IT subclasses strongly overlapping.
Families were less separable by morphology than by electrophysiology among inhibitory neurons, and most separable when electrophysiological and morphological features were combined.
Across 200 pairs of t-types from the same family, the transcriptomic distance and the electrophysiological distance between t-types were correlated with r = 0.60.
Among IT t-types, transcriptomic distances were strongly correlated with differences in average soma depth, r = 0.70.
Most t-types were classified into their own family from electrophysiology, but some, such as Sst Pvalb Calb2, Lamp5 Egln3_1 and Vip Mybpc1, were often classified into another family.
Many t-types had a normalized total variance of electrophysiological features well above that of k-means clusters, while some, such as Pvalb Vipr2_2, appeared homogeneous.

At physiological temperature, 185 neurons were sequenced from 8 adult mice (7 Sst-Cre/Ai9 and 1 Pvalb-Cre/Ai9); 177 got a t-type (110 Sst, 43 IT, 12 ET, 10 Pvalb, 2 NP); 175 were in layer 5; electrophysiological features were extracted for 184.
Cells at physiological temperature were stimulated with the same paradigm as the main data set, 600 ms current pulses from -200 pA upwards in 20 pA steps up to 1,380 pA, sometimes stopped earlier.
Follow-up experiments at 34 degrees C confirmed the electrophysiological overlap between IT and ET neurons seen at room temperature.
At 34 degrees C, the AP threshold showed a prominent difference between layer 5 IT and ET neurons.
Regression slopes of tp on ts are positive and less than one in every condition, so the animals estimated ts and their responses were biased toward the mean of the prior.
At the overlapping ts of 800 ms, biases were in opposite directions for the two priors (rank-sum test, p < 1e-43 in animal H over 17 sessions).
Increments of tp between neighbouring ts are smaller at the extremes of the prior than near its mean, as the sigmoidal Bayesian estimator predicts (signed-rank test, p < 1e-11 in animal H).
Biases are larger for the Long prior than for the Short prior, as scalar variability predicts; regression slopes are smaller for Long.
A Bayesian observer model with scalar measurement and production noise fit to the behaviour captures the bias and the variance of tp in all conditions.
About 30% of neurons were modulated by elapsed time (27% in monkey H) and more than 60% were sensitive to the prior (65% in monkey H), by a Poisson GLM of spike counts before Set compared by BIC.
At the overlapping ts of 800 ms, firing rates differ between priors, with the largest difference during the support of the prior, between 480 and 800 ms after Ready.
Population activity is low dimensional; 3 to 4 principal components in the estimation epoch and 5 to 10 in the production epoch explain about 75% of the variance.

Projections of estimation-epoch neural states onto the encoding axis match the Bayesian estimates from the model fitted to the behaviour (R2 = 0.993 for the Short prior, 0.996 for the Long prior, monkey H, Hand Left).
Neural projections are better explained by the Bayesian model than by a linear function of ts with the same number of parameters, for both priors (signed-rank test on RMSE, p = 0.008 for each prior).

In the Long prior during the period matched to the support of the Short prior ("Short In Long"), there is no sigmoidal representation; the Bayesian model is not better than the linear one (signed-rank test, p = 0.74).
Neural projections show more bias for the Long prior than for the Short prior, as a smaller regression slope of Xu on ts (signed-rank test, p = 0.008).
Larger projections on the encoding axis at Set are followed by slower neural trajectories in the production epoch (Pearson correlation, rho Short = -0.74, rho Long = -0.51).

The initial speed of production trajectories (Set to Set + 400 ms) is biased toward the middle of the prior; its dependence on ts is shallower than the unbiased profile proportional to 1/ts (signed-rank test, p < 1e-3 over conditions and animals).
The speed of neural trajectories in the production epoch predicts the mean tp (Pearson correlation, rho Short = -0.58, rho Long = -0.52).

Instantaneous speed of neural trajectories in the full neural space is not modulated during the support of each prior (signed-rank test for zero regression slopes, p = 0.64 for Short, p = 0.08 for Long).

In the first 200 ms after Set, trajectories for different ts run parallel; their distance to the middle ts trajectory does not change (signed-rank test for zero slopes, p = 0.92 for the shortest ts, p = 0.13 for the longest).

Aligned to the response, distances between trajectories for different ts decrease steadily up to movement initiation, without the converging then diverging pattern a ts-dependent threshold would produce.

The variance across single trials of the GPFA neural state at Set projected on the encoding axis has an inverted-U profile over ts, lower at the extremes of each prior (one-tailed signed-rank test on quadratic coefficients, p = 0.0273, monkey H).
The mean of the single-trial GPFA projections is sigmoidal (signed-rank test on increments, p = 0.0078) and has a higher slope for the Short prior (one-tailed signed-rank, p = 0.0625).
Recurrent neural networks trained on the two-prior task with scalar measurement noise behave like a Bayesian observer and show curved trajectories during the support of the prior, like DMFC.
In trained networks, compressing states along the encoding axis increases the regression to the mean of tp, and translating them shifts tp.
The behavioural and neural results hold in monkey G as in monkey H.
About 227 interneurons were imaged per mouse (226.6 ± 27.3, mean ± std over 16 mice), and 121.0 ± 28.4 per mouse were assigned a putative subtype.
The layer distribution of each subtype along the CA1 depth axis is consistent with earlier anatomical studies.
The majority of interneurons were positively correlated with running velocity, and about 10% were negatively correlated, across all subtypes (156 negative and 1429 positive in Figure 2D).
Negatively correlated cells were significantly enriched in CCKC, where nearly half of cells were more active during immobility.
The correlation with velocity differs between the six subtypes (one-way ANOVA, p < 1e-10, with Tukey's post hoc test).
IvC/NGFC were less modulated by locomotion than other subtypes.
Negatively correlated cells were enriched in stratum oriens and positively correlated cells in stratum pyramidale.

The activity of positively correlated cells followed changes in velocity by up to several seconds, while the activity of negatively correlated cells was more tightly linked in time to changes in velocity.
Run-start and run-stop responses show that immobility-triggered activation is specific to CCKC.
A deep network classified PV-expressing, SOM-expressing, CCK and IvC/NGFC cells from dF/F, velocity and depth with accuracies of 64, 71, 60 and 59%.
During sharp-wave ripples PVBC were generally strongly modulated while most SomC were not.
AAC and BiC showed bimodal modulation during sharp-wave ripples, and all subtypes but CCKC and IvC/NGFC split into a modulated and a non-modulated group.
17.5 ± 6.4% (mean ± sem over 6 mice, 3 sessions each) of interneurons, blind of subtype, passed the test for significant spatial selectivity.
12.7 ± 8.3% of interneurons (mean ± sem) had negative spatial selectivity, slightly fewer than had positive selectivity.

Position decoded from the small subset of spatially selective interneurons was about as accurate as from all interneurons, and more accurate than from as many randomly chosen interneurons or with position shuffled.
BiC had a higher probability than other subtypes of being spatially modulated again in other sessions.
The selectivity index of spatially selective cells did not differ between subtypes (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.35).
Spatially selective PVBC had a more stable within-session recruitment (odd-even lap correlation of tuning curves) than spatially selective SomC.
Within-session stability of tuning curves differed between subtypes, PVBC showing the highest and CCKC the lowest odd-even correlations.
Tuning curve correlations of the same cells after 1 hour and after 24 hours were lower than within-session correlations, and still higher than chance.
Interneuron tuning curves decorrelated on exposure to a novel belt, more than with the passage of time, and context could be decoded from population activity.
PVBC, SomC, BiC and AAC decreased their activity in the first laps on a novel belt; CCKC were not modulated.
In goal-oriented learning, SomC and BiC had higher reward modulation indices than other subtypes.
After the reward zone moved, SomC and BiC activity increased at the old zone above chance, and this decreased over the session.
VIP+/CCK+ and VIP+/M2R+ cells were negatively correlated with velocity, and all ISI subtypes positively.
VIP+/CR- cells and type III ISIs were less correlated with SomC and BiC than with PV+ cells.

During mating the probability of accepting behaviours (lordosis, wiggle) increases gradually over the interaction, while resistance behaviours (dart, top up, kick, turn) first increase and then slowly decrease.
Females spend 83.9% of their mating behaviour time in male-responsive behaviours (accepting, resistance, staying) and 16.1% in self-initiated ones (approach, sniff, check genital area).
Males spend 11.3 times more time in self-initiated mating behaviours (sniff, mount, intromission) than females do in theirs (approach, sniff, check genital area).
Male copulation (mounting and intromission) comes in bouts separated by interbout intervals with a mean of 13.7 s (1,685 bouts and 1,611 intervals in 74 trials).
Females show social behaviours (accepting, resistance and appetitive) for 62% of the duration of each male copulation bout and continue them for 23% of each interbout interval.
Only a small percentage of VMHvl alpha-cells (approximately 2 to 13%) are tuned to any one mating behaviour by choice probability; most show mixed selectivity.
A linear model of each neuron's activity from behaviour explains little of its variance, with mean cross-validated R2 of 0.08 from female behaviours, 0.14 from male behaviours and 0.15 from both.
Adding the activity of the other simultaneously imaged neurons as regressors raises the mean cross-validated R2 to 0.46.
About 30% of cells have an autocorrelation half-width (ACHW) longer than 25 s, and the mean ACHW is 20 s, longer than the mean interbout interval.
The ACHW of the same cells is shorter when the male is behind a perforated pencil cup (14.3 s) than during free interaction (19.6 s), 470 neurons from 5 mice.
An rSLDS fit to each receptive mating trial explains 64.08% (SD 6.8) of the variance of the neural trajectories, n = 15 mice.
The rSLDS reveals one integration dimension with a long time constant (110.7 +- 13.6 s) compared with the next (24.5 +- 5.1 s), forming an approximate line attractor; n = 15 mice, P = 6.5e-5.

A single-state linear dynamical system driven by male sniff, mount and intromission predicts activity in the integration dimension with cvR2 of 0.88 +- 0.02 and an intrinsic time constant above 200 s.
Of neurons contributing to the integration dimension, 56% correlate with an ideal ramp with r2 above 0.5, but they peak at different times.

Transient optogenetic inhibition of VMHvl pushes population activity off the line attractor, after which it relaxes back to the attractor, as the flow field fit to unperturbed data predicts; n = 3 mice.

Activity in the integration dimension during copulation interbout intervals is as high as in the preceding bout, so a decoder cannot tell bouts from intervals (0.52 against a shuffle of 0.49, n = 4 mice, P = 0.2).
When male mating is stopped for minutes by optogenetic activation of the male's VMH, activity in the female's integration dimension stays elevated; n = 4 mice.
Activity in the integration dimension peaks just before ejaculation and drops immediately after; n = 4 mice.

Over the natural oestrus cycle, rSLDS models fit on receptive days have a line attractor and those fit on unreceptive days do not (line-attractor score 1.9 +- 0.2 against 0.05 +- 0.02, n = 4 mice, P = 0.02).

Projected onto the integration dimension found on the receptive day, activity on unreceptive days does not ramp and stays low during male mounting (normalised value 0.09 on unreceptive against 0.69 on receptive days, n = 4 mice).

Cells weighted on the integration dimension have shorter ACHW on unreceptive than on receptive days (16.1 +- 0.8 s against 25.2 +- 1.5 s, P < 0.001), while cells that do not contribute to it do not change.
Attractor dynamics disappear after ovariectomy and return after hormone priming.

In oestrogen-injected females, the area under the curve of the integration dimension correlates with the percentage of time spent in accepting behaviours (r2 = 0.62, P < 0.0001, n = 50 trials), and not with resistance or appetitive behaviours.
In the same trials, the area under the curve of the population mean of all neurons does not correlate with the percentage of time spent in accepting behaviours.
Danionella cerebrum (DC) swim at a higher median velocity than zebrafish (ZF) across the visual stimuli.
Across the whole-field stimuli DC have a higher median velocity than ZF (9.8 against 6.4 mm/s), with a significant main effect of species in a two-way ANOVA.
ZF modulate their velocity with the direction of motion; forward motion increases their median velocity (static 5.0 mm/s, forward 8.8 mm/s).
DC lack the direction-dependent velocity modulation seen in ZF.
DC swim at a significantly higher velocity than ZF for oblique stimuli.
Both species follow the direction of optic flow, turning right (positive angular velocity) to rightward motion and left to leftward motion.
Across directional stimuli ZF have higher angular acceleration than DC, and the distributions of the two species differ for every stimulus.
DC generally respond less than ZF to monocular stimuli, suggesting that they need more visual motion input to drive the optomotor response.
ZF swim in discrete bouts separated by glides, while DC swim continuously at a relatively constant velocity.

In representative trials ZF bouts reach a peak velocity of 44.7 mm/s with a median of 1.8 mm/s, DC swim at a median of 13.7 mm/s to forward motion; to oblique motion ZF show a median angular velocity of 12.0 degrees/s and median peak angular acceleration of 174 degrees/s2, and DC an average peak of 103 degrees/s2 to rightward motion.
Both species have spatially intermixed, direction-selective neurons enriched in the pretectum and anterior hindbrain, and share the major functional response types.
The average direction selectivity index is similar in ZF and DC (0.62 against 0.66, p > 0.05, Student's t-test, 5 fish each).
ZF tend to have a higher proportion of motion-responsive neurons than DC (0.13 against 0.06, p = 0.059).
DC have a higher proportion of purely monocular neurons than ZF (0.37 against 0.16, p < 0.05).
The binocularity index ratio is higher in ZF than in DC (0.72 against 0.24, p = 0.010).
Head-fixed DC perform longer swims than ZF (median 0.75 s against 0.29 s, p < 0.0001).
Head-fixed ZF show larger directional tail angles than DC to turn-inducing stimuli, and shorten their swims for oblique stimuli while DC do not.
Swim-onset-associated neurons in DC have a longer active (ON) phase than in ZF, while non-motor-associated neurons have similar ON durations.
Motor-associated neurons in the putative ventromedial spinal projection neurons of both species encode turn direction in a lateralized way, correlating more with ipsilateral turns.

The data are 2286 single and multi-units from 29 patients (17 female), 30 to 137 units per patient, in the amygdala (580), hippocampus (794), entorhinal cortex (440), parahippocampal cortex (373) and piriform cortex (99).
Over half of the parahippocampal neurons responded to camera cuts (193 of 373, 51.74%).
Camera cuts evoked responses in a large share of neurons in every region (amygdala 46.90%, entorhinal cortex 45.68%, hippocampus 38.92%).
Few parahippocampal neurons responded to scene cuts (25 of 373, 6.70%), but the modulation was consistent across the responsive neurons (cluster permutation test, p = 0.018).
Only a few neurons responded to the onset of semantic features (Summer 46, Tom 216, Persons 6 and Outdoor 4 of 2286 neurons), in contrast to camera cuts (1025).
No neuron responded to the onset of indoor scenes.

By the cluster permutation test, parahippocampal neurons responded to the largest set of features (Summer, Persons, Camera Cuts, Scene Cuts, Outdoor), compared with the hippocampus (Tom, Camera Cuts, Outdoor), the amygdala (Camera Cuts) and the entorhinal cortex (none).
Thresholding the activity of single neurons does not reliably predict whether Summer is on screen; most neurons perform near chance, below the population decoder.
A logistic regression on spike counts decodes characters and location about as well as the LSTM; pooled over patients it reaches kappa 0.28 for Summer and 0.31 for Indoor/Outdoor.
For scene and camera cuts the logistic regression performs below the LSTM, by 0.1 and 0.07, that is about kappa 0.10 and 0.11.
Without temporal gaps between training, validation and test samples, decoding of Summer is almost perfect (kappa 0.99), and it falls to 0.31 as the gap grows to 32 s.
Decoding from a single patient's neurons is lower than from the pooled population; no patient matches the pooled performance, for Summer, Scene Cuts or Indoor/Outdoor.
For Summer, patients 7, 10, 15 and 22 exceed kappa 0.2; for Indoor/Outdoor, patients 2, 13, 20 and 25 exceed 0.2.
Decoding from single regions depends on the feature; the amygdala is best and the hippocampus worst for Summer, and the parahippocampal cortex is best and the amygdala worst for Indoor/Outdoor.
Face labels decode slightly better than character labels (Summer 0.33, Tom 0.27), and Summer Presence (0.27) is decoded best from the amygdala (0.26).

Responsive neurons drive decoding of camera cuts but not of Summer; without them, Summer is decoded about as well as from all neurons while camera cuts drop the most, and responsive neurons alone decode camera cuts about as well as all neurons but Summer less well.
Across the five rankings of neurons by logistic regression weights for Summer, the top 500 neurons share 78 neurons, against about 1 expected by chance.
Decoding Summer from the 500 top-ranked neurons gives the peak performance (kappa 0.38), above that of the full population.

An LSTM decodes every label above chance from the pooled population, with kappa 0.36 for Persons, 0.31 for Indoor/Outdoor, 0.31 for Summer, 0.32 for McKenzie, 0.23 for Tom, 0.20 for Scene Cuts and 0.18 for Camera Cuts.
Shuffling the order of time bins in the test data lowers the LSTM's performance, most for visual transitions.
The dataset holds 1863 single neurons recorded from the medial temporal lobes of 59 subjects.
The patients performed 87 sessions, listed by subject and session id in Online-only Table 1 (the Methods give 89).
Online-only Table 1 gives the age and sex of every subject; there are 25 female and 34 male subjects.
Each session has 100 encoding trials showing 100 novel images and 100 recognition trials, of which 50 show new and 50 old images, and the images come from 5 visual categories.
In the trials table, new_old_labels_recog is 0 for old stimuli (seen during encoding) and 1 for new stimuli.
The events stream holds the TTL markers 55, 1, 2, 3, 20 or 21, 31 to 36, 6 and 66 with the meanings of Table 1, and the events and experiment_ids streams have one entry each, in the same order.
The learning block is labelled with one of 80, 83 or 88 and the recognition block with one of 81, 84 or 89.
To protect patient information, session_start_time keeps only the year and month of the experiment, with the day set to the first of the month for all sessions.
The units table holds spike_times, waveform_mean_encoding, waveform_mean_recognition (sampled at 100 kHz), origClusterID, SNR, IsolDist and electrodes, with one electrode per neuron.
The electrodes table gives each electrode's brain area, MNI coordinates, impedance, the filter applied before spike sorting (300 to 3000 Hz) and the original hardware channel.
Clusters were accepted as units only when fewer than 3% of their interspike intervals were shorter than 3 ms.
All neurons were recorded from the medial temporal lobe, in the amygdala and the hippocampus.
Subjects distinguished new from old images; the behavioural AUC averaged over all sessions is 0.74 ± 0.10.
Performance was similar at the two study sites, with an average AUC of 0.74 ± 0.09 for CS sessions and 0.69 ± 0.13 for TWH sessions.
The ROC curve is asymmetric (p < 0.05), as expected for declarative memory.
Accuracy is significantly higher in high than in low confidence trials (P < 0.001, paired t test) across all sessions.

343 of the 1863 cells (18.4%) are visually selective, by a one-way ANOVA (P < 0.05) of the firing rate in recognition trials, in a 1 s window starting 200 ms after stimulus onset, across the 5 visual categories.

146 of the 1863 cells (7.8%) are memory selective, by a two-tailed bootstrap comparison of mean firing rates (1,000 runs, P < 0.05) between the 50 novel and 50 familiar recognition trials in a 1 s window starting 200 ms after stimulus onset.
26 cells (1.4%) are both visually and memory selective.
The percentages of VS, MS and dual cells are comparable between CS sessions (18.4%, 7.7% and 1.4%) and the new TWH sessions (19.4%, 10.4% and 1.3%).
The dataset includes 9 sessions from a new institution, Toronto Western Hospital.
Neuron 132-177-4-RA (session 132, channel 177, cell 4, right amygdala) is visually selective, responding most to images of animals.
Neuron 144-140-3-RH (session 144, channel 140, cell 3, right hippocampus) is visually selective for phones.

Optogenetically evoked dopamine release in the dorsolateral striatum (Anxa1+ projection region) at 0.5 mW is lower in LRRK2-G2019S than in LRRK2-WT mice (64 against 56 stimulations, p = 1.10e-20, one-tailed two-sample t-test).
Seven of eight individual G2019S mice show significantly reduced evoked dopamine release at 0.5 mW compared with the WT group; mouse 3743 does not.
The reduction of evoked dopamine release in Anxa1 G2019S mice holds at each of the four stimulation powers, 0.1, 0.5, 1 and 4 mW (p from 1.29e-15 to 1.10e-20).

Spontaneous dopamine transients in the dorsolateral striatum are smaller in G2019S than in WT mice (1064 against 798 transients, p = 2.75e-177, one-tailed two-sample t-test), with 57 to 285 transients per mouse.
Six of eight individual G2019S mice show significantly smaller spontaneous dopamine transients than the WT group; mice 4651 and 3743 do not.
In the dorsomedial striatum (Calb1+ projection region), spontaneous dopamine transients are not reduced in G2019S mice (970 against 682 transients, p = 0.98).
Evoked dopamine release in the dorsomedial striatum from Calb1+ neuron stimulation is reduced in G2019S mice at each of four powers (56 against 40 stimulations per power, p from 6.45e-05 to 0.001).
Only 2 of 7 G2019S mice show reduced Calb1+ evoked dopamine release relative to the WT group.
The G2019S reduction of evoked release at 0.5 mW is much larger for Anxa1+ (Cohen's d = 2.05) than for Calb1+ stimulation (d = 0.76).
Insertion yields were low, 21.4% (3 of 14 sensors) in monkey T and 33% (3 of 9) in monkey P, counted as recording sites that stayed functional after insertion until the end of the study.
The s-µIPs kept recording for more than a year after implantation; the example sites were recorded 483 days (c8dg), 496 days (c3bs-c3a) and 390 days (monkey P) after implantation.
FSCV applied a triangular waveform from -0.4 to 1.3 V at 400 V/s, every 100 ms (10 Hz).
EPhys was sampled at 30 kHz in monkey P and 32 kHz in monkey T, and band-pass filtered from 0.1 to 7500 Hz.
In the shape task, forced trials made up 25% of all trials, and the cue-reward association was reversed after blocks of 50 to 300 trials.

Dopamine was measured from two neighbouring channels of one dual-channel s-µIP (sites c8dg and c8ds, 0.1 to 0.2 mm apart), and both showed dopamine increases after the value cue in a single forced large-reward trial.
The single-trial FSCV colour plot shows dopamine redox current, with changes near 0.6 V (oxidation) and -0.2 V (reduction) after the value cue.
Single-trial bipolar LFP from site c3bs-c3a shows beta bursts (one to a few cycles of high beta power) whose frequency changes around the cue and other task events.
Trial-averaged dopamine at site c8dg is higher after large-reward than after small-reward value cues, in successful forced trials of the shape task.

Beta-band LFP power at c3bs-c3a in the direction task is more suppressed (stronger event-related desynchronization) after large-reward than after small-reward value cues, in a brief window after the cue.
With the reward fixed at large, beta-band LFP power is more suppressed when the cue is on the left (contralateral) than on the right (ipsilateral).
Spikes recorded from an s-µIP in the caudate of monkey P (site c33, 390 days post implant) fire at a different rate for large and small reward during the value cue fixation of the direction task.
The s-µIP recorded a spike-sorted unit in monkey P, shown by its average waveform and its interspike interval histogram.
In a single trial (trial 133 of the session), dopamine concentration changes at site c8ds fluctuate, especially after the value cue display.
Trial-averaged dopamine at site c8ds, aligned to the value cue, increases more for large than for small reward trials, especially between the value cue display and reward.
Spikes recorded at site c5d on a chamber-implanted CFE can be shown as a raster and a peristimulus time histogram aligned to the value cue display, for large and small reward trials.
The spikes at site c5d have a consistent waveform (mean and standard deviation) and an interspike interval distribution (1 ms bins) consistent with a single unit.
Trial-averaged beta-band LFP power at c7b referenced to c5c is suppressed more in the brief window after the value cue for large than for small reward cues.
The chamber system provided recordings of dopamine and electrical neural activity in two monkeys (T and J).
53% (21/40) and 25% (13/51) of implanted sCFEs retained functionality (background current above 500 nA and noise below 0.05 nA) in monkeys T and J.
73% (29/40) and 39% (20/51) of implanted sCFEs retained background current above 500 nA in monkeys T and J, of which 28% and 35% had noise above 0.05 nA.
21.4% (3/14) and 14.2% (2/14) of mCFEs retained functionality in monkeys T and J.
Of the functional CFEs, 63% (15/24) and 53% (8/15) in monkeys T and J displayed visible dopamine signals and were used during task performance.

Monkey T kept negative bacterial cultures for all samples; in monkey J, staphylococcus cultured at 29 days post-implant was cleared by 39 to 44 days and the chamber stayed aseptic for 286 days after treatment.
Fluid aspirated from the chamber per session ranged from 0.3 to 4.8 mL in monkey T and 0.2 to 9.8 mL in monkey J, and was sanguinous for the first 18 (T) and 217 (J) days.
Bone growth was observed within and around the chamber in both monkeys, and the chamber margins stayed relatively healthy.
The second-stage classification divided dentate excitatory neurons into 586 putative granule cells (GC) and 500 putative mossy cells (MC).

Narrow-waveform interneurons have a trough-to-peak latency below 0.425 ms, and among wide-waveform units the excitatory cells have a burst index above the threshold separating them from wide-waveform interneurons.
Narrow-waveform interneurons fire faster than wide-waveform interneurons (medians 7.97 and 2.11 Hz; Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.00001).
The waveform of granule cells is narrower than that of mossy cells.
In DRD2-Cre::Ai35 mice, 29 of 107 putative mossy cells were suppressed by green light, against none of 202 putative granule cells, 8 of 68 wide-waveform and none of 69 narrow-waveform interneurons.
Mossy cells are more active than granule cells during both waking and NREM sleep (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for each).
Granule cells fire most during NREM sleep and at similar rates during wake and REM.
CA3 pyramidal neurons are most active during wake and least active during REM.
Granule cells increase their firing in NREM sleep compared with waking, while mossy cells fire at equivalent rates in the two states.
Granule cells are more strongly phase-modulated by theta oscillations than mossy cells and fire at later theta phases (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).
Granule cells are more strongly phase-modulated by gamma oscillations than mossy cells and fire at earlier gamma phases (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).
Slow-firing neurons are more strongly coupled to gamma than fast-firing ones (GC r = -0.176, MC r = -0.184, P < 0.0001 for each).
Granule cells are more effectively recruited by type 2 dentate spikes than mossy cells and fire earlier (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.0001 for both).
5.5% of granule cells monosynaptically excite mossy cells (32 pairs), whereas no mossy cell significantly excites a granule cell.
Spike transmission probability from granule cells to mossy cells increases from the first to the second spike of a granule cell burst (P < 0.001).
GC to MC spike transmission is lower during NREM sleep than during waking (n = 31, P < 0.005).
Synchronous co-activation within 1 ms is found in 23% of mossy cells and 9% of CA3 pyramidal cells, but in fewer than 0.2% of granule cell pairs.

On the circular T-maze, the fraction of active neurons (above 1 Hz) is higher in the central arm than in the side arms, for granule cells, mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells (Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.00001 for each).
Few granule cells have two or more place fields on the T-maze (6.6%), against 57.8% of mossy cells and 36.1% of CA3 pyramidal cells (Kolmogorov-Smirnov P < 0.0001).
Granule cells have the lowest within-field peak firing rates (GC against MC, Kolmogorov-Smirnov P < 0.003) and the lowest spatial information of the three types (P < 0.0005).
The fraction of splitter cells, whose central-arm firing predicts the coming turn, is comparable in granule cells, mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells.
For neurons with stable place fields, the remapping index between open fields A and B is above zero in each group (Wilcoxon signed-rank; GC P < 0.05, MC and CA3 P < 0.00001).
Granule cells with stable place fields remap less than mossy cells (Kruskal-Wallis P = 0.034; post hoc GC against MC P = 0.028).
Only 36.7% of granule cells with place fields (11 of 30) remap, against 61.3% of mossy cells (68 of 111) and 55.6% of CA3 pyramidal cells (80 of 144).
Population-vector remapping is smaller for granule cells than for mossy cells and CA3 pyramidal cells, for populations of 5, 10, 15 and 20 place cells.
Mossy cells rarely inherit place fields from single presynaptic granule cells; of 10 place fields of connected granule cells, only 2 overlapped a field of the postsynaptic mossy cell.
In the open fields, the rate maps of connected granule cells and mossy cells are not correlated within the granule cell's place field (median near 0, n = 19, Wilcoxon P = 0.60).
Mossy cells are located deeper than granule cells relative to the reversal of the type 2 dentate spike (DS2) (Mann-Whitney P < 0.001).

K-means clustering on the DS2 amplitude at the unit's site, the NREM to wake rate ratio and two principal components of the waveform's second derivative separates excitatory dentate units into granule cells and mossy cells.
Granule cells reside 59 +- 35 um above the mossy cells they drive.
Granule cell spikes show a delay from the soma to the proximal dendrites, absent in mossy cells.
The recordings come from 11 rats and 27 sessions of 294 plus or minus 137 min, yielding 995 putative pyramidal cells and 126 putative interneurons.
Median firing rates of pE cells are 0.76 Hz in WAKE, 0.69 Hz in nonREM and 0.88 Hz in REM; of pI cells 5.59, 4.69 and 4.25 Hz.
The distribution of pE firing rates is strongly positively skewed and spans three orders of magnitude, from 0.05 to 5 Hz.
The fraction of pE cells firing above 2 Hz is 19.2% in WAKE, 19.2% in REM and 8.8% in nonREM (chi-square, p < 1e-10).

Per-cell nonREM and WAKE rates are highly correlated (R = 0.82), and the slope of their relation is below 1 (95% confidence interval 0.66 to 0.71), so state transitions act differently across the rate spectrum.
The burst index (fraction of spikes with inter-spike intervals under 15 ms) is highest in nonREM (median 11.8%), lowest in WAKE (4.0%), with REM (5.5%) slightly above WAKE (Kruskal-Wallis, p < 0.05).
The average spike autocorrelogram of pE cells peaks near 8 ms in nonREM, with a smaller peak near 125 ms (theta) in REM and WAKE.
The autocorrelogram of pE cells decays faster in nonREM than in WAKE and REM (decay fit exponent medians -1.35, -0.83 and -0.80; Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.05).
In nonREM, pairs of fast-firing pE cells are positively correlated, while pairs of one slow and one fast cell are negatively correlated.
Microarousals have a median duration of 15.9 plus or minus 3.3 s, occur 0.32 plus or minus 0.12 times per minute and occupy 9.1 plus or minus 3.5% of SLEEP (790 in total).
The fraction of time occupied by MAs decreases over the course of nonREM episodes (R = -0.85, p < 1e-10).
The duration of nonREM packets spans two orders of magnitude, with a median of 111 s.
The dataset holds 54 WAKE-SLEEP episodes (at least 7 min of WAKE followed by at least 20 min of SLEEP), an average of 2.0 per session, and sessions without one were discarded.
The mean firing rate of pE cells declines over the course of SLEEP, restricted to nonREM (R = -0.11, p < 1e-3).
The mean pE rate is lower in the last than in the first nonREM packet of SLEEP (1.04 plus or minus 1.20 against 0.88 plus or minus 0.91 Hz; Wilcoxon p < 0.02).

Comparing the same neurons in the first and last nonREM packets of SLEEP, the regression slope departs from 1 (95% confidence interval 0.827 to 0.880), as fast cells slow down and slow cells speed up.
pE rates are lower in the 5 min of WAKE after SLEEP than in the 5 min before (p < 1e-6, Wilcoxon), with a decrease in the top three sextiles and an increase in the lowest.
Over SLEEP, restricted to nonREM, the fastest sextile decreases its rate while the slowest shows a marginal increase.
The coefficient of variation of pE firing rates decreases over the course of SLEEP (R = -0.05, p < 0.01).
Within both nonREM episodes and nonREM packets, the fastest sextiles decrease their rates while the slowest increase.
The coefficient of variation of binned population rates decreases within nonREM episodes (R = -0.13) and packets (R = -0.12), both p < 1e-10.
The 15 ms burst index of pE cells increases within nonREM episodes (R = 0.09) and packets (R = 0.08), both p < 1e-10.
Delta and sigma power increase over nonREM episodes and packets, while gamma power decreases over episodes but not over packets.
Mean delta power within whole packets, normalized by nonREM delta power, is positively correlated with packet length (R = 0.31, p < 0.05).

Per packet, the rate of the fastest sextile is negatively correlated with delta power (R = -0.28) and positively with gamma power (R = 0.44), and the rate of the slowest sextile is positively correlated with sigma power in the last 20 s of the packet (R = 0.25), all p < 1e-10.
An intervening nonREM packet reduces the rates of the top two sextiles from one MA to the next (both p < 0.01).
An intervening WAKE episode increases the rate of the fastest sextile from one nonREM packet to the next (24 triplets).
An intervening MA increases the rates of slow-firing pE cells from one packet to the next and does not affect fast-firing cells.
An intervening REM episode decreases the rates of all sextiles from one packet to the next.
Longer REM episodes produce a proportionally larger decrease of rates from one packet to the next (R = -0.22, p < 1e-2).
Sigma power in the last 20 s of a packet between two MAs correlates with a larger increase of the slowest sextile from one MA to the next (R = 0.181, p < 0.01).
The increase of the slowest sextile's rate from one packet to the next is positively correlated with the change of delta power between the packets, regardless of the intervening state.
Within WAKE the two fastest sextiles increase and the two slowest decrease their rates; within REM all sextiles except the fourth increase.
WAKE periods with more movement have a larger effect on the rate increase of the fastest sextile from one packet to the next (R = 0.43, p < 0.05).
DOWN states have a median duration of 0.19 s and UP states 0.47 s.

Over SLEEP, the incidence of spindles (R = -0.093), UP states (R = -0.10) and DOWN states (R = -0.08) decreases and DOWN state duration increases, while spindle duration, frequency and amplitude do not change.
Within packets the incidence of UP and DOWN states increases, UP states shorten and DOWN states lengthen, and spindle incidence and duration increase.
pE cells fire in stable sequences early in UP states, and the latency of a cell's first spike is negatively correlated with its firing rate.
Within UP states, the fastest sextile and pI cells decrease and the slowest sextile increases from early to late SLEEP, and within packets the fastest sextile drops while pI cells increase.
Recordings were made in four rats, in eight novel exploration sessions, each a PRE sleep, a MAZE epoch on one of two linear tracks or a circular track, and a POST sleep.
The Bayesian decoder was built from 491 place cells over the eight sessions.
Sequence scores (rZ) of candidate events are higher in POST sleep than in PRE sleep (replay).
Sequence content is higher in MAZE immobility events than in PRE sleep events.
216 neurons showed significant PCC scores in PRE or POST and were considered to contribute strongly to sequences.
Most neurons strongly contributing to PRE sequences (73%) also contributed to POST sequences.
The PRE to POST increase in sequence score is eliminated when the place fields of the 10 to 20% of cells with the highest dPCC are shuffled, and remains after shuffling the bottom 75%.
The PRE to POST increase in sequence content is attributable to a small number of plastic cells; removing them, unlike removing rigid cells, removes the increase.
Rigid and plastic neurons were similarly distributed along the track.
Plastic neurons had higher place-specific indices and fewer place fields than rigid cells.
Plastic but not rigid neurons increased their spatial specificity (in-field versus out-of-field firing ratio) steadily during the MAZE session.
Session-wide firing rates of rigid neurons were higher than those of plastic neurons.
Ripple-related spiking, bursting and pairwise coactivation were higher in plastic than in rigid neurons.
In PRE sleep, coactivation was dominated by fast-firing neurons.
Slow-firing neurons showed the strongest increases in coactivation from PRE to POST sleep.
Slow-firing cells showed the greatest replay, the partial correlation between RUN and POST coactivation accounting for PRE.
Place cells divided into equal groups by sleep firing rate have medians of 0.39 Hz (low-rate) and 1.12 Hz (high-rate).
Low-rate neurons carried more spatial information per spike on the maze, and increased their within-ripple firing-rate gain from PRE to POST more than high-rate cells.
Slow-firing, but not fast-firing, neurons increased their contribution to sequences from PRE to POST sleep, in a decoding restricted to each group.
PRE to POST increases in sequence content were limited to cells with high ripple-specific recruitment (gain).
Of the recorded cells, 242 of 720 in the anterior thalamus and 111 of 357 in the PoS were classified as HD cells, 353 of 1077 in all.
The firing rates of HD neurons are strongly correlated between waking and SWS and between waking and REM sleep.
The pairwise correlations between HD neurons, within and across structures, are similar across brain states.

The zero-lag correlation between HD cell pairs falls with the offset of their preferred directions, positive below 60 degrees, negative above it and near zero at about 60 degrees, and this holds in waking, REM and SWS.
The angular velocity of the internal HD signal, estimated from the temporal profile of pairwise cross-correlograms, is about tenfold faster during SWS than during waking.
The angular velocity of the internal HD signal is similar during REM sleep and waking.

During waking, the observed correlations of HD cell pairs exceed those expected from independent rate-coded neurons for pairs with overlapping fields (0 plus or minus 15 degrees), and fall below them for pairs at about 60 degrees.
The HD signal decoded with a Bayesian decoder from the HD cells faithfully tracks the head direction of the waking mouse.
ADn HD cells have peak rates almost three times those of PoS HD cells (p < 1e-10, Mann-Whitney, 242 ADn and 111 PoS HD cells).
ADn HD cells convey 30% more head-direction information than PoS HD cells (1.44 against 1.11 bits per spike, p < 1e-6).
Ensembles of 8.4 plus or minus 5.1 (s.d.) HD units per session were recorded in the ADn and 5 plus or minus 2.8 in the PoS.
Pairwise correlations of HD cells closer than 60 degrees are stronger in the ADn than in the PoS in every brain state (p < 1e-5, 345 ADn-ADn and 55 PoS-PoS pairs).
The activity packets in the ADn and the PoS are coherent with the packet expected from the Bayesian decoded HD in waking, REM and SWS.
Noise correlations of HD cell pairs are stronger in the ADn than in the PoS (p < 1e-9, Kruskal-Wallis).
In the ADn the covariance-based optimal linear estimator of HD is about 50% better than the signal-based one, and this gain is larger than in the PoS (p < 0.05, 20 ADn and 8 PoS ensembles).

The HD signal decoded from ADn assemblies during sleep gives tuning curves of PoS cells more similar to their waking tuning than the signal decoded from PoS assemblies does for ADn cells, in all brain states.
ADn assemblies predict PoS spike trains in all brain states better than PoS assemblies predict ADn spike trains, with optimal readout windows of 123 ms (waking), 133 ms (REM) and 79 ms (SWS).
Fast synchrony between ADn HD cell pairs decreases with the difference of their preferred directions in all brain states (p < 1e-10, Kruskal-Wallis, 970 pairs).
Putative monosynaptic connections were found in 4.45% of 6960 ADn to PoS pairs and 0.35% of PoS to ADn pairs; among pyramidal PoS cells, 0.41% against 0.18% (p = 0.014).

PoS HD cells postsynaptic to ADn HD cells share the preferred direction of their presynaptic cell (12 pairs), and such PoS pyramidal cells convey more HD information than those without an identified presynaptic cell (p = 0.011).
ADn HD cell spikes are associated with high-frequency oscillations of the PoS LFP.
A session holds about 40 control trials, 20 to 60 cooling trials and 20 to 80 recovery trials, 80 to 200 trials in all with a mean of 150.
MS cooling peaked about 60 s after its onset and lasted about 10 to 12 minutes.
Theta frequency decreased linearly with MS temperature (R = 0.81, P = 5.4e-48).
Theta power also decreased with MS temperature, less tightly than frequency (R = 0.54, P = 1.2e-16).
The relationship of theta frequency with MS temperature was more consistent across animals than that of theta power.
Theta frequency and power were lower during MS cooling than before and after it.
During MS cooling LFP theta frequency decreased by 12%.
MS cooling increased choice errors about 3-fold, within each rat (P < 0.05 for all animals) and across all animals (P = 1e-6).
The error rate after cooling did not differ from the error rate before it.
The worst memory performance occurred between trials 4 and 8 after the onset of cooling, when MS temperature reached its minimum.
The incidence of errors correlated negatively with MS temperature (R = -0.35, P < 0.01).
The incidence of errors correlated negatively with theta frequency (R = -0.35, P < 0.01).
The incidence of errors correlated less with theta power; only 2 of 5 animals had a significant correlation (R beyond -0.3, P < 0.01).
The incidence of errors did not correlate with the running speed of the rat (R about 0.1, P > 0.05 for all animals).
Running speed decreased relatively monotonically within a session.
Mean running speed was 87.3 +- 8.0 cm/s in control trials and 86.2 +- 9.9 cm/s during MS cooling.
Within-field and peak firing rates of place cells decreased moderately during MS cooling (11% and 12%; P < 1e-9 and P < 1e-11).
Firing rates of interneurons decreased during MS cooling by about 14%.
The theta oscillation frequency of putative fast-spiking interneurons decreased during MS cooling, commensurate with the LFP theta.
The waveforms of hippocampal action potentials were not affected by MS cooling.

MS cooling decreased both the oscillation frequency of place cells (fp) and the LFP theta frequency in their fields (fLFP) by about the same degree, and both recovered (fLFP 8.4, 7.7, 8.5 Hz; fp 10.6, 9.5, 10.4 Hz before, during and after; n = 365).
fp and fLFP were correlated across place fields before, during and after cooling (R = 0.61, 0.59 and 0.36; P < 1e-6 each).
During MS cooling fp and fLFP decreased in parallel, so the difference fp - fLFP remained constant.
fLFP and fp measured within place fields decreased linearly with MS temperature (fLFP R = 0.66, slope 0.071 Hz per C; fp R = 0.38, slope 0.09 Hz per C).
Place field size was highly correlated before and during MS cooling (R = 0.91).
Place field size and fp were negatively correlated before, during and after cooling (R = -0.49, -0.40, -0.40; P < 1e-9).
Measured place field size correlated with the size predicted by SPF = v / (fp - fLFP) before (R = 0.55) and during (R = 0.54) cooling, and weakly after (R = 0.11).
The information content of place cell spikes was not altered by MS cooling (P > 0.26).
The spatial scale of the population vector correlation of pyramidal cells was not affected by MS cooling.
The phase precession slope decreased slightly but significantly during MS cooling (P < 0.007 and P < 0.0003).
fp depended on running speed more strongly than fLFP, and fp during cooling was lower at all velocities.

The theta-repeated cross-correlograms of place cell pairs had a period of about 85 ms before cooling, which lengthened during MS cooling (P = 0.002), while the period of the phase cross-correlograms was unaffected (P = 0.32).
Distance-time compression of place cell pairs (0.54 cm/ms before cooling) decreased during MS cooling (P = 0.02), while distance-phase compression was unchanged (P = 0.92).
During MS cooling the theta time lags between place cell pairs increased compared with before and after cooling (P = 8e-5 and P = 0.00032), and did not differ between before and after (P = 0.79).
Theta phase lags between place cell pairs were not affected by MS cooling (P > 0.24 between all conditions).
The fraction of place cells active in a theta cycle was not significantly affected by MS cooling (P = 0.2).
The number of spikes emitted by all neurons per theta cycle was preserved during MS cooling (P > 0.058 between all conditions).
Hippocampal temperature fell by less than 1.5 C at the time of the largest MS temperature decrease, and later than the MS cooling.
633 well-isolated units were recorded from the mPFC of four rats.
Rats performed the odor-place matching task at 92% correct (91.9% in the recording sessions).
About 10% (layer 2/3) and 20% (layer 5) of the recorded neurons fire at least one spike in any 100 ms window, a fraction that is relatively constant along the maze.
Neurons are active over similar standardized distances of the maze, 0.27 (62 cm) plus or minus 0.17 (39 cm) (mean and s.d.), from the 50% boundaries of the peak firing rate.

The fraction of neurons with significantly different firing on left and right trials is 16% (layer 2/3) and 18% (layer 5) in the central arm (positions 0 to 0.3), where the trajectories overlap, and 22% (layer 2/3) and 40% (layer 5) in the side arms (0.5 to 1).
Left and right trajectories overlap in the central arm and begin to differ significantly at position 0.3.
About one quarter of the neurons fire at significantly different rates (P < 0.05 per cell) during nose poking for the two odors.
Of all ordered pairs of simultaneously recorded neurons, 0.79% had short-latency, narrow peaks or troughs in their cross-correlograms (0.55% excitatory, 0.24% inhibitory), found with a jitter test.

By their connections, 32.5% of units are putative pyramidal cells and 12.5% putative interneurons, a ratio of 2.82 plus or minus 0.51 (s.d.), and 50.7% of the postsynaptic targets of putative excitatory cells themselves inhibit other neurons.
Most connected pairs were recorded on the same shank, and the probability of a connection falls with the distance between the neurons, though connections were found up to 1200 micrometres apart.
Out of 343 excitatory monosynaptic pairs, 67 showed position dependence of their short-latency coincidences in the maze (P < 0.01), beyond what the firing rates explain.
About equal fractions of connected pairs show firing pattern-dependent depression (12.7%) and facilitation (10.7%), comparing the transmission of the first spike of a train with that of later spikes.

Coincident firing of two or more presynaptic neurons within 5 ms on a common target is more effective than the sum of their separate effects (supralinear), while spikes spread over windows longer than 10 ms add linearly.
Large fractions of putative pyramidal cells (72.2% in layer 2/3, 84.7% in layer 5) and of interneurons (58.3% and 83%) are trajectory specific.

In the example layer 2/3 session, 117 neurons gave 1172 pairs with 48 excitatory and 30 inhibitory connections, 39 of the 117 cells formed one connected hub, 15 of 36 excitatory connections were active in particular maze segments, and the example pairs (156-136, 197-201, 49-52, 186-201, 197 and 186 onto one interneuron, a satellite on cell 135) show position-dependent, depressing, facilitating and supralinear transmission.

The two array datasets, monkey J-array recorded 2009-09-18 and monkey N-array recorded 2010-09-23, each present 108 reach conditions and comprise 146 and 218 isolations (a mix of single and multi-unit isolations).
In the first jPCA plane the neural state rotates in the same direction for all conditions of the J-array and N-array datasets, including reaches in opposite directions.
The rotations do not relate directly to reach curvature; the neural state rotates the same way for clockwise-curving, counter-clockwise-curving and straight reaches.
The rotation phase follows from the preparatory state; knowing the initial state in the jPC plane, the subsequent states are reasonably predictable.
The first jPCA plane captures an average of 28% of the total data variance (typically 20 to 35%).
The plane of PC2 and PC3 captures 29% of the total variance on average, about as much as the first jPCA plane, so the jPCA plane captures patterns already present in the top PCs.

In J-array the first three jPCA planes found within the top 10 PCs capture 22%, 19% and 12% of the variance (54% together), against 64% for the top six PCs, and each plane holds rotations coherent across conditions.
Every dataset contains two, and usually three, planes with rotations, together capturing 50 to 70% of the variance.
The distribution of the angle between the neural state and its derivative in the first jPCA plane, over all conditions and times, peaks near pi/2 (rotation), not near 0.
For the neural data the rotational (skew-symmetric) dynamics matrix fits the data nearly as well as the best unconstrained linear dynamics matrix, both in the 6-D space and in the first jPCA plane.
The rotations are brief and fast, up to about 2.5 Hz; the largest eigenvalues of M_skew in the monkey A and B datasets are 8.8 to 13.5 radians/s.

Three shuffle controls that keep preparatory activity and invert or reassign the peri-movement activity largely remove the rotational structure found by jPCA, so jPCA does not find rotations that are not there.
Analysed separately, the PMd and M1 arrays each show clear rotations; the jPCA plane captures 29% (PMd) and 29% (M1) in J-array and 32% and 28% in N-array.
The angular velocity of the rotations is slightly higher for M1 than for PMd in each dataset.

A simulated population of units tuned to hand velocity and speed, with preparatory activity tuned to reach endpoint, matched to the recorded data, shows no robust or consistent rotations; M_skew fits it poorly and its angle distribution peaks slightly above zero.
A simulated population tuned to hand position, velocity, acceleration and jerk (with the Methods' sensitivities) produces multiphasic responses but no consistent rotations; M_skew fits it poorly.
The population responses of the swimming leech and of premotor cortex in a walking monkey rotate in the jPCA plane, as expected for rhythmic movement.
Single neurons recorded with single electrodes show multiphasic, quasi-oscillatory responses lasting about 1 to 1.5 cycles, from 469 isolations in four monkeys averaging 810 trials per neuron.
The rotations are seen in the seven single-electrode datasets (monkeys A, B, J1 to J4 and N), for example monkey B, A, J3 and N in Figure 3a to 3d.
The recorded muscle populations (6 to 12 EMG recordings per dataset) show weak, inconsistent rotations, also when the neural population is down-sampled to their size.
A generator model of two rotations of fixed frequency fits deltoid EMG with correlations of 0.97 to 0.99, and its simulated units resemble real neurons.

Rotations have similar angular velocity for instructed fast and slow reaches; the largest M_skew eigenvalues are 8.8 against 9.8 radians/s (monkey A) and 12.2 against 13.5 (monkey B), with larger amplitude for fast reaches.
A significant fraction of virgin PVN units were activated during nest entry (6 of 21 OT-PVN and 33 of 126 PVN units; one-sided Fisher's exact test p = 0.01 and 0.0001).
A significant fraction of virgin PVN units were activated during shepherding by the dam (5 of 21 OT-PVN and 9 of 97 PVN units; p = 0.02 and 0.001).
Spontaneous pup retrieval by the dam, in which the virgin was not involved, activated a significant fraction of virgin PVN units (5 of 17 OT-PVN and 10 of 69 PVN units; p = 0.02 and 0.0007).
PVN units fired more when the virgin entered the nest after being shepherded than when she entered it voluntarily (18 units, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, p = 0.0056).
Dams shepherded virgins more often than the 0.2 events per hour at which dams chased virgins without pups, at 3.5 +/- 0.9 events per hour with pups present.
About once every two hours, dams dropped and then retrieved pups during co-housing (daily means 0.34 to 0.60 retrievals per hour, N = 14 dams).
Optically tagged OT-PVN units (21 units) were activated by shepherding, nest entry and dam retrieval, and pairs including OT-PVN units were more correlated than PVN pairs during these behaviours.
Units activated during shepherding fired less when the virgin chased the dam (6 units, Wilcoxon p = 0.03).
During 5-minute interactions, more virgin PVN units were activated by the dam than by pups (25 of 248 against 7 of 248), and units barely responded to pup calls (1 of 71).

Virgins co-housed with a dam and litter began retrieving pups earlier than virgins co-housed with pups alone (n = 14 and 10, P < 0.0001), and nest entry and shepherding on day 1 correlated with retrieval at the end of day 1 (r = 0.66 and 0.75).
Chemogenetic silencing of OT-PVN neurons delayed the onset of retrieval in co-housed virgins.

Non-co-housed virgins learned to retrieve after watching dams retrieve, with no barrier (11 of 15) or through a transparent barrier (12 of 19), but not through an opaque barrier (2 of 18) or when lacking the oxytocin receptor (3 of 10).

PVN units of non-co-housed virgins were activated while watching dam retrievals (15 of 65), some also during the virgin's own retrievals (15 of 41), and only in virgins that went on to retrieve (learners against non-learners, P = 0.0001).
Auditory cortex photometry responses to pup calls increased over co-housing up to the day of retrieval onset (P = 0.003, n = 3).
Single-trial PVN activity correlated with pup-call responses in auditory cortex during observation (r = 0.5, P = 0.00001, n = 4).
PVN to auditory cortex projections were activated during observation of dam retrieval in virgins that learned to retrieve (P = 0.02) but not in those that did not (P = 0.5), three animals per group.
An oxytocin receptor antagonist in auditory cortex prevented learning by observation (2 of 10 against 7 of 9), and stimulating OT-PVN fibres in auditory cortex enhanced it (4 of 4 against 2 of 4).
Superficial superior colliculus projects to OT-PVN neurons, and stimulating this input replaced visual experience (4 of 5 against 1 of 6 virgins retrieving).

The sessions are those the Methods list for each target configuration; for monkey R, ring on 2017-01-24 and 25, horizontal on 2017-01-17 and 18, vertical on 2017-01-15 and 16, and 3-rings on 2017-01-19; for J, ring, vertical and 3-rings on the dates listed.
Monkey R performed 3577 ring trials over two sessions, 3699 horizontal over two, 4040 vertical over two, and 912 3-rings trials in one session.
Monkey J contributed 6161 ring, 5017 horizontal, 6110 vertical and 7722 3-rings trials, over four sessions each.

Delays were uniform from 300 to 700 ms for J and 400 to 900 ms for R, 10% of trials had no delay; average reaction time was 346 ms (J) and 311 ms (R), average reach time 582 ms (J) and 482 ms (R), and reaction time was negatively correlated with delay (p < 1e-4 for both).
Of the 96 PMd electrodes, 74 for J and 80 for R had activity significantly correlated with the x and y location of the target (p < .05, Bonferroni over 96).
The top six PCs of the condition-averaged delay activity explain cumulatively 58, 82, 88, 92, 94 and 95% of the variance for J (120 conditions) and 81, 89, 92, 94, 95 and 96% for R (132 conditions).

The spatial plane captures a large part of the variance of the condition-averaged activity for the ring, horizontal, vertical and 3-rings tasks; 66.8, 64.4, 47.7 and 68.2% for J and 33.7, 30.7, 31.0 and 30.1% for R (p < 1e-4).
After target onset the neural state in the spatial plane starts at the center, diverges after 50 ms (R 75 ms) and converges to the steady delay state after 300 ms (R 400 ms).

On single trials, on-axis and off-axis deviations of the neural state in the spatial plane are positively correlated with the on-axis and off-axis deviations of the hand position at maximum speed (on-axis p = 1e-3 J, 4e-3 R; off-axis p = 4e-4 J, 2e-4 R).

The speed axis of delay activity varies with maximum speed for reaches to the same target distance, for 11 of 12 distances in J and 11 of 12 in R (p < 0.05), so it encodes speed independently of distance.
After regressing out speed from the neural activity, a positive correlation with target distance remains (p < 1e-4 for J and R).
Projected onto the top PCs, the distance dimension is about half as large as the speed dimension.
Across all single trials the speed dimension explains 2% (J) and 1% (R) of the variance of the neural state, and the spatial plane 20% (J) and 10% (R).
The distributions of single-trial neural states for each condition are elliptical, and for most conditions their major axis points along the direction of the mean neural state from the origin.

The mean absolute on-axis (distance) deviation of the neural state is larger than the off-axis (direction) deviation, in each task (J p = 9e-7 ring, 4e-7 horizontal, 1e-8 vertical, 3e-14 3-rings; R 8e-3, 4e-7, 2e-7 and 0.19).
Relative deviations of the neural state (deviation as a fraction of reach distance), on and off axis, decrease with reach distance.

Angular errors of direction classification decrease with ring distance, but errors measured as arc length are not significantly different between rings (F test, p > .05 for J and R).

A total of 1,647 LS neurons were recorded from five animals, in 62 sessions.
The hippocampal recordings hold 2,297 isolated CA1 units and 654 CA3 units (2,951 in all, Figure 3A).
Of the LS neurons, 840 fired at least 1.5 action potentials per trial on average.
The majority of LS neurons (751 of 840, 89%) showed position encoding in their spike theta phase, compared with shuffled data, in at least one condition.
Spike-phase decoding outperformed rate decoding of the rat's position for 786 of 840 LS neurons, 3,046 of 4,393 conditions, and 62 of 62 sessions.
Across LS neurons the spike-phase code is stronger than the rate code (two-sample t tests; N = 4,393 conditions, p < 1e-100; N = 62 sessions, p < 1e-10).
The mean phase minus rate MSE is about -1,000 for LS conditions and -33 for hippocampal place fields, and -1,024 and -25 for LS and hippocampal sessions.
For hippocampal place fields the distributions of rate and phase decoding errors are statistically equivalent (two-sample KS test; 1,820 place fields, p = 0.19; 45 sessions, p = 0.61).
Only 5.3% (232 of 4,393) of LS rate maps showed place fields by the criteria applied to hippocampal units, where 31.7% (1,820 of 5,735) did.
711 of 1,425 hippocampal neurons had at least one place field (1.27 fields per neuron on average); the median peak in-field rate was 8.5 Hz and the median field width 38 bins.
The few LS rate maps with a place field were less stable across trials than CA1/CA3 place fields (median coefficient of variance 41.5 against 10; two-sample t test, p < 1e-20).
Hippocampal place fields reach their peak information at smaller smoothing scales for phase than for rate (medians 15 and 29 bins; two-sample t test, p < 1e-40).
At smoothing below 6 cm (about one theta cycle) phase carries more spatial information than rate in hippocampal place fields, and above 10 cm rate carries more.
The strength of phase coding relative to rate coding increases with recording depth within the LS, within sessions and across animals.
The theta phase at the onset of LS phase fields varies with recording depth (DT5 r = 0.38, DT9 r = 0.25, DT2 r = 0.27; circular-linear correlation, p < 0.001).
Theta phase coherence between LS and the CA3 pyramidal layer increases from the beginning to the end of the run, while coherence between LS and CA1 stays relatively flat.
Coupling between hippocampal theta phase and LS gamma amplitude increases along the run for both CA1 and CA3, and is stronger for CA3-LS than for CA1-LS.

The firing phases of ensembles of simultaneously recorded LS neurons read out position better than the firing phases or rates of an equal number of hippocampal neurons (p < 0.001 at 15 to 25 neurons).
Spike trains of hippocampal neurons predicted LS firing in 18.5% (2,087 of 11,264) of hippocampal-LS pairs, with a median optimal timescale of 25 ms.
LS neurons that take part in at least one predictive assembly carry a stronger spatial phase code than those that do not (p < 1e-20).
CA3 place fields form progressively stronger gamma assemblies with LS along the track (r = 0.34) while CA1 coupling decreases (r = -0.11), and the two are anti-correlated (r = -0.88).
Only 2.8% (125 of 4,393) of LS conditions showed a significant correlation between running speed and the rate of phase precession, and 10.7% of LS rate maps were modulated by running speed.
LS rate maps have lower peak information rates than hippocampal place field maps (0.4 against 1.7 bits/cm; p < 1e-100).
After maze rotation many LS neurons kept their phase precession related to distal room cues, so the phase shift is a spatial code.

In a spiking model, CA1 and CA3 inputs weighted dynamically as the measured assemblies give a rate-independent phase code in the LS neuron, which static or random weights, or the loss of theta sequences, do not.
LS was recorded in 6 rats, with 1989 LS neurons; 37 recordings had CA1 and LS and 25 had CA3 and LS recorded simultaneously; LS HFO rates come from 89 recordings and CA1 ripple rates from 53.
Transient 120-180 Hz HFOs occur in LS in each of the 6 animals, with a robust increase in the firing probability of LS neurons at the events.
Across 6 animals, 29,955 LS HFO events were analysed.
On average 16% of LS neurons take part in a given HFO, firing an average of 0.23 spikes per event.
The vast majority of LS neurons (1840 of 1989, 92%) are significantly phase-locked to the 120-200 Hz band (Rayleigh P < 0.05), with a strong preference for the trough of each cycle.
LS HFOs are shorter than CA1 ripples from the same animals (27 +- 9 against 31 +- 14 ms; rank-sum P < 0.01).
LS HFOs are slower in frequency than CA1 ripples (147 +- 5.7 against 159 +- 8 Hz; rank-sum P < 0.01).
LS HFOs show no significant correlation between event amplitude and peak frequency.
HFO events are seen only at recording sites within LS, not at sites in neighbouring structures.
HFO power and the proportion of phase-locked neurons are highest in intermediate LS and taper towards its dorsal and ventral borders.
LS HFOs are travelling waves, posterior to anterior at 1.01 m/s (4 animals), medial to lateral at 0.53 m/s (1 animal) and dorsal to ventral at 2.19 m/s (4 animals).
The co-activation of LS neuron pairs during HFOs (excess correlation) is not modulated by waking experience on a familiar maze (PRE against POST, rank-sum P = 0.36).
Excess correlations during HFOs (PRE and POST) are higher than during maze traversal (rank-sum P < 0.001), and those of PRE and POST HFOs exceed chance from spikes jittered by +-200 ms (P < 0.01).
Only 7 of 53 sessions have significantly different excess correlations in PRE and POST (rank-sum P < 0.01), three with PRE below POST and four with PRE above.
The temporal ordering of LS spike pairs during HFOs before and after the maze correlates with the ordering during traversal to a similar degree (P = 0.85).

Cross-correlograms of LS pairs during HFOs correlate with those during traversal above chance up to about 20-fold temporal compression (P < 0.01), similarly for PRE and POST (P > 0.01 for all compression factors).
Firing rates increase during post-behavior NREM sleep in CA1, CA3 and LS.
LS HFOs occur primarily during NREM sleep, and their rates are lower than those of hippocampal SPW-Rs.
LS HFOs are reliably coupled to CA1 ripples, with a median peak-to-peak lag of 6.4 +- 4.2 ms, CA1 leading LS.
HPC-LS coupling is stronger in NREM sleep than in waking; the fraction of LS HFOs within +-25 ms of a CA1 ripple is 0.3 in NREM and 0.15 in WAKE (P < 6.6e-6).
LS firing around CA1 ripples is higher during NREM than during waking.
CA1-LS phase coherence in the 120-180 Hz band around CA1 ripples does not differ from that of randomly jittered windows, so LS does not inherit the ripple wave by wave.
Optogenetic activation of LS GABAergic neurons with a Gaussian light waveform induces local oscillations of about 140 Hz.
The number of CA1 spikes in a SPW-R significantly predicts the number of spikes of 38% of LS neurons.
Brain state (WAKE or NREM) in which a SPW-R occurs significantly predicts the spike count of 26% of LS neurons.
The duration of hippocampal SPW-Rs significantly predicts the spike count of about 20% of LS neurons.
The mean depth within the CA1 pyramidal layer of the neurons active in a SPW-R predicts the spike count of 23% of LS neurons.
The sequential content of SPW-Rs, by three replay scores, predicts the firing of only 7.9, 6.6 and 7.1% of LS neurons.
Template sequences extracted from SPW-Rs without supervision predict the firing of only 8.1% of LS neurons.
All spike-content-independent ripple features predict LS firing above chance, while all spike-content-based features do not.
In a model HPC-LS circuit, forward, reverse and scrambled compressed sequences evoke nearly identical responses of the LS neuron.
The initial dataset of 33 touch afferents comprises 54,647,500 video frames with simultaneous single-unit recordings, and the paper analyses 65,257,500 frames (2,175 min) in total.
During non-whisking periods most afferents spiked at low rates (0.0 plus or minus 0.2 Hz, median and IQR, n = 33).
All afferents responded with increased spike rates during whisker-pole contact (48.0 plus or minus 96.3 Hz, median and IQR, n = 33).

A subset of 13 of the 33 touch afferents (WT*) spiked especially strongly during whisking in air (19.1 plus or minus 58.2 Hz, median and IQR), and the other afferents divide into those sensitive to whisking and touch (WT) and to touch only (T).
A full statistical model of ten mechanical and kinematic variables strongly predicted ongoing spike rate during touch (r = 0.71 plus or minus 0.16, mean and SD, n = 33).
Models fitted to moment or its rate of change alone explained spiking relatively poorly (r = 0.45 plus or minus 0.19 and 0.42 plus or minus 0.21).
M0 and its rate of change together explained spiking (r = 0.63 plus or minus 0.20) better than any other pair of variables, and better than a model of M0, Fax and Flat (r = 0.48 plus or minus 0.19).

All 15 WT* afferents (13 touch WT* and 2 whisking-only) were dramatically modulated by whisk phase, with rates at non-preferred and preferred phases of 2.1 plus or minus 3.4 and 51.2 plus or minus 105.7 Hz (median and IQR).
Across the population of WT* afferents, preferred phase spanned the whisk cycle.
The preferred phase of each WT* afferent was largely invariant across whisk cycles of different amplitudes, frequencies and setpoints.

Statistical models fitted to whisker position, velocity, acceleration and jerk during whisking in air predicted phase tuning curves nearly perfectly (r = 0.97 plus or minus 0.04, n = 28), while single kinematic variables performed poorly.
Preferred phases of all 28 WT* afferents spanned the whisk cycle, with a slight abundance in the retraction phase.
Progressive whisker cutting eliminated spiking during whisking in air in 6 of 13 afferents (from 50.1 plus or minus 42.3 Hz intact to 0.9 plus or minus 0.7 Hz after the final cut, mean and SD).
In 7 of 13 afferents self-motion responses remained after cutting (86.1 plus or minus 71.5 Hz intact against 70.3 plus or minus 58.5 Hz after the final cut).
Cutting shortened the whisker to near its base (final length 0.37 plus or minus 0.43 mm, mean and SD, n = 13).
After whisker trimming, phase tuning curves of the 7 afferents that kept spiking were correlated with intrinsic protractor or nasolabialis EMG (r = 0.66 plus or minus 0.27).
