The spike rate lost after cutting was correlated with positive acceleration, negative acceleration or jerk (r = 0.71 plus or minus 0.19, n = 13).
In 5 afferents recorded with the whisker already cut near its base, phase tuning was strongly correlated with intrinsic protractor or nasolabialis EMG (r = 0.76 plus or minus 0.06).
Motor unit activity of m. nasolabialis was phase modulated and correlated with negative whisker velocity (r = 0.93) and anti-correlated with positive velocity (r = -0.75) within whisk cycles.
Intrinsic protractor EMG was correlated with positive whisker velocity within whisk cycles (r = 0.94, 0.97 and 0.96 in three mice).
The noise level of curvature estimates, curvature change during whisking in air as a percentage of that during contact, was 7.8 plus or minus 5.0% (mean and SD) across 33 sessions.
Identified Merkel afferents spiked at short latency (4.9 plus or minus 1.3 ms) and low jitter (SD of first-spike latency 0.91 plus or minus 0.29 ms) after brief light pulses.
In TrkC-CreER;Rosa-Ai9 mice, 99.2% of classified labelled afferent endings in whisker follicles were Merkel cell-associated (1,045 of 1,053).
Automatic contact classification agreed with manual curation for 99.5 plus or minus 0.2% of frames, with a false positive rate of 0.3 plus or minus 0.1%.
Silicon probe recordings gave 1537 single units and 303 multi-units from 57 recording sessions.
The population analyses of Figure 3 use 8 S1TJ, 9 M1TJ, 13 ALM and 5 S1BF sessions.
Regressions used the simultaneously recorded units of each session, 32 plus or minus 13 units (mean and SD).
Figure 3a averages 2684 trials of standard and backtracking sequences.
Tongue length L is decoded from population activity best in S1TJ and M1TJ and poorly in ALM and S1BF (R2 0.56, 0.42, 0.11 and 0.04).
Tongue velocity L' is decoded best in S1TJ and M1TJ and poorly in ALM and S1BF (R2 0.35, 0.32, 0.07 and 0.01).
Tongue angle theta is encoded comparably in S1TJ, M1TJ and ALM, but not in S1BF (R2 0.59, 0.57, 0.54 and 0.12).
Sequence identity I is encoded most strongly in ALM, then progressively less in M1TJ, S1TJ and S1BF (R2 0.67, 0.42, 0.23 and 0.14).
Relative sequence time tau is encoded most strongly in ALM, then progressively less in M1TJ, S1TJ and S1BF (R2 0.60, 0.45, 0.17 and 0.08).
Any pair of the five behavioural variables (L, L', theta, I, tau) is uncorrelated.
Across regions, the summed variance explained by the five coding axes reached about half that of the top five principal components.
The five coding axes were largely orthogonal to each other.

After canonical correlation, ALM trajectories in the top three PCs correlate best with the theta, I, tau coding subspace (group 2), more than with L, L', theta (group 1) or all five variables with five PCs (group 3); in S1TJ and M1TJ the correlation is high only when the coding subspace includes L and L'.
ALM and M1TJ activity predicts whether the port backtracked from the initial missed lick on; S1TJ shows only an insignificant trend and S1BF no prediction.
In the zigzag task, ALM population activity predicts the sequence identity (context) during subsequences with the same licking movements, across 6 sessions from 3 mice.
During the inter-trial interval, ALM populations encode the upcoming target position more strongly than the other regions.
None of the regions, including ALM, encoded time or distance to the trial start during the inter-trial interval.
Extended Data Fig. 4m counts 324 ALM, 233 M1TJ and 119 S1TJ neurons.
More ALM neurons are tuned to sequence initiation than neurons of the other regions.
S1TJ and M1TJ contain more neurons modulated by individual licks than ALM.
ALM contains neurons that fire during sequence execution and decrease firing abruptly when the tongue first contacts water, although licking continues.
Expert mice completed the 7 port positions in about a second.
Over training, 15 mice reduced their sequence initiation time and increased their sequence speed.
Mice reached proficiency in standard sequences after about 1500 trials of training.
Backtracking analyses used 7458 standard and 2695 backtracking sequences from 47 sessions of the 9 mice trained on backtracking.
After the port backtracked, mice took on average 1 to 2 missed licks before relocating it.
After the first lick that touched water, mice continued with about 5 consummatory licks.
Expert mice usually initiated sequences from the correct side without exploring the other side.
Inhibiting S1TJ increased the across-trial variability of lick angle, SD(theta_shoot), without reducing the lateral reach |theta_shoot|, and did not shorten licks.
Inhibiting ALM/M1TJ reduced the ability to direct licks to the sides and decreased lick length; inhibiting M1B only slightly increased angle variability; inhibiting S1BF or S1Tr changed nothing.
Inhibiting ALM/M1TJ at sequence initiation strongly suppressed licking (licks largely absent in 4 of 7 mice), and less strongly at mid-sequence.
Inhibiting S1TJ or M1B at water consumption impaired the stopping of ongoing licking.
With half the illumination power (2 mW) the effects were consistent with, though weaker than, those at 4 mW, and the termination deficit of S1TJ and M1B inhibition was similarly strong.
At 4 mW, light within 1 mm reduced the spike rate of putative pyramidal cells by 91%, at about 1.5 mm by 61% and at about 3 mm by 19%; FS neurons within 1 mm increased by 739%.
Hearing loss with earplugs did not increase missed licks during sequences.
Masking odours with an air flow did not change missed licks.
Numbing the tongue with lidocaine increased missed licks, so mice require tactile feedback from the tongue.
The maximal force of a lick was on average about 4 mN.
Clustering the PETHs of all neurons by NNMF was most consistent with 13 clusters.
In prolonged open loop, fish cycle between passive epochs lasting 24.4 +/- 2.5 s and active epochs lasting 36.1 +/- 4.2 s (mean +/- SEM, n = 74 fish), swimming 29 +/- 6 times per active epoch.

In closed loop fish swim in discrete bouts about once per second (inter-swim interval 1.2 +/- 0.05 s, n = 74), and within active epochs of open loop the interval is 1.19 +/- 0.047 s against 24.4 s in passive epochs.
Fish spend much more time in the passive state when swimming produces no visual feedback (open loop) than in closed loop with a naturalistic gain, where passivity is rare.
When switched from closed to open loop, fish first swim with higher vigor, then stop swimming.
Before the switch to passivity the inter-swim interval increases progressively, and fish swim more vigorously and less frequently in the seconds before passivity.
Whole-brain average neuronal activity is higher during active behavior than during passivity, and decays after passivity onset.
Whole-brain average radial astrocyte calcium increases before passivity onset and peaks soon after it.
Whole-brain average neuronal and glial calcium are higher and fluctuate more strongly in open loop than in closed loop.
When fish in closed loop stop swimming because the stimulus stops moving, glial calcium signals are weaker than during futility-induced passivity.

Non-negative matrix factorization of neurons and radial astrocytes gives components consistent across fish; glial component 1, in the lateral medulla oblongata (L-MO), is the most reliable, rising before and peaking after passivity onset (n = 5 neuron fish, 6 glia fish).
Of all brain regions, radial astrocytes in L-MO show the most consistent increases at passivity onset, with ramping signals before it.
Passive fish are less responsive to visual motion than active fish (p = 4.2e-7, n = 11).
Replaying in open loop the visual motion recorded in closed loop also induces passivity.
Ablating radial astrocytes, or blocking their IP3 receptors, halves futility-induced passivity, while random neuronal ablation does not change it.
Activating radial astrocytes with TRPV1, CoChR or Opto-alpha1-AR suppresses swimming, and astrocyte activation drives GABAergic neurons at the edge of L-MO.
The neuronal population whose activity rises fastest before passivity overlaps the noradrenergic neurons of the medulla oblongata (NE-MO).
NE-MO activity precedes astrocyte activity at passivity, NE-MO ablation reduces passivity, and NE-MO stimulation activates radial astrocytes through alpha1B receptors.
NE-MO neurons respond to swims without visual feedback, encoding sensory-motor mismatch.
Radial astrocyte calcium grows with the number of consecutive failed swims and with the probability that a swim fails.
The data come from 459 sessions of 139 mice recorded in 12 laboratories.
699 Neuropixels insertions yielded 621,733 units, an average of 889 per probe.
Stringent quality metrics identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, an average of 108 per probe.
The main analyses use a canonical dataset of 201 regions with at least 2 sessions of 5 well-isolated neurons and at least 20 neurons in total, 62,857 neurons.
The probes covered 279 brain areas.
The 139 mice were 94 male and 45 female.
On the day of recording the mice were aged 13 to 178 weeks (mean 44.96, median 27.0) and weighed 16.1 to 35.7 g (mean 23.9, median 23.84).
The insertions used Neuropixels 1.0 probes of versions 3A (109) and 3B2 (586), and Neuropixels 2.4 probes (4).
Recorded sessions lasted on average 645 trials (median 602, range 401 to 1,525).
Receptive-field mapping after the task (504 of 699 insertions) found a relatively small fraction of cells with significant receptive fields, with large fractions in VISp, VISl and SCs.
After training, mice made correct choices on 81.4 +/- 0.4% (mean +/- s.d.) of trials.
On 0% contrast trials mice were rewarded on 58.7 +/- 0.4% (mean +/- s.e.m. across mice) of trials, better than chance (t138 = 20.18, P = 5.2e-43).
22.8% of first wheel-movement times occurred under 80 ms after stimulus onset.
Mice performed better and faster on trials with high visual contrast.
Towards the end of the sessions, performance decreased and first wheel-movement times increased.
After a block switch, mice took around 5 to 10 trials to adjust their behaviour, as shown by the fraction of correct choices on 0% contrast trials after the switch.
For all contrast values mice chose the side of the block's likely stimulus more often, responding right more often in right blocks than in left blocks.

The visual stimulus side, decoded from the first 100 ms after stimulus onset, was represented in a narrower set of regions than choice or feedback, with strong signatures in visual cortex such as VISp.
Choice, decoded from the 100 ms before the first wheel movement, was represented in a larger number of regions than the visual stimulus, with strong effects in hindbrain regions such as GRN.
Whether the trial was correct could be decoded from the 200 ms after feedback onset in nearly all recorded regions, almost perfectly in many.

Single-cell tests controlling for choice and block found few stimulus-selective neurons (0.5% of all neurons); even in the regions with the largest fractions, such as visual cortex, the fraction did not exceed about 10%.
More neurons responded to choice than to the visual stimulus (4% of all neurons), with the largest fractions in hindbrain, midbrain and thalamic regions.
The latency of the stimulus trajectory separation ordered the visual regions as LGd < VISp, which is about equal to LP, < VISpm < VISam, at about 34, 42, 42, 57 and 78 ms.
The early visual wave was followed by later stimulus encoding in the MRN, SCm, PRNr, IRN and GRN, with latencies of about 100 to 120 ms.
The stimulus trajectory distance was significant in 104 regions.
During reward delivery, activity showed coherent oscillations of about 10 Hz that were missing after negative feedback and were closely related to licking.
Wheel speed was decodable from 163 of the 201 regions.
In the encoding model the kernel for correct feedback explained the most variance of all kernels (mean delta R2 of 8.6e-3 over all neurons).
More than half of the neurons in most brain regions were significantly correlated with at least one behavioural variable from video (nose, paw, pupil, tongue).
High Granger interaction scores were found for region pairs from all major brain regions, weakly correlated with anatomical distance and mostly bidirectional.
Chronic recordings were made from 17 adult mice (12 males, 5 females) electroporated at E13.5 (n = 4), E14.5 (n = 3), E15.5 (n = 6) and E16.5 (n = 4).
The recordings comprise 92 sessions lasting 113.7 to 475.6 min (median 309.1 min), each including a homecage period of sleep and wake.
SPW-Rs were detected with duration limits of 20 to 200 ms, and their median duration across all recordings was 36.4 ms.
The dataset includes 9,471 well-isolated units, 7,411 putative pyramidal cells and 2,060 putative interneurons.
Nine mice (E13.5 n = 2, E14.5 n = 2, E15.5 n = 2, E16.5 n = 3) ran a spatial alternation task on a familiar figure-eight maze, and a cohort of three mice also explored novel environments.
On the figure-eight maze each trial was 205 cm long, position was tracked at 30 Hz, and animals ran at least ten trials along each arm in every session.
The novel-environment cohort of three mice made 16 novel environment explorations in six distinct environments (two linear tracks, three open fields and one figure-eight maze).

Population firing-rate vectors at the same linearized position decorrelate between left and right trials once the animal leaves the common stem of the figure-eight maze (median correlations stem 0.93, turn 1 0.412, arm 0.372, turn 2 0.394).
Individual pyramidal neurons preserve their theta-related firing rates between the familiar and novel environments (Spearman rho = 0.7378, n = 2,544 neurons).
Pairwise spatial ratemap correlations between pyramidal neurons are higher in novel environments (median 0.048) than in the familiar environment (median -0.045).
Spatial information is lower in novel environments than in the familiar one (median 0.39 against 0.88 bits/s).
Theta-related firing rates are slightly lower in novel environments than in the familiar one (median 0.69 against 0.77 Hz).
664 of 7,411 putative pyramidal neurons (8.96%) were light-responsive, that is, birthdated.
The fraction of light-responsive pyramidal cells per session follows a bell-shaped wave over birthdates, peaking at E15.5 (E13.5 5.39%, E14.5 11.16%, E15.5 14.74%, E16.5 9.16%; ANOVA p = 4e-4).
Neurons born on later days lie more superficially in the pyramidal layer (median normalized depth 0.71, 0.48, 0.28 and 0.19 for E13.5 to E16.5).
Earlier-born light-responsive neurons more often shift their preferred theta phase in REM sleep (30.89% at E13.5 to 19.7% at E16.5; regression slope -3.42% per day).
Earlier-born light-responsive pyramidal neurons have higher firing rates (medians 1.57, 1.63, 1.62 and 1.16 Hz; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.016).
Burst index is an inverted-U function of birthdate (medians 0.1167, 0.1272, 0.136, 0.1082; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.0044).
Same-birthdate (SBD) pairs fire more synchronously than different-birthdate (DBD) pairs in 11 of 13 animals.
SBD pairs cofire more than DBD pairs in theta cycles (median 0.0189 against 0.0087).
Intermediate-birthdate neurons have lower theta depth modulation in waking but not in REM sleep.
SPW-R firing rates and participation of light-responsive neurons are an inverted-U function of birthdate.
SBD pairs cofire more than DBD pairs in SPW-Rs (median 0.0399 against 0.0231).
Assembly members cofire more in SPW-Rs than member-nonmember pairs, and segregation from nonmembers depends nonlinearly on the members' birthdate.
Assemblies with intermediate-birthdate members are expressed in SPW-Rs at higher rates (E13.5 8.16, E14.5 9.25, E15.5 8.16, E16.5 6.9 Hz; ANOVA p = 0.0158).
A model with a bell-shaped rate of neurogenesis and correlations among SBD neurons reproduces the assembly expression rates, and a uniform-neurogenesis model does not.
Spatial information and coverage on the maze are largest in intermediate-birthdate neurons.
SBD pairs have higher spatial ratemap correlations than DBD pairs on the familiar maze (median 0.0152 against -0.0256).
The ratemap overlap of SBD pairs depends on their anatomical distance, larger within 250 micrometres.
Between left and right trials, ratemaps of SBD pairs reorganize closer together than those of DBD pairs.
In novel environments SBD pairs have higher ratemap correlations than DBD pairs (median 0.117 against 0.046).
Ratemaps of SBD pairs remain closer together than those of DBD pairs between the familiar and novel environments.
SBD pyramidal pairs converge onto the same interneurons more than DBD pairs (median convergence 0.2727 against 0.2).
Convergence onto interneurons and spike transmission probability are bell-shaped functions of the presynaptic neurons' birthdate.
Of all pyramidal pairs, 65.27% share at least one postsynaptic interneuron, and cofiring in SPW-Rs, theta cycles and ratemap overlap all increase with convergence.

DLS dopamine fluctuations are significantly negatively correlated with translational velocity at short timescales (under 10 s), and the correlation reverses and becomes positive at longer timescales, for both dLight transient rates and binned amplitudes.
Average syllable-associated dLight amplitudes differ across syllables (Kruskal-Wallis H = 209.29, P < 1e-25, n = 518 mouse-syllable pairs).
Random forest classifiers cannot predict which syllable is being expressed from the coincident dLight peak amplitude or waveform.
Syllables associated on average with more DLS dopamine in an experiment tend to be used more.

Mice string together less predictable sequences after syllables associated with more dopamine; average syllable-associated dLight correlates positively with the entropy of the syllable's outgoing transitions.
When an instance of a syllable coincides with a higher-amplitude dopamine transient, that syllable is used more over the following minutes.
dLight recordings in dorsomedial striatum (DMS) show less frequent dopamine transients than in DLS.
DMS dopamine transients do not predict future syllable usage.

Pairing a target syllable with optogenetic dopamine release (Opto-DA) increases its use relative to baseline more than in no-opsin controls (log2 fold change in target counts, one-sided Mann-Whitney U = 197, P = 0.002, f = 0.82).
The cumulative increase in target counts relative to baseline is larger in Opto-DA mice than in controls (one-sided Mann-Whitney U = 184, P = 0.007, f = 0.77).
Only a fraction of Opto-DA mice learn; nine mice exceed the largest change in target counts of any control ("learners").
In learners, the change in target usage during stimulation predicts the change in the post-stimulation sessions (Pearson r = 0.89, P = 0.005).
Brief (250 ms) Opto-DA does not change movement at the moment of stimulation; no comparison between stimulation and catch trials in any mouse is significant.
Extending stimulation to 3 s (pulsed, 25 Hz) makes mice increase their velocity.

Spontaneous syllable-associated dopamine transients roughly match those during consumption of an unexpected chocolate chip (mean spontaneous peak 2.12 +- 0.80 z, n = 5,247; reward 2.36 +- 0.92 z, n = 10).
The average syllable-associated dLight transient exceeds that associated with movement initiation (P = 0.0006, n = 14 mice).
A higher-amplitude dopamine transient at a syllable instance is followed by less predictable syllable choices over the next several seconds.
Behavioural sequences right after Opto-DA stimulation are less predictable than after catch trials.
Opto-DA delivered on the fastest (slowest) quartile of target instances makes later instances faster (slower).
Per mouse, the influence of endogenous dopamine on syllable counts and on sequence entropy are correlated (r = 0.69, P = 0.001).
Mice whose syllable use is more influenced by endogenous dopamine learn more from Opto-DA (r = 0.51, P = 0.001).
Syllables with higher endogenous dLight on catch trials are more reinforced by Opto-DA (r = 0.32, P < 0.001).
A model in which endogenous and exogenous dopamine add predicts held-out syllable choices better than shuffled and noise controls (median r 0.20 against 0.04).
A Q-learning agent rewarded by syllable-associated dLight learns a transition matrix similar to the observed one, best when dopamine also transiently raises choice variability.
CA1 pyramidal neurons were recorded and probed in four CaMKIIa-Cre::Ai32 mice, 822 pyramidal neurons in all, 43.3 plus or minus 8.37 per session.
uLEDs were driven with 20 ms pulses at random sites with randomly variable 20 to 40 ms offsets, so that the stimulation of each site recurred at about 0.3 to 0.6 s intervals.
Of 822 pyramidal neurons, 611 responded to light from the uLEDs.
Light-induced spike responses of individual pyramidal cells decreased during sharp-wave ripples (n = 485 neurons, P < 1e-55, Wilcoxon paired signed-rank test).
The firing-rate change of pyramidal neurons during SPW-Rs is negatively correlated with their baseline firing rate (rho = -0.19, P < 1e-7).
During track running, the light-induced rate gain is largest at the trough of the theta cycle (P < 1e-6, Wilcoxon test).
More than half of the pyramidal neurons were place cells, 73% of light-responsive and 71% of non-responsive neurons, with no difference between them (P = 0.90, chi-squared test).
The light-induced rate increase is higher within than outside the place field (n = 553 place fields, P < 1e-115, Wilcoxon test).
The in-field gain is positively correlated with the out-of-field firing rate (rho = 0.17, P < 1e-5) and with the home-cage firing rate of the neuron (rho = 0.25, P < 1e-7).
Light responses in the home cage before the track were stronger in place cells than in non-place cells (P < 1e-4, Kruskal-Wallis test).
Optogenetic depolarization revealed place fields in the majority of non-place cells, 289 of 417 (69.3%).

The spatial location of light-induced spikes matches that of spikes without stimulation, both for place fields of place cells (P < 1e-40) and for unmasked place fields of non-place cells, whose sparse control spikes form ghost fields (P < 1e-10).

Place fields during light stimulation were more stable between the first and second halves of the session than during control epochs, for both true place fields and unmasked place fields (P < 1e-9 and P < 1e-19, two-way ANOVA).

Spatial information of control and light-stimulated epochs is correlated, and the light-boosted increase is stronger for unmasked place fields of non-place cells than for place cells (P < 1e-15, Kruskal-Wallis test).

Cofiring of place cell pairs during SPW-Rs in the home cage is positively correlated with their spatial overlap on the track (P < 1e-27), while pairs of a place cell and a non-place cell show no such relationship (P = 0.11).
With light-induced spikes, the relationship between SPW-R cofiring and spatial overlap appears for pairs that include non-place cells (P < 1e-5, Spearman correlation).

Stronger light (three intensities) decreased the light-induced response during SPW-Rs, increased the in-field gain of place cells several-fold, and increased the in-field gain of unmasked fields (Figure 1J, Figure 2F, Figure 3D; Friedman tests).
Intracellular recordings in which the membrane potential was varied reproduce the decreased gain during SPW-Rs (five cells in anesthetized rats and five in head-fixed mice, P = 0.002).
During SPW-Rs, excitatory neurons increased their firing rates more than inhibitory neurons.

Decoding of position is most accurate from light-boosted spikes of place cells, and light-induced spikes of non-place cells predict position better than control spikes of place cells (P = 0.001, Tukey test).

ICA assemblies of place cells in the home cage show higher spatial correlation than chance, mixed assemblies of place and non-place cells do not, and with unmasked place fields they reach the level of place-cell assemblies.

Sequential firing of place cells is correlated with spike sequences during SPW-Rs, and the fraction of SPW-Rs with significant trajectories increases when unmasked place fields are included in the template (P < 1e-4, Friedman test).
In the calcium imaging and EEG/EMG experiment, high-shock mice froze more during aversive recall than low-shock mice (t7 = 8.99, p = 0.020).
During offline periods, hippocampal population bursts occur more often than expected from shuffled neuronal activity, so CA1 neurons fire in a more coordinated way than chance.
The mean population activity during offline periods is more right-skewed than in shuffled data, showing brief burst-like activations that need coordinated activity of groups of neurons.
Offline population bursts coincide with the mouse briefly slowing down about 1 s before the burst and resuming its movement about 1 to 2 s later.

After a strong (high-shock) aversive experience, during wake in the offline period the overlap ensemble co-bursts more with the neutral ensemble than with the aversive ensemble (t4 = 4.94, P = 0.016).

Fear spreads from an aversive context to a neutral context experienced 2 days before (retrospective linking) but not to one experienced 2 days after (prospective), with no difference in aversive recall between the groups.
High-shock mice froze more than low-shock mice in the aversive context, and froze more in the neutral than in the novel context, while low-shock mice did not.
In high-shock mice, aversive recall freezing correlates with the strength of retrospective memory linking (R2 = 0.45, P = 0.016), but not in low-shock mice.
Chemogenetic inhibition of the hippocampus in the 12 h after aversive encoding prevents retrospective memory linking and leaves the aversive memory intact.
A cocaine experience also drives retrospective memory linking to a neutral context experienced 2 days before.
Cells active during aversive encoding are reactivated offline and preferentially during aversive recall.
During offline 2 the neutral ensemble is less active than the aversive and overlap ensembles in low-shock mice but no differently active in high-shock mice.
During offline 1 a greater percentage of the neutral ensemble participates in bursts than of the remaining ensemble, in both shock groups.
During offline 2 the neutral ensemble preferentially participates in bursts relative to the remaining ensemble in high-shock mice (t7 = 4.88) but not in low-shock mice.
During burst periods the overlap ensemble participates independently in more bursts than the aversive and neutral ensembles, with no difference between shock groups.

In the one-hour offline experiment, high-shock mice show more overlap-neutral than overlap-aversive co-bursting during bursts (t7 = 4.95), low-shock mice do not, and there is no such difference outside bursts.
The overlap ensemble is enriched in putative inhibitory neurons identified by chemotagging.
Without a shock, overlap-neutral co-bursting does not exceed overlap-aversive co-bursting and no memory linking occurs.
Neural activity during neutral and aversive encoding is highly discriminable, with no difference between low- and high-shock mice.
In the calcium imaging and EEG/EMG experiment, high-shock mice froze more in the neutral than in the novel context (t4 = 4.02, p = 0.03), while low-shock mice did not.
During NREM and REM sleep, overlap-neutral and overlap-aversive co-bursting do not differ in either shock group.
In low-shock mice, overlap-neutral and overlap-aversive co-bursting during wake do not differ (t3 = 1.20, P = 0.32).
Mice wearing a Miniscope sleep normally, the intermittent recording scheme captures the time spent in each state, and sleep structure is not changed by neutral or aversive encoding.
The overlap ensemble is reactivated more during neutral recall than during novel-context exposure in high-shock mice compared with low-shock mice (t12 = 3.2, P = 0.007).
In high-shock mice the neutral encoding-to-recall population correlation is lower than in low-shock mice and lower than the aversive encoding-to-recall correlation.
209 single units met the criteria to be included as GPi neurons (105 in NHP G, 104 in NHP I) and 185 as VLa neurons (66 and 119).
The resting firing rate of GPi neurons (mean 70.1 spikes/s) is significantly higher than that of VLa neurons (13.5 spikes/s), and the rates are consistent between the two animals.
Action potentials of GPi neurons are shorter than those of VLa neurons (trough to peak 0.24 against 0.50 ms; rank sum p = 1e-33).

The firing rate of most units ramps during the start-position hold period (97% of GPi and 98% of VLa units with a significant linear trend); slopes are distributed symmetrically around zero, without a difference between GPi and VLa (rank sum p = 0.29).
Nearly all units change their discharge around movement for at least one direction (GPi 99%, 206 of 209; VLa 88.1%, 163 of 185 in Table 1, 94% in the text).

Monophasic increases are the most common form of response in both GPi and VLa (48.7% and 65.3% of responses), and increases make up most detected changes (61.5% and 68.8%, biphasic responses counted twice), more than decreases (chi-squared p = 1.2e-17).
Monophasic changes are more common in VLa than in GPi (88.9% against 66.7% of responses; chi-squared p = 2.8e-12), and polyphasic responses more common in GPi.
The mean integrated change in firing over the peri-movement epoch is positive in both GPi and VLa (3.89 and 1.75 spikes), significantly different from zero.
Peri-movement changes begin later in GPi than in VLa (median onsets -47 and -90 ms; rank sum p = 2.4e-5).
GPi decreases lag behind VLa increases (median onsets -27 and -88 ms; rank sum p = 4.9e-4), against the gating prediction.
VLa decreases precede GPi increases (median onsets -108 and -62 ms; rank sum p = 0.01).
Comparing every GPi response with every VLa response, 96% of comparisons conflict with gating (178,846 of 187,154); only 4% have a GPi onset 0 to 50 ms before the VLa onset with the opposite sign.
A majority of GPi neurons (109 of 206) and some VLa neurons (56 of 179) respond significantly more strongly to one movement direction.

Short-time-scale spike-to-spike correlations between simultaneously recorded GPi and VLa units are rare (3.5% of 427 pairs over whole recordings, 2.2% of 183 at rest, 5.2% of 172 during movement) and their peaks are not larger than those of jittered controls (p = 0.975, 0.675 and 0.998).

Trial-to-trial noise correlations between GPi and VLa are rare (5.4% of 332 pairs at rest, 7.2% of 372 during movement), not different from shuffled controls (p = 0.07 and 0.388), and equally often positive and negative.
At rest, GPi burst onsets, burst offsets and pause onsets are each followed by a small, slow decrease of the population VLa firing rate.
Reaction times do not differ between the animals or reach directions; movement durations are longer for reaches to the right target, and NHP G moves more slowly than NHP I.
Thalamic neurons inhibited by GPi stimulation lie dorsal and anterior to neurons excited by SCP stimulation, with a narrow border between VLa and VLp.

Mice trained on RI60 accept more shocks in the shock probes than mice trained on RR20 (main effect of schedule, F1,43 = 6.37, p < 0.05; schedule by time interaction, F1,43 = 4.54, p < 0.05), and RI60 mice accept more shocks on the late probe than on the early one (p < 0.01).
RI60-trained mice take longer to complete the omission probe than RR20-trained mice (unpaired t-test, p < 0.05; n = 20 and 7).
Among RI60 mice, shocks received on the late probe and omission completion time are not significantly correlated (r = 0.42, ns).

RI60 mice are split by their shock probe counts into 9 punishment resistant (PR), 9 delayed punishment resistant (DPR) and 18 punishment sensitive (PS) mice, by the rule in the Methods (DPR when the count rises by more than 85%; otherwise PR when the early count exceeds 13).
There is an interaction of phenotype and probe on shocks received (p < 0.0001), and only DPR mice receive significantly more shocks on the late probe than the early one.
During RI60 training PR and DPR mice nosepoke at higher rates than PS mice (main effect of phenotype, p < 0.0001).
PR mice take longer than PS mice to complete the omission probe (PR 51.50 +- 17, PS 27.92 +- 13.65; one-way ANOVA F2,18 = 4.36, p < 0.05; Tukey PR vs PS p < 0.05).
After a reward PS mice wait longer before nosepoking again (38 +- 15 s) than PR (21 +- 5 s) and DPR (22 +- 4 s) mice (one-way ANOVA p < 0.01; Tukey p < 0.01 for each).
PS mice make fewer extra nosepokes between a rewarded nosepoke and the rewarded port entry than PR mice (PS 1.28 +- 0.85, PR 3.23 +- 1.65, DPR 2.1 +- 2.63; Tukey PS vs PR p < 0.05).
PS mice have longer inter-reward intervals (79.77 +- 26.54 s) than PR (71.2 +- 32.3 s) and DPR (69.58 +- 35.18 s) mice (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, p < 0.0001 for each).
Averaged over RI60 training, PS mice earn fewer rewards per session (39.91 +- 7.39) than DPR mice (46.56 +- 4.49; PR 45.33 +- 4.33); one-way ANOVA p < 0.05, Tukey PS vs DPR p < 0.05.
PR mice escalate their nosepoking as soon as they enter RI30, while DPR mice escalate later, during RI60.
RI60-trained mice earn more rewards per training session than RR20-trained mice (unpaired t-test, p < 0.0001).
Male mice accept more shocks than female mice in the shock probes (main effect of sex, F1,35 = 26.19, p < 0.0001).
Peaks in DMS dopamine axon activity at rewarded nosepokes emerge during RI30 in PR mice, and more slowly across RI60 in DPR mice.
The DMS rewarded-unrewarded peak score differs by phenotype (F2,33 = 8.16, p < 0.01) and changes across training (p < 0.001).
The DMS rewarded-unrewarded peak score correlates with the shocks a mouse receives in the shock probes (r = 0.53, p < 0.0001).
The DMS rewarded-unrewarded peak score does not correlate with omission completion time (r = 0.1, ns).
The DLS rewarded-unrewarded peak score has no significant effect of phenotype.
The DLS rewarded-unrewarded peak score does not correlate with shocks received (r = -0.01, ns).
The DLS rewarded-unrewarded peak score does not correlate with omission completion time (r = -0.21, ns).
Mice receiving DMS dopamine terminal stimulation on rewarded nosepokes (ChR2) escalate their nosepoking faster than EYFP and ChR2 Scrambled controls during FR1 and RI30.
On the first shock probe ChR2 mice accept more shocks than EYFP mice (interaction of time and manipulation, F2,35 = 3.65, p < 0.05; Tukey p < 0.05); the difference fades by the second probe.
ChR2 mice are very likely to be classified PR, while EYFP and ChR2 Scrambled mice are distributed across phenotypes as expected.
Under DMS ChR2 stimulation 100% of male mice and about 71% of female mice are PR.
DMS dopamine terminal stimulation does not change omission probe performance.
DMS dopamine terminal inhibition impairs initial learning; 25% of NpHR and 22% of NpHR Scrambled mice in group 1 failed FR1, and 29% of NpHR mice in group 2 failed RI30, and were dropped.
DMS dopamine terminal inhibition on rewarded nosepokes delays punishment resistance; NpHR mice accept fewer shocks than EYFP mice on the second probe (Tukey p < 0.01).
The NpHR group has more PS mice, and the NpHR Scrambled group more PR mice, than the EYFP group.
DMS dopamine terminal inhibition does not change omission completion time.
Mice receiving DLS dopamine terminal stimulation (ChR2, EYFP, ChR2 Scrambled) escalate their nosepoking at the same rates.
DLS dopamine terminal stimulation does not change the number of shocks received.
DLS ChR2, EYFP and ChR2 Scrambled mice have similar distributions of PR, DPR and PS.
DLS dopamine terminal stimulation does not change omission completion time.
The 0.2 mA shock is aversive in a fear conditioning test, in males and females.
Heterozygous DAT-IRES-cre mice are not hyperactive in a novel open field.
GCaMP7b is expressed in TH-positive dopamine neurons of medial SNc (n = 572 cells) and of medial and lateral SNc (89.56% of GCaMP neurons TH-positive).
The striatal recordings that pass the locomotion criteria number 42 from 12 Vglut2 mice, 22 from 6 Calb1 mice, 47 from 10 Anxa1 mice, 74 from 14 DAT mice and 75 from 14 Aldh1a1 mice.
The striatal recordings in the reward analysis number 28 (Vglut2), 17 (Calb1), 51 (Anxa1) and 63 (DAT), and in the air puff analysis 29, 17, 57 and 69.

Cross-correlations between dF/F and acceleration show a trough at positive lags for Calb1 and Vglut2 axons (transients after decelerations) and a peak at positive lags for Anxa1 axons (transients after accelerations).
Calb1 transients follow decelerations with a shorter lag than Vglut2 transients; the trough of the cross-correlation is at 0.42 s for Vglut2 and 0.17 s for Calb1 on average (P = 1e-6).
In a PCA of the cross-correlations of all Vglut2, Calb1 and Anxa1 striatal recordings, PC1 explains 64.2% and PC2 20.1% of the variance (84.3% together).
The PC1/PC2 angles of the cross-correlations separate the subtypes, with mean angles of 141 degrees for Vglut2, 208 for Calb1 and 239 for Anxa1 (P = 2e-7 V-C, 4e-11 V-A, 2e-4 C-A).
Triggered averages on large accelerations and decelerations average 135 +/- 77 accelerations and 138 +/- 101 decelerations per recording (mean +/- s.d.).
The probability that a dF/F increase follows an acceleration is 57.5% for Anxa1, and that one follows a deceleration is 62.4% for Vglut2 and 62.3% for Calb1.
In averages triggered on decelerations, the dF/F peak comes later for Vglut2 (0.35 s) than for Calb1 (0.23 s), P = 0.01.
Transient amplitude grows with the size of the deceleration (Vglut2 214%, Calb1 243%) or acceleration (Anxa1 206%) from the smallest to the largest quintile (P = 0.01, 0.002, 0.002).
Vglut2 and Calb1 axons respond to unexpected rewards (means 7.9 and 12.4 normalized dF/F s), as do DAT recordings (5.9).
Reward responses are almost entirely absent from Anxa1 axons (mean -0.5, P = 0.1, not significant).
Air puffs evoke increases in Vglut2 (15.8), Calb1 (5.3) and DAT (5.3) axons and a decrease in Anxa1 axons (-3.7).
Vglut2 axons respond more to air puffs than to rewards, and Calb1 axons more to rewards than to air puffs.
Calb1 axons respond more to large than to small rewards (mean difference 3.9, P = 9e-3), as do DAT recordings (1.9, P = 8e-5), while Vglut2 (0.9, P = 0.6) and Anxa1 (0.04, P = 1) do not.
Reward responses of Vglut2 and Calb1 axons are the same for rewards delivered at rest as for the others (P = 1 for both), so the reward signal is not a movement response.

Unsupervised k-means clustering on locomotion (PC1, PC2 scores), reward and air puff responses assigns recordings to clusters that match the genetic subtypes with 91% accuracy (14/16 Vglut2, 10/11 Calb1, 15/16 Anxa1).

Within genetic subtypes, simultaneously recorded SNc somas and striatal axons are highly correlated (mean peak cross-correlation 0.65 Vglut2, 0.67 Calb1, 0.58 Anxa1), more than in DAT recordings (0.37); P = 3e-4, 3e-3, 3e-4.
Like their axons, Vglut2 and Calb1 somas in SNc respond to rewards and air puffs, while reward responses are largely undetectable in Anxa1 somas.
The striatal PCs explain most of the variance of the SNc cross-correlations, 77.6% (PC1 52.4%, PC2 25.2%).
Aldh1a1 axons are heterogeneous; dorsal recordings are acceleration-correlated (Type 1) and more ventral ones deceleration-correlated (Type 2).
In Aldh1a1 recordings, larger reward responses go with deceleration-correlated signaling, and small or negative reward responses with acceleration-correlated signaling.

Where Calb1 and Anxa1 axons overlap in striatum, Calb1 recordings remain deceleration-correlated and Anxa1 recordings acceleration-correlated (Calb1 4 mice, 5 recordings; Anxa1 5 mice, 16 recordings).

Where Calb1 and Anxa1 axons overlap, Calb1 recordings respond to rewards and Anxa1 recordings do not, and Anxa1 recordings decrease to air puffs (Calb1 4 mice, 9 recordings; Anxa1 5 mice, 13 for rewards, 17 for air puffs).
Activity was recorded from 113 WT-background animals, each for up to 40 min, while a neuron was stimulated once every 30 s with a 0.5 s train of light pulses.
Responses to stimulation were imaged for 23,433 pairs of neurons (66% of all possible pairs in the head), from 186 of the 188 head neurons, and some pairs were observed as many as 59 times.
Stimulation of the interneuron AVJR evoked activity in AVDR.
Activation of the premotor interneuron AVER evoked activity transients in AVAR.
Activation of SAADL inhibited the activity of the sensory neuron OLLR.
Stimulation does not elicit responses in most close neighbours of the targeted neuron; at 75% of the cumulative distribution, neighbours' responses are below a dF/F0 of 0.1.
1,310 of the 23,433 measured neuron pairs (6%) are functionally connected at q < 0.05.
Bilaterally symmetric neurons are eight times more likely to be functionally connected than pairs chosen at random.

The probability of a functional connection decreases with the minimal anatomical path length, functionally connected pairs are on average 2.1 hops apart, and pairs with long paths are more often functionally non-connected.

Signal propagation differs from predictions of a connectome-constrained model; pairs predicted to respond strongly respond more, but agreement over all pairs is poor (R2 < 0), improves when weights and signs are fitted, and is better in unc-31 animals.
Kernels of one neuron pair are more similar to each other than to kernels of other pairs, and kernel rise times characterize the speed of signal propagation.
unc-31 mutants have a smaller proportion of functionally connected pairs than WT animals.
URX, ADL and AWB, predicted from anatomy to have no response, respond strongly to RID stimulation in WT animals.
Fifty-three pairs are functionally connected in WT (q < 0.05) and functionally non-connected in unc-31 (q_eq < 0.05), with timescales similar to all functional connections.
In a D1-cre mouse expressing GCaMP7f in D1 spiny projection neurons, fluorescence under 470 nm excitation shows Ca2+ transients across fibers that are absent under 405 nm (isosbestic) excitation.
Pairwise correlations of D1 SPN Ca2+ signals are generally low but variable, and drop off significantly with the distance between fiber tips.
After accounting for distance in the brain, signal correlations do not depend on the distance between fibers on the bundle surface, so nearby fibers in the bundle do not cross-talk.
Dopamine release to unpredicted water reward is reliable and of comparable amplitude over at least 12 weeks after implantation (median over 44 fibers, normalized to week 5).
The light evokes transient increases in dopamine release across many striatal locations.
Light-evoked dopamine increases follow an amplitude gradient from the anterior striatum into the posterior tail, where increases are less prevalent and smaller.
The tone evokes the strongest dopamine increases at sites in the posterior tail, while anterior to the tail it evokes primarily decreases.
Tone-evoked decreases are slightly more prevalent in the anterior lateral and ventral striatum, with many sites showing both increases to the light and decreases to the tone.
The modality-specific release patterns are consistent within and across mice.
Locomotor changes to the stimuli are variable and bi-directional, while the dopamine release patterns to light and tone are consistent, so the patterns are stimulus and not movement driven.
With isosbestic (415 nm) excitation, large fluorescence changes and spatial patterns to light and tone are not observed, ruling out a hemodynamic origin of the release patterns.

Latencies to half-maximum are shorter for dopamine increases to light than to tone, and shorter for increases than decreases to tone (light increase 221.6 ms, SD 42.5; tone increase 305.4 ms, SD 100.0; tone decrease 428.3 ms, SD 197.1).
Dopamine release latencies to light follow an anterior-posterior gradient, with faster increases in the anterior striatum, consistent with wave-like dynamics.
Dopamine release latencies to tone follow a different gradient, faster in the posterior striatum than in the anterior striatum.
The spatial latency gradients are also present in individual mice.

In the mouse with ChR2 in dopamine axons and rDAm3.0 in the striatum, 24 recording locations lie within or on the border of the striatum; 18 of the 24 stimulated locations evoke a significant response at another location, and 22 of the 24 recording locations respond to at least one stimulation.
Stimulating dopamine axons through one fiber evokes release at neighbouring non-stimulated sites that drops off sharply with distance in all three dimensions.
Evoked release drops off less with distance dorsal to the stimulated fiber than ventral to it, consistent with dorsally extending dopamine axon branches.

In control mice expressing tdTomato in place of rDAm3.0, single-fiber stimulation evokes no significant fluorescence increase at non-stimulated sites (0 of 48 sites, 26 stimulations in 2 mice), so the release is not a hemodynamic effect.
In mice expressing rDAm3.0 without opsin, light through one fiber raises fluorescence at the stimulated site by photoswitching, but at no other site (0 of 22 non-stimulated sites for 3 stimulations).
The magnitude and type of targeting errors (fiber tip relative to its intended target) vary across mice and fibers.

The mouse block-protocol data (four odors, 5 s pulses, 55 s between trials, blocks of ten, 15 min between blocks) come from seven imaging sessions in four mice, with a median of 215 glomeruli per imaging session.

In the mouse OB the angle between glomerular ON and OFF response vectors is greater than 90 degrees for each odor (mean 121.8 +/- 2.98 SEM, 4 odors, 7 sessions), so ON and OFF responses are inverted relative to each other.
Time-averaged glomerular ON and OFF responses to the same odor are anticorrelated; glomeruli active during the odor tend to be suppressed after it and the reverse.
In the mouse OB the ON response to a reference odor is closer in angle to the ON responses of the other odors than to any OFF response, including its own, and this holds for every odor of the panel.
Hierarchical clustering of glomerular responses cleanly separates ON responses from OFF responses.

Methyl salicylate presented 1 s after another odor evokes a response less correlated with that odor's solitary response than the solitary methyl salicylate response is (history dependent contrast enhancement; one-tailed t-test p < 0.01, 3 sessions from 2 mice).
Acetophenone presented 1 s after another odor evokes a response less correlated with that odor's solitary response than solitary acetophenone (one-tailed t-test p < 0.05, 4 sessions from 2 mice).
After odor offset the glomerular population activity stays negatively correlated with the odor-evoked ON response for several tens of seconds, although overall activity returns to baseline quickly.
Glomerular activity averaged over the 50 s after each odor offset classifies the preceding odor with high accuracy (k-NN, k = 20).

A time-bin k-NN classifier identifies the preceding odor from glomerular activity throughout the 55 s inter-trial interval; accuracy stays high for its whole duration and falls to chance with shuffled labels.
During the 15 min between blocks odor-specific information is no longer present; classification of 1-min bins of the inter-block interval by the preceding odor is near chance (34.8%).
When eleven odors are presented in random order (1 s pulses, 19 s apart), odor information after offset is variable across odors and on average declines to chance after several seconds.
Photoionization detector recordings at the nostril show odor concentration rising and decaying quickly at onset and offset, for every odor.

The variance of ACh3.0 and jRCaMP1b signals explained by a ridge regression on FaceMap PCs 1 to 25, locomotion speed and pupil area differs across cortical areas (Friedman's ANOVA p < 0.001 for both, n = 6 mice).

The coupling of behaviour to fluorescence has anterior-posterior gradients that are inverted between the signals, with ACh most strongly linked to behaviour in frontal areas and calcium in posterior areas.

For ACh3.0, facial movement (FaceMap PC1) predicts activity better than locomotion or pupil, in single-variable models (Friedman p = 0.006, face against locomotion and against pupil p = 0.031) and as unique contribution (Friedman p = 0.003).
For jRCaMP1b, facial movement (FaceMap PC1) is the most robust predictor of activity (single-variable Friedman p = 0.006; face against locomotion and pupil p = 0.031).
Facial movement onset without locomotion is associated with significant whole-cortex transients in ACh (0.64 ± 0.09 ΔF/F, p = 0.001) and calcium (0.69 ± 0.15 ΔF/F, p = 0.006).
Locomotion onset is associated with transient increases in ACh (0.68 ± 0.17 ΔF/F, p = 0.010) and calcium (1.50 ± 0.11 ΔF/F, p < 0.001).
ACh transients vary across cortical areas (p < 0.001) but do not differ between locomotion and facial motion onsets (p = 0.734, two-way repeated measures ANOVA).
Calcium transients vary across cortical areas (p < 0.001) and states (p = 0.005), with locomotion onset associated with the largest signal.
Transient magnitudes show a significant anterior-posterior gradient for ACh but not for calcium.
Sustained facial movement and locomotion are associated with progressively increasing 30 to 100 Hz ECoG power.
Sustained facial motion elevates whole-cortex ACh (low face -0.13 ± 0.04, high face 0.18 ± 0.08 ΔF/F; low against high p = 0.046, post hoc LSD), with a main effect of state (p = 0.015).
Locomotion does not further increase whole-cortex ACh beyond high facial motion (locomotion 0.16 ± 0.06 ΔF/F; locomotion against high face p = 0.717).

Sustained facial movement and locomotion both increase whole-cortex calcium (low face -0.02 ± 0.02, high face 0.17 ± 0.04, locomotion 0.63 ± 0.19 ΔF/F; low against high p = 0.020, locomotion against high p = 0.044), with a main effect of state (p = 0.005).

Differences across sustained states have significant anterior-posterior gradients, for ACh comparing high and low facial movement, with larger increases in anterior areas, and for calcium comparing locomotion and high facial movement.
During high facial motion ACh3.0 amplitude is higher in frontal-motor areas than in visual areas (paired t-test, p < 0.05).
The muscarinic blocker scopolamine decreases cortical activity in motor but not visual areas, and the nicotinic blocker mecamylamine has no significant effect.
Increased facial movement is associated with significant increases in between-area correlations of ACh in anterior somatosensory and motor areas.
Locomotion is associated with a reduction in between-area correlations of ACh that is significant across the cortex.
Increased facial movement is associated with broad, significant increases in between-area calcium correlations.
Locomotion occurs with modest decreases in calcium correlations that are significant primarily across posterior cortical areas.
Sustained facial movement is associated with a significant increase in the correlation between ACh and calcium signals broadly across the cortex.
Sustained locomotion is associated with a significant reduction in the correlation between ACh and calcium that is restricted to the frontal cortex.

The spatial regression on 395 nm signals removes stimulus-evoked and behaviour-related negative hemodynamic transients better than pixel-wise regression, shown in GFP and mCherry control mice and in ACh3.0 mice.
ACh3.0 specifically reports cholinergic signalling, ex vivo (carbachol, blocked by scopolamine) and in vivo (basal forebrain stimulation).
The relationship between behavioural state and cholinergic signalling is also seen with mesoscopic imaging of GCaMP6s in cholinergic axons.

The number of mice per experimental group is as given in the figure legends; SNr GABA neurons STN 7 and PPN 8 (Figure 2); SNc pan-DA neurons STN 11 and PPN 9 (Figure 3); GRAB-DA in TS and DLS, STN 6 and 7, PPN 9 and 9 (Figure 4); DA terminals in TS and DLS with STN stimulation, 9 and 9 (Figure S3); Vglut2+ DA neurons STN 10 and PPN 10, Anxa1+ terminals in DLS STN 8 and PPN 10 (Figure 5); Anxa1+ cell bodies in SNc STN 5 and PPN 4 (Figure S4).
Optogenetic stimulation of STN or PPN inputs increases SNr GABA neuron activity (paired t-test on the 1 s train, STN t = 3.8, p = 0.008; PPN t = 9.2, p < 0.0001).
The SNr GABA response scales with stimulation frequency from 5 to 40 Hz (Friedman test on 1 s trains, STN F = 21.0, p = 0.0001; PPN F = 18.2, p = 0.0004).
A 250 ms 40 Hz train of STN inputs elicits a net increase in SNc pan-DA neuron activity that peaks after stimulus offset (latency to peak 0.50 +/- 0.03 s, mean +/- SEM).
For SNc pan-DA neurons the STN-evoked response varies with train duration; with 1 and 4 s trains an initial increase is followed by inhibition (Friedman test, F = 13.0, p = 0.005).
The amplitude of the SNc pan-DA response during STN stimulation does not scale with frequency (Friedman test, F = 4.2, p = 0.24).
PPN stimulation also evokes SNc pan-DA responses that vary with train duration (Friedman test, F = 11.5, p = 0.009).
The SNc pan-DA response to PPN stimulation does not vary with frequency (repeated-measures one-way ANOVA, F2,15 = 1.35, p = 0.28).

STN or PPN stimulation evokes opposite DA release in TS (increase) and DLS (decrease) (two-way ANOVA, striatal site, STN F1,11 = 40.9, PPN F1,16 = 36.4, p < 0.0001; site by time interaction of the same size).

In TS, the DA increase evoked by either input scales with frequency, for all train durations (STN, repeated-measures ANOVA, 0.25 s F2,8 = 7.5, 1 s F2,7 = 13.6, 4 s F2,9 = 16.9; PPN, Friedman, F = 20.0, 24.0, 23.2).

In DLS, the DA inhibition scales with frequency and is most prominent at higher frequencies (STN, repeated-measures ANOVA, 0.25 s F = 7.5, 1 s F = 12.8, 4 s F = 46.8; PPN, 0.25 s Friedman F = 12.3, 1 s and 4 s repeated-measures ANOVA F = 12.8 and 10.2).
Low-frequency (5 Hz) stimulation of either STN or PPN increases DLS dopamine.
In DLS the DA inhibition is followed by a post-stimulus rebound above baseline.
Calcium in DA terminals in TS and DLS shows opposite responses to STN stimulation, as the GRAB-DA recordings do.

Stimulation of STN or PPN inputs increases the activity of Vglut2+ DA neurons in SNc (STN, Wilcoxon, 0.25 s W = 41, p = 0.012, 1 s W = 43, p = 0.008, 4 s W = -5, p = 0.82; PPN, paired t-test, 0.25 s t = 2.9, p = 0.02, 1 s t = 3.4, p = 0.008, 4 s t = 3.0, p = 0.01).

The Vglut2+ DA neuron increase scales with frequency for short STN trains and for all PPN durations (Friedman, STN 0.25 s F = 15.5, p = 0.001, 1 s F = 5.9, p = 0.11, 4 s F = 7.0, p = 0.07; PPN F = 18.8, 24.8, 20.2, p <= 0.0003).

In DLS terminals of SNc Anxa1+ neurons, STN and PPN stimulation produce inhibition (STN, 0.25 s t = 6.4, p = 0.0004, 1 s W = -36, p = 0.005, 4 s W = -36, p = 0.008; PPN, 0.25 s t = 3.9, p = 0.004, 1 s W = -55, p = 0.002, 4 s t = 3.8, p = 0.004).
The Anxa1+ terminal inhibition scales with frequency (STN, 0.25 s F = 18.0, 1 s F = 15.5, 4 s F = 15.3; PPN, 0.25 s F = 11.5, 1 s F2,15 = 11.0, 4 s F2,18 = 7.2).
Anxa1+ terminals in DLS show a transient increase in activity at stimulus offset, for both inputs.

Anxa1+ SNc cell bodies show stimulation-induced inhibition (paired t-test, STN 0.25 s t = 3.1, 1 s t = 4.0, 4 s t = 7.2, n = 5; PPN t = 4.8, 8.4, 3.3, n = 4) followed by post-stimulus rebound activation.
Excitatory inputs from STN and PPN activate PD-resilient Vglut2+ DA neurons but inhibit PD-vulnerable Anxa1+ DA neurons.
In human SNc, TH+ neurons (Mann-Whitney U = 2.0, p = 0.002) and TH+/ANXA1+ neurons (U = 1.0, p < 0.0001) are fewer in PD cases (n = 7) than in controls (n = 12).
Among remaining DA neurons in PD, ANXA1+ neurons are de-enriched to 10 +/- 7% of control, ALDH1A1+ to 41 +/- 12%, while CALB1+ neurons trend toward enrichment (301 +/- 103%).
TH+/CALB1+ neuron counts are not significantly changed in PD (U = 19.5, p = 0.08) while TH+/ALDH1A1+ counts are reduced (U = 1.0, p < 0.0001).

Immunofluorescence confirms fewer TH+ and TH+/ALDH1A1+ neurons and a lower fraction of TH+ neurons expressing ALDH1A1 in PD (n = 11) than in controls (n = 15), and counts agree with RNAscope in four cases processed both ways.
In dSPNs the rheobase is lower in the LID on-state than in the off-state.
In on-state dSPNs suprathreshold current steps evoke more spikes than in off-state dSPNs across a range of intensities.
Bath application of the D1R antagonist SCH 23390 does not reverse the lower rheobase of on-state dSPNs.
The dendritic excitability index of dSPNs is higher in the on-state than in the off-state.
SCH 23390 reverses the higher dendritic excitability of on-state dSPNs.
The amplitude of Sr2+-oEPSCs evoked from cortical afferents is larger in on-state than in off-state dSPNs.
The frequency of Sr2+-oEPSCs in dSPNs does not differ between states.
dSPN spine density falls in the off-state, and mushroom spines are more common in the on-state than in the off-state.
In iSPNs the rheobase is higher in the on-state than in the off-state.
The F-I relationship of iSPNs shifts to the right in the on-state.
Sulpiride does not alter the somatic excitability of on-state iSPNs.
The dendritic excitability index of iSPNs falls in the on-state compared with the off-state.
Sulpiride does not significantly alter dendritic excitability in on-state iSPNs.
The amplitude of Sr2+-oEPSCs is smaller in on-state than in off-state iSPNs.
The frequency of Sr2+-oEPSCs in iSPNs does not differ between states.
Apparent iSPN spine density (2PLSM) falls after the lesion, returns in the off-state and falls in the on-state, in total and mushroom spines.

Confocal spine density of iSPN proximal dendrites is higher than the 2PLSM estimate (median 2.084 against 1.243 spines per um), falls after the lesion, rises modestly in the off-state and falls in the on-state.
Evoked ACh release (GRAB-ACh3.0) in slices from LID off-state mice is greater than in unlesioned striatum.
Evoked ACh release in the off-state is similar to that after a 6-OHDA lesion.
Evoked ACh release is markedly elevated in 6-OHDA-lesioned striatum compared with unlesioned striatum.
In unlesioned striatum sulpiride increases and quinpirole suppresses evoked ACh release.
Dopamine (50 nM) strongly suppresses evoked ACh release in 6-OHDA-lesioned and off-state striatum, and sulpiride has no effect after the lesion.
M1R antagonism throughout the off-state does not have a strong impact on the elevated somatic excitability of off-state iSPNs.
M1R antagonism prevents the off-state elevation of iSPN dendritic excitability.
M1R antagonism prevents the off-state elevation of apparent iSPN spine density.
Deletion of CDGI does not blunt the oscillation of iSPN somatic excitability between on- and off-states.
The off-state elevation of iSPN dendritic excitability is absent in CDGI KO mice (off against on not different), while it is present in wild type.
The off-state increase in apparent iSPN spine density is absent in CDGI KO mice.
Axial, limb, orolingual and total AIMs are less severe in CDGI KO mice than in wild type.
Deletion of M1Rs from iSPNs does not alter the elevated somatic excitability of off-state iSPNs.
Deletion of M1Rs from iSPNs blunts the off-state increase in apparent spine density.
AIMs are attenuated by deletion of M1Rs in iSPNs.
The study used 26 male Long-Evans rats, aged between 6 and 24 months.
Rats performed on average 542 trials per session.
On average, rats switched across 14.6 context blocks per session.
Behavioural sessions lasted 2 to 4 hours.
Block switches occurred after a minimum of 30 trials per block, and when a local estimate of performance reached 80% correct.
Twenty rats each contributed more than 120,000 trials after training.
After training, choices are mostly driven by location in the location context and by frequency in the frequency context.
Rats switch the feature they attend to within about four trials of a new context block.
Most rats learned the task in two to five months.
Differential behavioural kernels predominantly converge towards the end of the pulse train, that is the difference between contexts in the weight of a feature shrinks for later pulses.
Across rats, the shape of the differential behavioural kernel for one feature does not predict the shape for the other feature.
The behavioural slope index computed from the first half of a rat's trials is correlated with the index from the second half (r = 0.58, p = 0.000013).
Bilateral optogenetic silencing of the frontal orienting fields during the stimulus impairs performance of the task (three rats).

Across 174 sites in 5 mice, the dominant DA-ACh cross-correlation (the largest magnitude Pearson r within 1 s lags) during spontaneous behavior is negative at 132 sites, 127 of them with DA leading, and positive at 42 sites, 31 of them with ACh leading.
The dominant correlations form a significant hotspot, identified by local Moran's I, in the anterior dorsolateral striatum (aDLS), where the strongest correlations are negative.
Sites inside the aDLS hotspot have more negative dominant correlations than sites outside (Wilcoxon rank-sum p = 1.67e-16).
Dominant positive correlations lie in the posterior striatum.
The hotspot is consistent across mice; in each mouse, sites inside the group hotspot have more negative dominant correlations than sites outside.
Mice expressing non-functional sensors (a mutant ACh sensor and tdTomato, n = 3) show only sparse, weak positive red-green correlations with no anatomical organization; no hotspot is found.

For coincident transients of opposite polarity (ACh trough with DA peak, ACh peak with DA trough) the DA transient leads; for same-polarity pairs (peak with peak, trough with trough) the ACh transient leads.

Magnitudes of paired transients are negatively correlated at many sites for opposite-sign pairs (121 of 174 for ACh troughs with DA peaks, 81 of 174 for ACh peaks with DA troughs) and positively for same-sign pairs (97 of 174 peak-peak, 78 of 174 trough-trough), with no site significant in the other direction.
Magnitude correlations of opposite-sign pairs, but not same-sign pairs, are stronger inside the aDLS hotspot than outside (rank-sum p < 0.05 for opposite-sign pairs, p > 0.05 for same-sign pairs).
The frequency of paired transients is highest in aDLS, in a region overlapping the correlation hotspot, for all four pair types (volume overlap test, p < 0.01 for each).
DA and ACh transient rates are higher at sites inside the global correlation hotspot than outside.

After unpredicted rewards, trial-by-trial DA peak magnitude correlates with ACh; dominant correlations are negative at 114 of 174 sites with DA leading (mean latency 177.9 +/- 96.7 ms) and positive at 58 of 174 with ACh leading (-41.2 +/- 218.9 ms).
Reward-evoked DA-ACh correlations are significantly more negative inside the global hotspot than outside.
Reward anti-correlations form an aDLS hotspot that significantly overlaps the hotspot of spontaneous correlations (volume overlap test, p = 0.008).
After Pavlovian conditioning, the conditioned light cue evokes an ACh peak, then a DA peak, then an ACh dip at a majority of sites (49 of 75).

For conditioned light cues, ACh correlates with the trial-by-trial DA peak negatively at lagging times at 39 of 75 sites (ACh lagging, 202.28 +/- 128.4 ms) and positively at leading times at 26 of 75 (ACh leading, -79.1 +/- 224.0 ms).

After cue-specific extinction (light cue rewarded on 20% of trials), cue-evoked DA dips correlate negatively with lagging ACh (DA dip then ACh late peak) at 41 of 74 sites, mean lag 117.9 +/- 176.2 ms.
Conditioned-cue DA-ACh correlations are more negative at sites inside the global aDLS hotspot than outside.
After extinction, DA dip to ACh correlations are more negative at sites inside the global aDLS hotspot than outside.
At locomotion initiations, ACh rises and then falls at 131 of 174 sites; DA dips at 119 of 174 sites, rises at 73, and both rises and dips at 32.
Initiation-related signals occur in sequence; DA dips first (median latency 111.11 ms), then ACh peaks (222.22 ms) and DA peaks (227.78 ms), then ACh dips (611.11 ms).
Initiation-related DA dips are concentrated in the aDLS and DA peaks in dorsomedial and posterior striatum; ACh dips are localized to the aDLS.
At sites with initiation-related DA dips (119 sites), trial-by-trial DA dip magnitudes correlate negatively with ACh with DA leading (mean latency 193.80 +/- 177.68 ms).
Initiation DA dip to ACh correlations are concentrated in the aDLS and more negative inside the global hotspot than outside.

At locomotion invigorations, GLM-estimated DA peak magnitudes correlate negatively with ACh at lagging times, and these correlations are concentrated in the aDLS, more negative inside the global hotspot (131 sites with invigoration DA peaks).
Optogenetic stimulation of midbrain DA neurons evokes significant DA release at 179 of 180 sites.
DA stimulation evokes significant ACh suppression at a subset of sites (116 of 180, 64%).

The stimulation cohort replicates the aDLS anti-correlation hotspot in spontaneous release outside stimulation periods; its dominant correlations are more negative inside the original hotspot, and its own hotspot overlaps the original.
Stimulation-evoked ACh dips are larger inside the cohort's correlation hotspot than outside, and their own hotspot overlaps it.
406 units were recorded from 7 juvenile WT rats and 372 from 5 juvenile Fmr1-/y rats; 543 units from 6 adult WT rats and 507 from 6 adult Fmr1-/y rats.
Juvenile recordings held 8 to 83 putative excitatory units each, adult recordings 30 to 114.
Juvenile Fmr1-/y and WT rats do not differ in the time spent inactive, the time spent in the centre of the arena, or the speed while active.
Adult Fmr1-/y and WT rats do not differ in the time spent inactive, the time spent in the centre of the arena, or the speed while active.
In juveniles, cluster contamination, mean and peak firing rates, and the resultant vector length of PoSub cells do not differ between genotypes.
In adults, cluster contamination, mean and peak firing rates, and the resultant vector length of PoSub cells do not differ between genotypes.
PoSub cells of juvenile Fmr1-/y rats are more sharply tuned to head direction than those of WT littermates, with higher HD information and narrower tuning curves.
In juveniles the HD information of a cell is stable between the two halves of an exploration session (WT r = 0.90, Fmr1-/y r = 0.95).
Within a session, the tuning curves of juvenile Fmr1-/y cells drift less relative to the room than those of WT cells; the angular offset between the two halves is smaller.
Bayesian decoding shows less drift of the HD signal relative to the room in juvenile Fmr1-/y rats than in WT rats.
In juveniles HD information is preserved between the two exploration sessions (WT r = 0.85, Fmr1-/y r = 0.85).
In juveniles the drift of tuning curves between the two exploration sessions does not differ between genotypes.
In juveniles the HD information of tuning curves computed against the Isomap angle of the waking population activity matches that of real HD tuning curves (WT r = 0.84, Fmr1-/y r = 0.92).
Juvenile Fmr1-/y cells are better tuned than WT cells to the internal HD signal of the waking manifold, independently of any reference frame.
In juveniles the HD information of tuning curves computed against the Isomap angle of REM sleep activity matches that of real HD tuning curves (WT r = 0.73, Fmr1-/y r = 0.90).
Juvenile Fmr1-/y cells are better tuned than WT cells to the internally generated HD signal during REM sleep.
In adults HD tuning does not differ between Fmr1-/y and WT rats, in HD information or tuning curve width.
In adults HD information is stable between the two halves of an exploration session (WT r = 0.94, Fmr1-/y r = 0.94).
Within a session the tuning curves of adult Fmr1-/y cells drift more relative to the room than those of WT cells.
Bayesian decoding shows more drift of the HD signal relative to the room in adult Fmr1-/y rats than in WT rats.
In adults HD information is preserved between the two exploration sessions (WT r = 0.90, Fmr1-/y r = 0.76).
In adults the tuning curves of Fmr1-/y cells drift more than those of WT cells between the two exploration sessions 90 min apart.
In adults the HD information of Isomap tuning curves from waking activity matches that of real HD tuning curves (WT r = 0.95, Fmr1-/y r = 0.90).
In adults tuning to the internal HD signal of the waking manifold does not differ between Fmr1-/y and WT rats.
In adults the HD information of Isomap tuning curves from REM activity matches that of real HD tuning curves (WT r = 0.82, Fmr1-/y r = 0.80).
In adults tuning to the internally generated HD signal during REM sleep does not differ between Fmr1-/y and WT rats.
In every rat the probe tracts passed through PoSub, confirmed histologically.
Mice of both genotypes show sigmoidal psychometric curves, with the proportion of rightward choices increasing as the stimulus contrast increases on the right.
Psychometric bias, slope and lapse rates do not differ between WT and KO mice (bias p = 0.94, slope p = 0.95, left lapse p = 0.16, right lapse p = 0.22).
Reaction time (time to first movement) is longer at lower contrasts in both genotypes.
Reaction times do not differ between genotypes on correct (p = 0.234) or incorrect (p = 0.522) trials.
WT and KO mice learn the task with similar trajectories, reaching asymptotic performance after about 20 sessions.

Mice use the block prior; rightward choices are more frequent in right-likely blocks than in left-likely blocks, most clearly when contrast is low, shifting the psychometric curve toward the likely side (shown for WT, and present but smaller in KO).
KO mice shift their choices less between biased blocks than WT mice, with a difference in psychometric bias and none in slope or lapses.

After a block switch, mice adapt their choices toward the newly likely side, and the proportion of choices toward the block side rises from an initial value A to an asymptote B with a time constant tau.
KO mice adapt more slowly after a block switch (longer tau, p = 0.004) and have lower initial performance after the switch (p = 0.041) than WT littermates.
Visual cortex (VISp) responds robustly to contralateral visual stimuli.
KO mice show elevated dF/F across cortex in the ITI (most prominent in motor regions), stimulus and feedback periods compared with WT.
KO mice show globally increased pairwise correlations between regional dF/F time series during the task.
KO mice show higher pixel-wise trial-to-trial variance across all cortical regions and task periods.
The full linear encoding model explains more than half of single-trial cortical variance (cvR2 0.60 +/- 0.02 in KO and 0.54 +/- 0.02 in WT).

Movement predictors account for most of the explained variance; shuffling them reduces cvR2 by much more than shuffling task predictors (delta R2 for movement 0.40 +/- 0.02 in KO and 0.33 +/- 0.02 in WT; task shuffle beta -0.02).

KO mice lose more explained variance than WT when movement predictors are shuffled (Group x Movement beta = 0.071, p = 0.006; delta R2 KO 0.40 against WT 0.33, p = 0.032), with no group difference for task predictors; full-model cvR2 tends to be higher in KO (p = 0.076).
KO mice show elevated baseline motion energy relative to WT, with comparable stimulus-evoked movement dynamics after baseline correction.
Individual movement variables explain more unique variance in KO than in WT mice, and task variables explain little unique variance in either group.

Each frame holds seven MARS keypoints (nose, left ear, right ear, neck, left hip, right hip, tail base) for each of two mice, the resident (mouse 0) and the intruder (mouse 1), in pixel coordinates of a 1024 x 570 image, at 30 Hz, with a confidence score from 0 to 1 for each keypoint.
Mouse 0, the resident, is the black C57Bl/6J mouse, and mouse 1, the intruder, is the white BALB/c mouse.
Task 1 frames are annotated by one annotator (annotator id 0) with exactly one label per frame from the vocabulary attack 0, investigation 1, mount 2 and other 3.
The source videos of Task 1 are released, recorded at 30 Hz and 1024 x 570 pixels.
Close investigation, attack and mount are behaviors in which the resident is in close contact with the intruder; other frames include the animals apart.
Errors in pose estimation are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly.

Grin2b+/- rats have more SWDs than WT across the 24-h day; hour of day has no effect and does not interact with genotype (linear mixed model, genotype F = 55.36, p < .00001; hour p = .16; interaction p = .49).
Grin2b+/- rats have more SWDs over 24 h than WT (Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 4.5, p = .0002).
SWDs are longer on average in Grin2b+/- rats than in WT (two-sample t test, df = 22, T = -5.26, p = .00003).
The total time in SWDs over 24 h is higher in Grin2b+/- rats than in WT (Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 5.5, p = .0002).
Over 24 h, Grin2b+/- rats spend on average 59.97 min in SWDs, while WT littermates average less than a minute.
The number of SWDs does not differ between the light and dark phases, and Grin2b+/- rats have more SWDs than WT in both (linear mixed model, genotype p < .00001, phase p = .28, interaction p = .53).
Sex does not affect the number, mean duration or total duration of SWDs (two-way ANOVA sex x genotype, sex p = .74, .99 and .99).
The EEG spectrum during SWDs has a clear peak in the theta range with a harmonic, in both genotypes.
Delta power during SWDs is higher in Grin2b+/- rats than in WT (two-way ANOVA genotype x band, interaction p = .015; Tukey delta p = .039).
Grin2b+/- rats have less REM sleep per hour than WT across the day, and the reduction is not specific to certain hours (linear mixed model, genotype F = 9.98, p = .0045; hour x genotype p = .53).
Grin2b+/- rats spend less total time in REM sleep over 24 h than WT (two-sample t test, df = 22, T = 3.16, p = .0045).
Grin2b+/- rats have fewer REM bouts than WT (two-sample t test, df = 22, T = 3.94, p = .00069).
REM bouts are longer on average in Grin2b+/- rats than in WT (Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 33, p = .043).
Total NREM sleep over 24 h does not differ between genotypes (two-sample t test, df = 22, T = -.09, p = .93).
Grin2b+/- rats have fewer NREM bouts, which are longer, than WT (Wilcoxon rank-sum, bouts W = 29.5, p = .025; mean bout duration W = 26, p = .015).
Grin2b+/- rats spend less total time awake over 24 h than WT (Welch t test, df = 10.25, T = 2.26, p = .047).
Grin2b+/- rats have more wake bouts of shorter duration than WT (Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 18, p = .0035; Welch t test on mean bout duration, df = 8.91, T = 2.97, p = .016).
EEG spectral power during REM sleep does not differ between genotypes (two-way ANOVA genotype x band, genotype p = .14, interaction p = .69).
During NREM sleep Grin2b+/- rats have higher beta power than WT (two-way ANOVA genotype x band, interaction p = .038; Tukey beta p = .0008, other bands p >= .82).
During wake, spectral power is reduced in Grin2b+/- rats overall, without a difference in single bands (two-way ANOVA genotype x band, genotype p = .01, interaction p = .86).
Over both genotypes, SWDs occur mostly in wake (94.8%), then NREM (4.4%), and rarely in REM sleep (0.5%).
Compared with WT, Grin2b+/- rats have a higher share of SWDs in NREM and a lower share in wake (two-way ANOVA genotype x state, interaction p = .00008; Tukey NREM p = .0011, wake p = .0022).
All Grin2b+/- rats have SWDs that start at wake-NREM transitions, against 3 of 9 WT rats (Fisher's exact test, p = .00062).
In Grin2b+/- rats 24.2% of SWDs occur during the wake-NREM transition, similar to the 22.39% of the WT rats that have such SWDs (two-sample t test, p = .74).
In Grin2b+/- rats, total SWD duration is negatively correlated with total time awake (Pearson, R = -.51, p = .048).
In Grin2b+/- rats, total SWD duration is not correlated with total REM or NREM time, the number of REM, NREM or wake bouts, or the mean REM, NREM or wake bout duration (Pearson, all p >= .066).
GluN2B protein is reduced by about 50% in somatosensory cortex and hippocampus of Grin2b+/- rats (homogenate t test p = .000104; synaptosome Wilcoxon p = .00094).
GluN2A, GluR1 and PSD95 expression are unchanged in Grin2b+/- rats.
Grin2b+/- rats survive, grow and develop motor reflexes like WT littermates (survival 48% and 52%; body weight, righting reflex and negative geotaxis do not differ).
The automated sleep scorer agrees with visual scoring on 90.8% of epochs (Cohen's kappa 0.83).
Systemic ethosuximide reduces the number of SWDs relative to saline and memantine in both genotypes (linear mixed model, treatment p = .0049; ethosuximide-saline p = .0081).
Systemic ethosuximide and memantine reduce the mean SWD duration in Grin2b+/- rats but not in WT (treatment x genotype p = .044).
Systemic ethosuximide reduces the total SWD duration in both genotypes (treatment p = .0011; ethosuximide-saline p = .0005).
Infusion of ethosuximide or memantine into the reticular thalamic nucleus reduces the number and total duration of SWDs in Grin2b+/- rats but not their mean duration.

Mice touched the pole often when it was within reach (lick trials, 5.7 +- 5.3 touches per trial over 4,147 trials) and rarely when it was distal (0.9 +- 3.4 over 4,173 trials); performance was 0.72 +- 0.11 in cortical and 0.71 +- 0.07 in VPM recordings.
VPM neurons respond to active touch with a sharp, short-latency increase in spike rate (0.6 +- 0.5 spikes per touch, median 0.4; latency 3.2 +- 1.0 ms, median 2.5 ms).

VPM neurons fire at 5.1 +- 5.5 spikes/s without whisker movement or touch; most (25 of 29) increase their rate during whisking without touch, and the mean rate rises from 5.1 to 13.5 spikes/s. Three of 29 do not increase with whisking but still respond to touch.
The spike rate of VPM neurons is modulated by the phase of whisker movement.

In L4 excitatory neurons (37 whole-cell), resting Vm spans -76 to -45 mV (-63 +- 8 mV); every neuron depolarizes after touch (latency 4.8 +- 0.8 ms, amplitude 6.0 +- 2.9 mV), while whisking causes only a small depolarization or hyperpolarization (1.2 +- 2.1 mV).
Touch moves the membrane potential of L4 excitatory neurons much closer to spike threshold than whisking does (shift 6.1 +- 3.2 mV against 1.1 +- 2.0 mV).

The effective reversal potential of the touch response of L4 excitatory neurons is more depolarized than resting Vm, while that of whisking is close to rest and more hyperpolarized than that of touch.
With L4 excitatory neurons depolarized near 0 mV to reveal inhibition, touch evokes strong, transient inhibition that follows excitation by 0.4 +- 0.8 ms at half maximum.

In L4 excitatory neurons held near 0 mV, inhibitory inputs occur spontaneously but are more prevalent at the onset of whisker movement; after whisking onset, excitation and inhibition increase gradually, with indistinguishable time courses, over about 100 ms.
L4 FS interneurons fire at 9.3 +- 8.5 spikes/s without whisker movement and fire 1.9 +- 1.0 spikes per touch, with a spike latency of 5.3 +- 2.1 ms.
In whole-cell L4 FS interneurons (n = 7), touch depolarizes the membrane by 7.0 +- 5.2 mV with onset 4.0 +- 0.6 ms, and whisking depolarizes it by 2.7 +- 2.1 mV toward threshold.
Most L4 FS interneurons (23 of 26) increase their spike rate during whisking without touch and 3 of 26 decrease it; over the population the rate roughly doubles (to 21.1 +- 15.8 spikes/s).
Spikes of L4 FS interneurons are coupled to whisking phase.
Touch- and whisking-evoked spikes are typically multiplexed in individual L4 FS neurons, as in VPM neurons.
