L4 excitatory neurons respond mostly to touch (0.3 +- 0.4 spikes per touch, n = 85) and only weakly to whisker movement; their rate does not change significantly between nonwhisking and whisking (0.4 to 0.6 spikes/s, P = 0.20).
Photoactivating TRN axons in VPM of VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice reduces thalamic activity to 17% of control.

Thalamic photoinhibition hyperpolarizes L4 excitatory neurons and reduces their Vm fluctuations, with an onset latency of 4.2 ms, longer than the 2.8 ms latency of direct cortical GABAergic activation.

Photoinhibiting the thalamus reduces the spike rates of L4 FS interneurons during nonwhisking (to 4% of control), whisking (to 13%) and touch (to 32%), so FS interneurons are driven by thalamic input.
Monosynaptic rabies tracing from L4 PV interneurons labels thalamic neurons mostly in VPM (>90%) and few in POM (<10%).
After infraorbital nerve transection, L4 excitatory neurons do not depolarize after touch.

After ION transection, whisking-evoked depolarization of L4 excitatory neurons is reduced (0.62 +- 0.50 mV, n = 9) relative to control neurons with matched resting potential (1.54 +- 0.79 mV, n = 15).
After ION transection, phase-locking of L4 excitatory Vm to whisker movement is abolished (coupling 0.12 +- 0.04 mV against 0.38 +- 0.31 mV in controls).
After ION transection, touch does not evoke spikes in L4 FS interneurons.
After ION transection, the whisking-related activation of L4 FS interneurons is absent in most cells (P = 0.80, n = 10), so their movement-related modulation is reafference driven by sensory input.
After ION transection, phase-locking of L4 FS spikes to whisker movement is reduced but not entirely abolished.
After infraorbital nerve transection, mice still search for the pole by whisking but, unable to sense it, perform the task at chance (48% correct).
Yellow light in PV-IRES-Cre mice expressing eNpHR3.0 strongly inhibits most L4 PV interneurons (3 of 4); their rate falls 3 ms after laser onset and L4 excitatory activity rises 2 ms later.
Partially suppressing PV (FS) interneurons increases the spike rate of L4 excitatory neurons during nonwhisking (0.6 to 1.6 spikes/s) and whisking (0.8 to 2.7 spikes/s).

With PV interneurons suppressed, L4 excitatory neurons become driven by whisker movement (whisking rate above nonwhisking, P = 0.02), while in control trials they are not (P = 0.55); their selectivity for touch is normally maintained in part by FS interneurons.

PV interneuron suppression does not change mean touch-evoked spiking of L4 excitatory neurons significantly (0.27 to 0.32 spikes per touch, P = 0.09); its effect is heterogeneous, with weakly responding neurons responding more and strongly responding neurons unchanged or less.
Suppressing PV interneurons improves touch detection (AUC) for L4 excitatory neurons with weak touch responses and diminishes it for neurons with robust touch responses.

Neurons whose AUC rose with PV suppression gained touch-evoked spiking (3.4 to 8.7 spikes/s); neurons whose AUC fell kept their touch-evoked response (7.3 to 7.0 spikes/s) but had higher baseline rates (0.9 to 2.6 spikes/s).
With PV interneurons suppressed, most mice (6 of 8) are more likely to report touch with the pole out of reach (false alarms on no-lick trials).
smFISH confirms Slco2a1 as a PTlower marker and Npnt as a PTupper marker (Slco2a1 puncta IQR 1-2.5 in PTupper against 6-22 in PTlower; Npnt IQR 16-40 in PTupper against 1-9 in PTlower).
The recordings yield 61 identified PTupper cells from 8 mice and 69 identified PTlower neurons from 4 mice after exclusions (130 of 143 tagged units kept).
Identified PTupper cells are at more superficial recording depths than PTlower neurons.
Baseline and trial-averaged peak spike rates do not differ between PTupper (baseline 4.3 +/- 3.5 Hz, peak 17.7 +/- 13.8 Hz, median +/- s.d.) and PTlower cells (5.2 +/- 4.8 Hz, 17.2 +/- 22 Hz).
Spike rates are more heterogeneous across the PTlower population than the PTupper population, for baseline (P = 0.02) and peak rates (P = 3 x 10^-4).
A substantial proportion of PTlower neurons fire bursts (18.8%), which are rare among PTupper cells (3.3%).
Most recorded PT neurons (122 of 130, 94%) have significant trial-type selectivity in at least one task epoch.
Trial-averaged activity patterns are nearly as diverse within each PT population as across all neurons recorded in ALM; cell type explains relatively little of the variance.
Along the late delay coding direction (CDlate) selectivity is substantial in both PT types, with 40 of 61 PTupper and 44 of 69 PTlower neurons selective.
Along the early coding direction (CDearly, first 400 ms of the sample epoch), selectivity is larger and more consistent across trials in the PTupper population than in the PTlower population.
In the PTupper population, selectivity along CDearly remains constant through the sample and delay epochs until the go cue.
In the PTlower population, selectivity along CDearly decays rapidly, with no significant selectivity in the 400 ms before the go cue (P = 0.34, bootstrap).

The coding direction stays more similar across the sample and delay epochs in the PTupper population than in the PTlower population, whose delay-epoch coding directions are largely orthogonal to those of the sample epoch.
Individual PTupper neurons have higher early selectivity than PTlower neurons (0.41 +/- 0.04 against 0.25 +/- 0.02, mean +/- s.e.m., P < 0.01).

Single PTupper neurons decode trial type better than PTlower neurons in the first 400 ms of the sample epoch; 24.6% (15 of 61) of PTupper and 4.4% (3 of 69) of PTlower neurons reach 70% accuracy, mean accuracy is 64.4 +/- 1.0% against 58.9 +/- 0.6%, and the ten most discriminative neurons are all PTupper.

Decoding from spike rates rectified at baseline, no PTlower neuron reaches 70% accuracy while the same 24.6% of PTupper neurons do, PTupper neurons make up 20 of the 21 most predictive, and mean accuracy is 62.7 +/- 1.1% against 56.7 +/- 0.4%.
Along CDgo, significant selectivity emerges 24 ms after the go cue in PTlower neurons, faster than in PTupper neurons (48 ms), consistent with a role in movement initiation.

PTlower neurons carry late preparatory activity (selectivity along CDlate) and a movement command; along the go cue coding direction (CDgo) selectivity is larger, emerges faster and persists longer in PTlower than in PTupper.
The first detectable movement occurs about 50 ms after the go cue (99% confidence interval 38 to 56 ms).
The coding direction changes rapidly at the go cue in the PTlower population, and more slowly, over several hundred milliseconds, in the PTupper population.

In PTlower neurons, selectivity along both CDlate and CDgo ceases with the offset of movement (the last lick), together with an abrupt change in the coding direction; this transition is not seen in the PTupper population.

Differences in coding between PTupper and PTlower neurons are not explained by the animal cohorts; unidentified neurons recorded in the two cohorts give similar coding direction projections, nearly indistinguishable once depth-matched.

The two PT types have different roles in time; PTupper populations carry early preparatory activity that persists until movement, while PTlower populations mainly carry late preparatory activity and movement commands.
1,329 cells from 266 mice passed the initial quality control and were sequenced; the paper's recordings come from these cells.
The mice were 35 to 245 days old, with a median of 75 days and an interquartile range of 64 to 100 days.

The 266 mice were wild-type C57Bl/6 (27), Viaat-Cre/Ai9 (24), Sst-Cre/Ai9 (75), Vip-Cre/Ai9 (46), Pvalb-Cre/Ai9 (76), Npy-Cre/Ai9 (2), Vipr2-Cre/Ai9 (7), Slc17a8-Cre/Ai9 (6), Gnb4-Cre/Ai9 (1) and Slc17a8-iCre/Ai9 (2).

Each neuron was stimulated with 600 ms current pulses from -200 pA upwards in 20 pA steps up to 1,380 pA (sometimes stopped earlier), with 1.3 or 1.4 s between pulses, and for most neurons the series was repeated several times.
Soma depth was measured for 1,284 of the 1,329 neurons; 45 neurons were recorded with too little biocytin, and the depth could be measured for only 2 of them.

The features of the example cell of Extended Data Fig. 4 are an input resistance of 274.80 MOhm, a membrane time constant of 21.95 ms, ISI adaptation index 1.26, ISI average adaptation index 1.15, AP amplitude adaptation index 0.91 and its average 0.99, AP threshold -40.18 mV, AP amplitude 81.17 mV, AP width 0.80 ms, AHP -12.60 mV, ADP 0 mV, UDR 1.62, latency 69.28 ms, rheobase 20.44 pA, 32 APs in the highest firing trace, ISI CV 0.27, ISI Fano factor 0.0014, AP CV 0.17, AP Fano factor 1.32, sag ratio 1.17, sag time 0.26, sag area 31.16 mV ms and rebound 17.84 mV.
All 17 features used for statistics could be computed for 1,320 cells, of which 1,219 had a t-type assignment.
Pvalb neurons are characterized by high firing rates, while Sst neurons have high hyperpolarization sag and rebound.

In a k-nearest-neighbour classification of cells into seven transcriptomic families from electrophysiological features, the confusion matrix is mostly diagonal, with only the ET and IT subclasses strongly overlapping.

At room temperature, the features that differ most between layer 5 IT and ET neurons by a two-sided Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test, after omitting the upstroke-to-downstroke ratio, sag time and sag area, are the sag ratio, input resistance, AP width and rebound.
After quality control 1,227 neurons had a t-type (817 inhibitory, 410 excitatory), covering 77 of the 90 neuronal t-types of the reference taxonomy.
Within-type distributions of soma depth agree with the layer-specific names of the excitatory t-types.
The L4/5 IT_1 t-type is located on the boundary between L2/3 and L5, and probably corresponds to the quasi-L4 neurons described before in motor cortex.

Most t-types are classified into their own family from electrophysiology, but some lie between two families; many Sst Pvalb Calb2 neurons are classified as Pvalb, Lamp5 Egln3_1 neurons have Vip- and Sst-like firing, and Vip Mybpc1 neurons often have Sst-like firing.

Many t-types have a normalized total variance of electrophysiological features well above that of k-means clusters; some, such as Pvalb Vipr2_2 (chandelier cells), appear homogeneous, while Vip Mybpc1_2 is highly variable.
An alternative analysis using the entropy of Leiden cluster assignments within each t-type often highlights the same t-types as variable.
Mice performed the delayed-response task at 77.6% correct on average, with 10.3% lick-early trials and 1.1% no-response trials.
Unilateral photoinhibition of ALM during the delay epoch biased responses to the ipsilateral side, lowering performance on contra trials and raising it on ipsi trials.
Unilateral photoinhibition of thalALM during the delay epoch lowered performance on contra trials and caused a small, non-significant improvement on ipsi trials.
Photostimulating TRN axons in thalamus of Gad2-IRES-Cre mice reduced thalALM spike rates, recorded near VM/VAL, to 67.8% of control during the delay epoch.
In VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, thalamus photoinhibition reduced activity 0.5 to 1.1 mm from the fibre tip to 15.9% of control.

Small doses of muscimol infused near VM/VAL produced an ipsilateral bias in licking responses, while infusions outside thalALM, anterior or dorsal (1.1 to 1.6 mm anterior or 1.6 to 1.9 mm dorsal to VM/VAL in the Results; about 0.3 to 0.8 mm anterior to VM/VAL and 0.2 to 0.5 mm dorsal to MD in the legends), did not, even at ten-fold higher doses.
Of 1214 ALM units, 1006 were putative pyramidal neurons (spike width > 0.6 ms), 166 putative fast-spiking (< 0.4 ms) and 42 unclassified; the spike-width distribution was bimodal.
Most ALM putative pyramidal neurons (70%, 704/1006) distinguished trial types; 145 had preparatory activity only, 272 peri-movement selectivity only and 287 both.
Approximately equal numbers of selective ALM neurons preferred contra and ipsi movements.
Of 790 thalamic units, 672 were putative thalamic neurons (spike width > 0.5 ms) and 313 lay within 0.4 mm of the VM/VAL centre; 295 VM/VAL units were analysed.

A majority of VM/VAL neurons (69%, 204/295) distinguished trial types, a fraction indistinguishable from ALM; 43 had preparatory activity only, 82 peri-movement selectivity only and 79 both, a distribution similar to ALM.
Strong photoinhibition of thalALM (VGAT-ChR2-EYFP) decreased ALM activity to 6% of control, inhibiting 309 of 314 neurons (155 significantly) and significantly activating none.
Thalamus photoinhibition reduced ALM activity across all cortical layers.
ALM neurons with preparatory activity, peri-movement selectivity or both were equally inhibited by thalamus photoinhibition.
Strong photoinhibition in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice abolished thalALM activity nearly completely, to 2% of control.
Photoinhibition reduced thalALM activity 2.5 ms after photostimulus onset, and ALM spike rates were reduced 8.2 ms after onset, a latency difference consistent with direct thalamocortical drive.
During the delay epoch the mean membrane potential of ALM neurons was close to spike threshold, 12.7 mV below it on average.
Thalamus photoinhibition hyperpolarized ALM neurons by 18.7 mV, preventing spiking, with an onset 7.9 ms after photostimulus onset.
The hyperpolarization of ALM neurons during thalamus photoinhibition was caused mainly by a loss of excitation, not by an increase in inhibition; it was larger with negative current injection.
Photoinhibition of M1 during the delay epoch caused only a slight hyperpolarization (3.3 mV) and a small drop in spike rate (1.4 spikes per s) in ALM neurons.
Photoinhibition of contralateral ALM barely changed the membrane potential of ALM neurons (1.4 mV).
thalALM drives ALM more strongly than M1 or contralateral ALM, the other reciprocally connected structures tested.

The latency of ALM hyperpolarization is too short for the thalamus to M1 to ALM pathway; thalamus photoinhibition hyperpolarized M1 neurons after 11.0 ms and M1 photoinhibition hyperpolarized ALM neurons after 13.9 ms, so that pathway would give a latency difference above 14.3 ms against the 5.4 ms observed.
Photoactivating thalamus in Olig3-cre x Ai32 mice depolarized ALM neurons after 3.6 ms, an estimate of the thalamocortical conduction delay.
A model ALM neuron with 200 thalamic inputs predicts at least 1.8 ms between full loss of thalamic input and a detectable change in membrane potential.

Weak thalamus photoinhibition (20-fold weaker, 0.5 mW) significantly changed the spike rate of 83 of 160 ALM neurons, with a mean reduction of 1.2 spikes per s; 39% of the changed neurons (32/83) increased their rate.

Weak thalamus photoinhibition reduced the selectivity of ALM neurons, both contra- and ipsi-preferring; the change in selectivity was anti-correlated with selectivity (slope -0.33, r = -0.75), even in neurons without a change in mean rate.
The data are inconsistent with linear network models with specific or non-specific thalamocortical connectivity, but do not exclude non-linear models of either kind.
ALM photoinhibition decreased the activity of VM/VAL neurons to 25% of control, inhibiting 190 of 201 neurons (139 significantly) and significantly activating none.
VM/VAL neurons selective during the sample, delay or response epochs were equally inhibited by ALM photoinhibition.

The few VM/VAL neurons not changed by ALM photoinhibition were significantly less selective in the delay epoch, while neurons strongly reduced by it carried trial-type information; the change of rate and delay selectivity were negatively related (regression slope -0.73, r -0.33).
The reduction of thalamic activity by ALM photoinhibition was mainly limited to VM/VAL; neurons within 1.0 mm of the VM/VAL centre were inhibited to 36% of control, and neurons farther away less.
Photoinhibiting vibrissal M1 did not reduce thalALM activity (Results), or reduced VM/VAL activity less than ALM photoinhibition in the same neurons (Extended Data Fig. 8g legend).
After ALM photoinhibition onset, ALM pyramidal neurons were silenced after 8.1 ms and VM/VAL activity reduced after 10.9 ms; SNr neurons changed later, after 15.2 ms.

ALM photoinhibition changed only a small fraction of SNr GABAergic neurons (48/181 significantly inhibited, 23/181 activated), more decreasing than increasing, and reduced SNr activity overall by 3.6 spikes per s (8.3%), which argues against SNr mediating the thalamic reduction.
Putative GABAergic SNr neurons had high spike rates (40.9 spikes per s) compared with the other SNr units (23.4), and most of them (152/181) were selective for trial type, like ALM and VM/VAL.

ALM is reciprocally connected with ipsilateral thalamic nuclei, most consistently the VM/VAL complex; a retrograde injection into ALM labelled 17375 thalamic neurons, against 38062 in contralateral ALM and 26599 in M1.

In ALM and in VM/VAL, population selectivity emerged in the sample epoch and increased throughout the delay epoch; it peaked at the beginning of the response epoch in ALM and during the response epoch in VM/VAL.
GABAergic neurons in ALM do not project to thalALM, so ALM photoinhibition does not inhibit thalamus directly.

Over 61 sessions in 4 rats, 7,390 well-isolated units were recorded (rat 1, 2,444; rat 2, 1,294; rat 3, 1,138; rat 4, 2,514), of which 2,038 were in the BLA, 782 in the central nuclei, 1,560 in the piriform cortex and 1,210 in the hippocampus.
Rats learned the daily location of the air puff. The speed ratio between the previous and the current danger zone rises from pre-run to run and post-run, reversing between pre-run and post-run.
The speed ratio changes across pre-run, run and post-run in each of the four rats taken alone, indicating that every rat learned the new air puff location.
Speed in the current danger zone is lower in post-run than in pre-run, and in run and post-run rats run slower in the current than in the previous danger zone.
The location of the air puff on the track does not correlate with the speed in the current danger zone in pre-run, run or post-run.
The aversive valence of the air puff diminishes over training days; rats run more laps per unit time as they habituate.
BLA pyramidal cells fire faster in REM sleep and, to a lesser extent, in NREM sleep than in wakefulness.
BLA interneurons do not change their firing rate between REM sleep and wake, and fire slightly less in NREM sleep than in wake.
Hippocampus-BLA pyramidal cell pair correlations of the run are reinstated in post-sleep NREM, measured as explained variance (EV) exceeding the reverse explained variance (REV) across sessions.
Hippocampus-BLA NREM reactivation holds when pyramidal cells and interneurons are both included.
Hippocampus-BLA reactivation decays over the first hour of post-sleep NREM (mean EV - REV 2.89, 1.72 and 1.31% in successive 20-min NREM periods).
Hippocampus-BLA and hippocampus-piriform cortex reactivations are not significant in REM sleep.
Piriform cortex neurons show weaker reactivation with hippocampal CA1 neurons than BLA neurons do, though still significant in NREM.
There are no reactivations between the central amygdala nuclei and the hippocampus.
Within the hippocampus and within the BLA, pair correlations are reactivated in NREM but not in REM sleep.
A subset of BLA neurons is positively modulated during hippocampal SPW-Rs, 25.8% of interneurons (42 of 163) and 11.1% of pyramidal cells (137 of 1,233).
Another subset of BLA neurons is negatively modulated during hippocampal SPW-Rs, 14.7% of interneurons (24 of 163) and 8.3% of pyramidal cells (102 of 1,233).
Reactivation (EV - REV) is larger for hippocampus-BLA pairs whose BLA cell is ripple-modulated than for pairs with a non-modulated BLA cell.
During run, 6.69% of hippocampus-BLA pyramidal pairs (2,521 of 37,660) are significantly positively correlated, 3.34% (1,258) negatively, and 89.96% (33,881) not reliably correlated.

Among nine groups of hippocampus-BLA pyramidal pairs formed by run correlation and BLA ripple modulation, the pairs with a significant positive run correlation and an upmodulated BLA partner show the largest pre-NREM to post-NREM increase in correlation, and differ from every other group.
EV computed within each of the nine pair groups confirms the dominant contribution of the pairs with positive run correlation and an upmodulated BLA partner.
Upmodulated BLA cells in the quartile contributing most to the reactivation increase their SPW-R gain from pre-NREM to post-NREM, while upmodulated cells of the other three quartiles do not.
Hippocampus-BLA EV does not depend on firing rates; EV exceeds REV across firing-rate octiles of the pairs, of the BLA cells and of the hippocampal cells.
Reactivation strength of the whole-run template around hippocampal ripple peaks is higher in post-NREM than in pre-NREM, for pyramidal pairs and for all cell pairs.
The hippocampus-BLA correlation pattern of the air puff trajectory is reactivated more around post-NREM ripples than around pre-NREM ripples.
The hippocampus-BLA correlation pattern of the safe trajectory is not significantly more reactivated around post-NREM ripples than around pre-NREM ripples (pyramidal pairs).
The post-NREM minus pre-NREM change in reactivation strength at the ripple peak is larger for the air puff trajectory than for the safe trajectory (pyramidal pairs).

With all cell types included, both the air puff and the safe trajectory patterns are more reactivated around post-NREM than pre-NREM ripples, and the post minus pre difference does not differ significantly between the two trajectories.
Firing rates of BLA cells do not differ significantly between the safe and the air puff trajectories.
The occurrence rate of SPW-Rs does not differ between pre-NREM and post-NREM.

For the 2.5% most strongly contributing hippocampus-BLA pairs, the pre-run to post-run change in correlation correlates with the pre-NREM to post-NREM change (r = 0.27), but not for the 2.5% least contributing pairs.
The coupling between run and sleep correlation changes holds when the most and least contributing quartiles of pairs are compared (r = 0.13 against r = 0.013).

The proportion of cells with grid structure depended on layer. Most well-separated layer II cells were grid cells (66 of 108), against a smaller proportion in layers III (78 of 223), V (17 of 110) and VI (42 of 186).
Grid cells with tessellating firing fields were found in all four principal cell layers of MEC (II, III, V and VI).
Among deeper-layer cells with periodic firing, the range of gridness did not differ from that of layer II cells.
All 203 grid cells had stable periodic firing patterns within and between trials.

In every layer grid spacing increased with distance from the postrhinal border, by a factor of 1.5 to 2 over the sampled range, with the densest spacing (about 35 to 40 cm) near the border; the correlations (0.46 to 0.94) were significant in every layer and did not differ between layers.
In every layer grid field size increased with distance from the postrhinal border (0.44 ≤ r ≤ 0.94, all P < 0.005), with the smallest fields (about 500 cm2) near the border.
In all layers the spatial phase of nearby grid cells was distributed (their vertices were offset), while grid orientation was consistent across simultaneously recorded cells.
No head-direction cells were found in layer II, whereas a large proportion of the cells in layers III to VI had directional preferences (273 of 385 cells, counting conjunctive cells).
Beneath layer II, head-direction cells were usually recorded together with grid cells.
The breadth of directional tuning did not differ between layers III, V and VI (mean U2 18.2, 25.2 and 18.3; mean angular standard deviation 55.9, 52.2 and 58.2 degrees; P > 0.05).
The entire range of head directions was represented by the preferred directions of head-direction cells in each of layers III, V and VI.
Preferred directions of simultaneously recorded head-direction cells in the same area were widely distributed; in most ensembles of five or more cells (8 of 12) they showed no significant clustering.
Directional tuning curves were always stable across the two trials (circular correlation r = 0.84, P < 0.001).
In head-direction cells, firing rose from a low background rate (typically below 0.5 Hz) to a high maximum rate (5 to 40 Hz) when the rat's head faced the cell's range of directions.

The proportion of grid cells with conjunctive head-direction tuning depended on layer (66% in layer III, 90% in layer V, 28% in layer VI, none in layer II); the difference was significant across all four layers and across layers III to VI.

Grid cells and head-direction cells formed overlapping populations; the joint distribution of gridness and directional tuning was continuous, with some grid cells directionally tuned and some head-direction cells having grid structure.
Directional tuning of conjunctive cells did not differ from that of pure head-direction cells (mean U2 18.0 against 19.4, P > 0.05).

Cells with different degrees of gridness and directionality always responded as a coherent ensemble to rotation of a polarizing cue card; in the example (layer VI, Fig. 3F and fig. S8), a grid cell and four head-direction cells were recorded together, the head-direction cells all rotated 90 degrees with the card, and the grid cell's map is shown following it.
Regression showed a consistent positive speed-rate relation in nearly all grid cells (141 of 150), head-direction cells (153 of 220) and conjunctive cells (45 of 53).
The slope of the speed-rate regression was steeper for conjunctive cells and grid cells than for head-direction cells, and did not differ between conjunctive and grid cells.

The intercept of the speed-rate regression was positive in all cells but one (422 of 423), and mean rates at the lowest speeds (0 to 3 cm/s) were about 2.3 to 2.5 Hz in each cell class, so firing persisted during brief stops.
The Kiloscope records thousands of neurons at once in a freely behaving mouse; in the mouse with the best expression EXTRACT gave 2,948 footprints.
In the mouse with the most footprints, manual curation leaves 2,382 putative neurons.
The Kiloscope was used in four mice, and more than a thousand neurons were recorded at once in more than one of them; EXTRACT gave 2,948, 401, 1,029 and 112 footprints.
The Featherscope recorded hundreds of neurons in juvenile songbirds; curation gave 177, 46 and 225 footprints in three birds.
Birds carrying the Featherscope sang 3,861 to 23,545 syllables per day, within the normal range.
The activity of almost all LMAN footprints during song shows the sparse random bursting seen in earlier recordings of LMAN.
The Kiloscope's field of view is 4.8 x 3.6 mm (about 4 mm in the abstract).
The two microscopes weigh 1.4 g (Kiloscope, large field of view) and 1.0 g (Featherscope, 1.0 mm field of view).
Images of a USAF 1951 target resolve elements of 2.19 um line width with the Featherscope and 4.38 um with the Kiloscope, and 2.2 um with Kiloscope optics on a sensor with 1.4 um pixels.
The onboard analog-to-digital converter records test tones with a root-mean-square residual of 0.2% of full scale.
Lateral shifts of the image due to the mouse's movement are small, with a root-mean-square displacement of 0.13 pixels (0.7 um).

Linear SVM decoders trained on half of the data decode the mouse's combined quadrant and movement direction on the other half at an accuracy at least three times chance, above that of decoders trained on shuffled data.
Decoding accuracy depends on the number of footprints used, with P at or below 2.7 x 10^-4 (Mann-Whitney U) for every decoder size from 2 to 2,048 footprints.
Decoders built from the 32 footprints closest to a point decode quadrant and direction with accuracies that differ substantially across the field of view.
The correlated activity in each NMF component is driven by footprints spread across the field of view.
Position within the maze can be decoded with octant resolution from the activity, above decoders trained on shuffled data.
Decoders built from the 32 footprints closest to a point decode octant position significantly in parts of the field of view, with accuracy that varies across it.
Some footprints have activity localized to subregions of the maze.

In flight, after an initial period, hippocampal place cells on the Escher staircase showed normal, spatially specific firing, with spatial information per spike not different from the same rats' preflight cells.

For rat 2, the spatial information per spike of the 16 active cells recorded on the Escher staircase on flight day 9 (1.13 +/- 0.09 bits) did not differ significantly from that of its 19 active preflight cells (1.12 +/- 0.08 bits), by Mann-Whitney test.
For rat 1, the mean spatial information of its 21 active cells on flight day 9 (1.19 +/- 0.09 bits) did not differ significantly from its preflight cells (1.37 +/- 0.10 bits, n = 28).
For rat 3, the mean spatial information of all 7 active place cells on flight day 4 (1.12 +/- 0.27 bits, session 2) was not different from its preflight cells (1.48 +/- 0.11 bits, n = 24).
On the first experience of the Escher staircase on flight day 4, place cells of rats 1 and 2 showed abnormal patterns of spatial selectivity, which differed between the two rats.

For rat 3 on flight day 4, most of the 7 cells kept the same firing fields in a third session that followed the second immediately; the fourth cell lost its field, and a few other cells gained a field in session 3.
Some cells had place fields only when the rat moved counterclockwise through a location, showing the direction selectivity seen on such tracks on Earth.
Hippocampal EEG showed normal theta rhythm during active locomotion, in all rats on flight days 4 and 9.
Hippocampal EEG showed normal sharp waves and ripples during quiet inactivity in the sleeping pouch, on both flight days.
Hippocampal cells formed distinct, reliable representations of position on the three orthogonal surfaces of the Escher staircase in microgravity.
Pcdh-gamma proteins (Pcdh-gamma-GFP in fusg mice) are present in all five retinal layers and in all six retinal cell types (photoreceptors, horizontal, bipolar, amacrine, RGCs and Mueller glia).
Pcdh-gamma is present in the IPL, neuroblast layer and RGC axons at P0, appears in the developing OPL by P7, and reaches the adult pattern by P14.

Pcdh-gammas are present in pre- and postsynaptic compartments of rod and cone synapses in the OPL, though little is in horizontal cell varicosities, and at many but not only synaptic sites in the IPL.
Chx10-Cre recombination is extensive (above 90%) in the INL and ONL, while about half of the cells in the GCL are not recombined.
At P18, retinas lacking Pcdh-gammas in Chx10-Cre mutants are properly laminated but about 25% thinner than controls, from a selective reduction of about 40% in INL and IPL thickness.
The INL and IPL are thinned to the same extent in Chx10-Cre;Pcdh-gamma fcon3/fcon3 and fdel/fdel retinas, so fcon3 is functionally a null.

In peripheral Pax6alpha-Cre;Pcdh-gamma fcon3/fcon3 retina at P18, bipolar, amacrine and retinal ganglion cells are reduced by 45 to 65%, Mueller glia by about 20%, while horizontal cells and photoreceptors differ little from controls.
Mutant and control retinas do not differ perinatally (E17.5 to P3); INL and IPL are thinner in mutants by P7, about 40% thinner by P14, and change little over the following months.
Apoptosis (cleaved caspase-3) follows the normal time course but is significantly higher in mutant than control retinas during the first postnatal weeks.

In central retina of Pax6alpha-Cre;Pcdh-gamma fcon3/fcon3 mice, where only the Pax6alpha amacrines lack Pcdh-gammas, these amacrines are 58% fewer than in controls, a loss equivalent to that in peripheral retina.

Loss of Pcdh-gammas from Pax6alpha amacrines in central retina does not affect the survival of bipolar cells, horizontal cells, Mueller glia or starburst amacrines, but causes a small (about 15%) significant loss of Brn3a-positive RGCs.
In Pcdh-gamma mutant retina at P18, processes of all ten examined amacrine and bipolar subtypes are arrayed in their appropriate IPL sublaminae, though with occasional gaps.

Deleting Bax rescues the neurons that die in Pcdh-gamma mutant retina; INL and GCL thickness and Chx10+ bipolar number do not differ between Pcdh-gamma-positive and -negative Bax-/- retinas, and the IPL expands to the Bax-/- thickness.
Synapse density in the IPL and OPL (PNA or Bassoon staining) does not differ significantly between Pcdh-gamma-positive and Pcdh-gamma-negative Bax-/- retinas.
Neurons rescued from death by Bax deletion target their processes to the appropriate IPL sublaminae as specifically as in Pcdh-gamma single mutants, and the gaps of the single mutants are absent.
Figure 9C to 9H report 115 RGCs from mutant retinas and 143 RGCs from control retinas.
RGCs in mutant and control retinas show a similar variety of responses to small flashing spots, including sustained and transient ON, OFF and ON-OFF responses.
The proportions of ON- and OFF-dominated responses are the same in mutant and control retinas.
Mutant RGCs respond to very dim flashes, which excite only rods, and to bright flashes, which mainly excite cones, so both rod and cone pathways function.
Both ON and ON-OFF direction-selective RGCs are found in mutant retinas.
Receptive field centre size varies greatly among RGCs, but its distribution is similar in control and mutant retinas.
Some control and mutant RGCs have receptive field surrounds of opposite sign to the centre, so lateral inhibition functions in mutant circuits.
The time course of the light response is significantly slower in mutant retina, measured as the time to peak of the temporal integration function a(t).
Mutant RGCs fire at much lower rates than control RGCs in response to flickering gratings.
In a Linear-Nonlinear model fitted to the flicker responses, the response threshold of mutant RGCs is unaltered.
In the same Linear-Nonlinear model, the gain of mutant RGCs is reduced.

Unilateral photoinhibition of ALM during the delay epoch biases licking to the ipsilateral side, raising performance on ipsilateral (lick left for left ALM) trials and lowering it on contralateral trials, with the reverse pattern for right ALM.
The ipsilateral bias is smaller when ALM is photoinhibited during the sample epoch than during the delay epoch.
1,408 single units were recorded from left ALM in 19 mice over 99 sessions; by spike width 124 were fast-spiking, 1,245 putative pyramidal and 39 intermediate.
73% (912 of 1,245) of putative pyramidal neurons distinguished the trial types in at least one trial epoch.
Among selective neurons, 219 of 912 had selective preparatory activity only, 389 peri-movement activity only, and 304 both.
Selectivity emerges in the sample epoch, increases through the delay epoch and peaks at the beginning of the response epoch.

Individual neuron responses are dynamic although selectivity is stable at the level of the population (Fig. 2c, bottom, population selectivity and the correlation of the population response with that at the go cue).
On error trials ALM activity predicts the direction the mouse licked, so most selective neurons switch their trial-type preference relative to correct trials.

Contra-preferring and ipsi-preferring neurons are present in equal proportions in left ALM, and the overall spike count shows no significant contralateral bias (P = 0.13; 8% spike rate modulation across all task-selective neurons).
Fast-spiking neurons have higher baseline firing rates and are less selective than putative pyramidal neurons.

Of 73 neurons antidromically activated from pyramidal tract axons, 45 passed the collision test (PT neurons), 22 failed and 6 could not be tested; of 134 activated from IT axons, 27 passed (IT neurons), 106 failed and 1 could not be tested.

PT neurons had shorter antidromic latencies (mean 2.7 ms) than IT neurons (4.6 ms), and both had smaller jitter (0.1 and 0.2 ms) than activated neurons that failed collision (latency 8.3 and 9.8 ms, jitter 2.8 and 2.4 ms).
Both PT and IT neurons show preparatory and movement-related activity.
Contra-preferring neurons outnumber ipsi-preferring neurons among PT neurons (P < 0.05, bootstrap) but not among IT neurons (P = 0.74).
Contralateral population selectivity emerges in PT neurons from 570 ms before the response epoch (34% spike rate modulation, P < 0.05), but not in IT neurons (-19%, P = 0.40).

In two-photon imaging of ALM (59 fields of view, 4 mice), 58% of cells (2,740 of 4,706) were task-related and 57% of those (1,575) trial-type selective, with a slight majority of contra-preferring cells (61%, 971 of 1,575).

Contra- and ipsi-preferring neurons are found in all fields of view and are spatially intermingled; nearest-neighbour selectivity and same-type distances do not differ from shuffled data (P = 0.34 and P = 0.61).

Among layer 5 neurons, about a quarter of labelled PT (182 of 534) and IT (174 of 542) neurons were selective; 67% of selective PT neurons were contra-preferring (P < 0.001, binomial test) but only 48% of IT neurons, and PT neurons were more often contra-preferring than IT neurons (P < 0.001, chi-squared test).
The reaction time after the go cue was 61.1 +/- 10.5 ms (mean +/- s.d. across mice).
Subthreshold photostimulation of PT neurons during the delay epoch biases licking contralaterally; in left ALM it lowers performance on lick left trials, and the reverse holds for right ALM.
Stimulation of PT neurons during the sample epoch also causes a significant contralateral bias.
The effect of PT photostimulation on licking depends monotonically on laser power.
Subthreshold photostimulation of IT neurons changes behaviour, but the changes vary across mice and depend non-monotonically on laser intensity.

High-power unilateral photostimulation of ALM PT or IT neurons triggers contralateral licking with short latency, also in untrained mice, and in trained mice produces premature licking in the contralateral direction; vibrissal motor cortex stimulation does not cause licking.

Subthreshold sample-epoch stimulation of PT neurons, with simultaneous recordings (2 mice, 8 sessions, 91 neurons), changes ALM activity and causes a directional bias that persists for seconds after the photostimulus ends.

Retrograde tracers in the ipsilateral pontine nucleus and the contralateral ALM label non-overlapping populations of PT and IT neurons (under 4% double-labelled, 2 mice), intermingled in layer 5B; ALM PT neurons project to the contralateral intermediate reticular nucleus, which is presynaptic to the hypoglossal nucleus.

1012 single units were recorded in left ALM during behaviour in 58 sessions (20 unilateral, 38 bilateral experiment sessions); by spike width 72 were fast-spiking, 890 putative pyramidal, and 50 intermediate and excluded.
Most putative pyramidal neurons distinguished trial types (634 of 890); 176 in the sample epoch, 337 in the delay epoch and 493 in the response epoch.
Unilateral photoinhibition of ALM (0.5 s) ending at the go cue caused an ipsilateral response bias.
Unilateral photoinhibition ending at least 0.3 s before the go cue had minimal behavioural effects.

Performance was not significantly affected when photoinhibition (0.5 s or 1.3 s) ended more than 0.3 s before the go cue, and 0.5 s photoinhibition just before the go cue had an effect similar to photoinhibition over the whole delay epoch.
Neurons whose spike rates decreased during the delay epoch also recovered after unilateral photoinhibition, returning to the time-matched control trajectory and not decaying to the end-point rate.
Within 400 ms after unilateral photoinhibition, spike rates became indistinguishable from control in 90% of neurons; 10% retained a sustained change.

After unilateral photoinhibition ALM neurons recovered more than 80% of their control selectivity within about 0.5 s; recovery times were 373 ms (sample), 510 ms (early delay) and 327 ms (late delay).
After transient photoactivation of layer 5 intratelencephalic neurons, ALM selectivity recovered on a time course similar to recovery after photoinhibition.
Photoactivation during the sample epoch excited 19% and suppressed 22% of neurons; during the late delay epoch it excited 15% and suppressed 17%.

Ipsilateral and bilateral photoinhibition reduced the activity of putative pyramidal neurons by more than 90%, similarly in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP and PV x ReaChR mice; contralateral photoinhibition had little effect on the average rate.
Photoinhibition with one laser spot silenced activity in a cortical area of 1 mm radius at half-maximum, through all layers.
No rebound excitation was detected on average after photoinhibition offset; a small fraction of neurons showed rebound, balanced by weak sustained inhibition in a larger fraction.
Unilateral photoinhibition in the early delay epoch only slightly reduced performance (one spot 70.3%, four spots 67.7%).
Bilateral photoinhibition degraded performance severely (two spots 58.0%, eight spots 51.4%, near chance), more than four-spot unilateral photoinhibition.
Bilateral photoinhibition biased movements inconsistently across mice and sessions, toward lick left in some and lick right in others.

After ipsilateral (one spot) photoinhibition spike rate (more than 90%) and selectivity (more than 80%) recovered within 600 ms; contralateral photoinhibition hardly affected activity; after bilateral photoinhibition spike rates recovered on average but selectivity did not.
Selectivity recovered to 80% of control 538 ms after ipsilateral and 192 ms after contralateral photoinhibition, and did not recover after bilateral photoinhibition.

Bilateral photoinhibition with one spot per side changed selectivity more persistently than unilateral photoinhibition with four spots; selectivity recovered to 80% of control 490 ms after ipsilateral and 235 ms after contralateral four-spot photoinhibition, and did not recover after bilateral one-spot photoinhibition; recovery after unilateral photoinhibition was less robust with larger photoinhibition (Extended Data Fig. 7e).

Trajectory separation along cd at the end of the delay was 0.80 in control, 0.64 after ipsilateral and 0.68 after contralateral four-spot photoinhibition, and 0.54 after bilateral one-spot photoinhibition.
The direction of the lick right minus lick left difference vector was stable over the sample and delay epochs (correlation 0.61 between late sample and late delay).

Projection on cd captured 65.6% of population selectivity and 36.4% of task-related activity variance over the sample and delay epochs; modes 1 to 5 together captured 98.5% of variance and 95.8% of selectivity.

Along cd, trajectories recovered after ipsilateral photoinhibition (ROC 0.73 against 0.76 in control) and were little changed by contralateral photoinhibition (0.74), but were permanently altered by bilateral photoinhibition (0.58).
During photoinhibition trajectory separation along cd fell to 0.54 (ipsilateral), 0.64 (contralateral) and 0.54 (bilateral), against 0.72 in control.
Activity along cd predicts the upcoming movement trial by trial; deviations toward the lick right trajectory predict more lick right responses, and vice versa.
A persistent mode, built to capture the sustained effect of ipsilateral perturbation, stays altered past movement onset but neither discriminates trial type nor predicts behaviour on control trials.
A ramping mode capturing most remaining variance shows non-selective ramping in the delay epoch, does not predict behaviour, and is resistant to unilateral and bilateral perturbation.
Even after bilateral photoinhibition destroys average selectivity, single-trial activity along cd predicts the upcoming movement.
In each session the behavioural bias after bilateral photoinhibition followed the side of the control trajectory that the perturbed cd trajectory ended closer to.
Reaction times were faster on trials whose cd trajectory was far from the decision boundary at the go cue.
The recovery along cd after unilateral perturbation does not depend on the window used to compute cd (first or last 400 ms of the delay epoch).
Bisecting the ALM corpus callosum did not affect performance on control trials.

After callosotomy, performance became highly sensitive to unilateral (one spot) photoinhibition, with a significant interaction between callosotomy and photoinhibition, and dropped to the level of bilateral photoinhibition in control mice.
Preparatory activity after callosotomy was similar to control; 254 of 496 putative pyramidal neurons were selective.

After callosotomy, ipsilateral photoinhibition left spike rates recovered on average but selectivity failed to recover; contralateral photoinhibition selectivity recovered in 217 ms; bilateral did not recover.
After callosotomy, selectivity along cd was reduced following ipsilateral photoinhibition.

Monolithic network models (integrator, integrator with corrective feedback, trained random recurrent networks) do not recover the unperturbed trajectory after transient silencing of half their neurons.

Modular networks of two coupled modules (attractor, integrator, trained recurrent network) recover after silencing of one module; the modular attractor drifts to a random fixed point when both modules are silenced.

Across the 52 sessions the fraction of trials correct was 0.740 +- 0.086 (mean +- s.d.).

Spike rates were low in both whisking (0.67 spikes/s) and non-whisking (0.23 spikes/s) periods.

L5 neurons near C2 have much higher spike rates than L4 neurons, with more diverse touch responses.
Modulation by whisking phase does not differ between L4 neurons inside and outside C2.
L4 neurons, inside and outside C2, are more modulated by whisking phase than L5 neurons.
Across L4 neurons, inside and outside C2, spike rate does not change between whisking and non-whisking periods.
