Pooling the activity of only 15 L4 C2 neurons, integrated over 10 ms, is enough to detect 95% of touches.
Touch detection by neurons from surrounding barrels, outside C2, is poor.

A naive Bayes decoder reading 200 L4 C2 neurons integrated over 10 ms decodes the time elapsed since touch with high precision, a minimum uncertainty of 0.55 ms (95% confidence) at 10 ms after touch onset.
Even 1000 L4 neurons give only a rough estimate of whisking phase, a resolution of 24 deg in C2 and 33 deg outside C2 at d' = 1 (76% correct discrimination).

Touch response magnitude of L4 C2 neurons is strongly modulated by touch order, whisker velocity before touch and maximum curvature during touch, with mean modulation indices of 0.71 +- 0.25, 0.71 +- 0.27 and 0.72 +- 0.23.
Across cells, responsiveness to pre-touch velocity and to maximum curvature covary strongly (r = 0.80), and responsiveness to touch order is somewhat less correlated with both (r = 0.70 and 0.65).
The clustering of touches into five groups finds subsets with significantly less variability in touch properties than random samples of touches.
Across L4 C2 neurons, the Fano factor following touch drops below one, lying close to the binomial limit (the theoretical minimum) for most cells.
The low Fano factor after touch cannot be explained by a Poisson process with a 2.3 ms refractory period and rates matched to each neuron.
Counting spikes over the whole sample epoch, ignoring the millisecond structure of behavior, gives a very large Fano factor of 6.57 +- 5.41 (mean +- s.d. over L4 C2 cells).
Counting spikes in random 38 ms windows, as many per trial as there are touches, gives a Fano factor of 1.59 +- 0.49.
Counting spikes in 38 ms windows aligned to touch onset (after a 6 ms latency) gives a Fano factor of 1.37 +- 0.74.
A narrower 10 ms window after touch reduces the Fano factor to 0.73 +- 0.19.
Computed only across similar touches, the 10 ms Fano factor falls further to 0.54 +- 0.27, so that L4 responses to touch are almost noiseless.
L4 neurons fire few spikes during whisker movements, on average fewer than 0.15 spikes per whisk cycle, which hinders decoding of whisking phase.
Mice licked early, during the delay epoch, on 13.3% +- 10% of trials, and these trials were not analysed.
Two-photon imaging covered 12 locations in 6 mice with 8.8 +- 2.6 planes per location, 105 planes in all, each imaged for 92 +- 26 trials at 73% +- 9% correct, 3 +- 1 planes per session.
Each imaged plane had on average 34 +- 13 CR, 36 +- 14 CL, 12 +- 5 ER and 10 +- 4 EL trials.
15,431 neurons were imaged across 6 mice, 8,837 in ALM and 6,594 in MM.
A large fraction of neurons distinguished between trial types, 23% in MM (1,523 of 6,594) and 31% in ALM (2,754 of 8,837).
The selectivity of most neurons can be attributed to one of the three coefficients, especially early in the trial, so most neurons mainly encode one behavioural variable at a time.

Different neurons coded for lick direction in different epochs, some during the sample and delay epochs before licking, some during the response epoch, and some after the mouse stopped consuming water.

Many object-location-selective neurons were selective during the sample epoch, and a subset coded object location mainly in the delay epoch after the pole was removed, some up to the end of the delay.
Outcome-selective neurons typically became selective after the answer lick; some preferred correct and others error trials, and some kept the outcome long after the trial ended.
Most neurons with mixed selectivity were seen during the response epoch; a subset responded in only one trial type and a few switched the variable they coded during the trial.
During the sample and early delay epochs, object location was represented mainly in MM.
Neurons selective for lick direction appeared first in the deep layers of ALM, early in the delay epoch.
Lick-direction selectivity, in number of neurons and strength, kept increasing and spread across ALM layers and to a minor extent into MM, peaking after the go cue.
Outcome-selective neurons were seen only during the response epoch, scattered roughly uniformly through ALM and MM; mixed neurons were also seen mainly in the response epoch in both areas.

Throughout the trial preparatory activity, as the fraction of lick-direction-selective neurons or the average coding coefficient, was most pronounced in ALM, while object location selectivity was mainly limited to MM.
Optogenetic inactivation during the delay epoch affected lick direction more in ALM than in MM.

In wide-field imaging, activity during the sample and early delay was most pronounced in MM, and spread forward and laterally to ALM as the delay progressed; after the response it rose across much of motor and somatosensory cortex.
Early wide-field activity in MM was contralateral to the whiskers touching the object, and the later ALM activity was in both hemispheres.
In two-photon imaging, the peak of activity shifted from MM to ALM over the delay.
IT neurons were found in both superficial and deep layers, PT neurons only in deep layers; 719 PT and 2,631 IT neurons were imaged in three mice.
In ALM the strongest lick direction selectivity was in the deep layers, where PT and IT neurons were intermingled.
During the delay epoch, ALM PT neurons showed a bias toward contralateral (lick right) selectivity.
In ALM, lick direction selectivity (|beta|) was stronger and earlier in PT than in IT neurons, with an onset difference of 1.4 +- 0.6 s (p < 0.01, bootstrap).

MM neurons showed strong object location selectivity in superficial and deep layers and in PT and IT cells, PT cells particularly in the early delay; neither PT nor IT neurons in MM showed prominent lick direction selectivity before licking.
MM neurons were more active in posterior trials, when the pole was within reach of the whiskers, than in anterior trials.
Overall, neurons preferring error trials outnumbered those preferring correct trials.
Coding is mainly determined by cortical location; cortical area (ALM against MM) and cell depth explain most of the variance of selectivity, more than projection type.
Whisker movements were similar across the four trial types, so neurons coding whisker movement were likely classed as non-selective.
Even in ALM, less than 20% of PT or IT cells displayed lick direction selectivity at any given time, and the onset timing was variable.

Three subjects with high-density ECoG (two left, one right hemisphere) read aloud CV syllables made of 18 or 19 consonants followed by /a/, /i/ or /u/, each CV produced 15 to 100 times, with the microphone recorded with the ECoG at 3052 Hz.
About 30 active vSMC electrodes were found per subject during syllable articulation, an electrode being active when its high-gamma z-score changed by more than 2 for any syllable.

In one subject, dorsal electrodes (e124, e108) were active for /b/ (lips), mid vSMC electrodes (e129, e133, e105) for /d/ (front tongue), and a more ventral electrode (e104) was most active for /g/ (back tongue).

Fricatives with different tongue-tip constriction locations (/th/, /s/, /sh/) engaged different electrodes; front-tongue consonants of different manner (/l/, /n/, /d/) engaged overlapping electrodes with different magnitudes; for /ja/, /ji/, /ju/ the activity was similar before the C-V transition, while a dorsal electrode was active during /u/ only.
Each articulator is represented across vSMC; the lip representation lies in dorsal vSMC and the tongue representation is spread over its ventral part.

Across subjects the articulator representations are laid out from dorsal to ventral as larynx, lips, jaw, tongue and larynx, with a laryngeal representation at the dorsal end of vSMC as well as a ventral one.
Electrodes with similar articulator representations lie closer together than chance; the mean spatial autocorrelation within 3 mm is 0.45 against 0.26 for permuted electrode positions.
Each articulator's representation lies in a more consistent place across subjects than chance (mean cross-subject correlation within 3 mm 0.195 against 0.031).

Within each subject, adjacent articulator representations (larynx-tongue, tongue-jaw, jaw-lips) are spatially sequenced along the dorsal-ventral axis, with positive cross-correlation on one side of the diagonal (0.099) and negative on the other (-0.102), both beyond chance.

The observed map is neither a perfect linear somatotopy nor random; the mean distance between electrodes preferring the same articulator (11.06 mm) and between those preferring different ones (15.11 mm) lie between the two null models.
Single electrodes show a clear preferred articulator and also carry weights for other articulators.

Articulator correlations follow a staggered sequence consistent across subjects; lip and tongue correlations begin well before sound onset, jaw and larynx align to the C-V transition, and the high and back tongue vowel features peak near the vowel midpoint (~250 ms).
Onset latencies of the articulator model fit do not differ between electrodes just anterior and just posterior to the central sulcus (within 10 mm), nor across the guenon.
The cortical state-space has nine spatial PCs in every subject, the eigenvalues falling fast up to the ninth and slowly after, together explaining about 60% of the variance.

At the consonant time (-25 ms) k-means clustering of the cortical state-space groups syllables by major oral articulator (labial, coronal, dorsal), and three clusters are more parsimonious than two or four (mean silhouette 0.47 against 0.45 and 0.43).

Clusters of the cortical state-space match the major articulators at the consonant time (median co-clustering 0.50 against 0.32 by chance) and the vowels at the vowel time (0.65 against 0.37), across subjects.

Hierarchical clustering of the state-space puts the major oral articulator (dorsal, labial, coronal) at the top tier for consonants, superordinate to constriction location, with constriction degree only at the lowest level; for vowels the first split is lip rounding (/u/ against /a/ and /i/).

Over early times (-375 to 120 ms) constriction location correlates with the state-space structure more than constriction degree, which correlates more than the upcoming vowel; over later times (125 to 620 ms) vowel configuration correlates most.
Cluster separability, averaged over subjects, rises from about -300 ms and peaks about 200 ms before the C-V transition for consonants, and rises from about 50 ms and peaks at +250 ms for vowels.
Cluster separability and the correlation of the state-space with phonetic features are tightly linked over time for consonants and vowels in each subject (R2 0.42 to 0.98, all P < 1e-10).

Consonant and vowel representations occupy distinct regions of the state-space; consonant-vowel distances are larger than consonant-consonant and vowel-vowel distances, and consonant-consonant distances are larger than vowel-vowel ones.
The first three PCs are weighted toward tongue over lips, and toward lips over jaw and larynx, while jaw and larynx do not differ.
In monkey V, 112 neurons were studied before MPTP and 159 after, of which 49 and 54 were PTNs and 31 and 48 CSNs; three neurons in all were activated from both the peduncle and the putamen.
In monkey L, 57 of 115 neurons before MPTP and 35 of 73 after responded to torque perturbations of the wrist, and the monkey L responses enter all pooled results.

Before torque onset, the firing rate of M1 neurons was lower after MPTP, because PTN rates fell (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001) while CSN rates did not change (p = 0.5). In monkey V the rates were 12.6 and 8.9 spikes/s for all cells, 20.3 and 14.8 for PTNs, and 3.5 and 3.4 for CSNs, before and after MPTP.
Before MPTP, PTNs fired much faster than CSNs at rest (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001).
PTN antidromic latencies did not change after MPTP (1.9 ms, p = 0.9), while CSN latencies were longer (5.1 against 6.1 ms, p < 0.05/3).
The detection threshold, p < 0.01 divided by 5 independent comparisons, holds the chance of a false response over the 200 ms epoch near 0.01.
In monkey V, 84 of 112 M1 neurons (75%) were torque-related before MPTP and 108 of 159 (68%) after; for PTNs 27 of 49 (55%) and 37 of 54 (68%); for CSNs 14 of 31 (45%) and 10 of 48 (21%).
MPTP did not change the fraction of torque-related neurons, in M1, in PTNs or in CSNs (chi-square, p > 0.05/3).
PTNs responded to torque more often than CSNs (68% against 31% over both monkeys, chi-square 32.3, p < 0.001).
About half of the torque-related cells (124 of 284, 44%) responded to only one direction of rotation.
Most torque responses were increases in firing (86% of M1 responses before and 88% after MPTP; 70% and 75% for PTNs), and MPTP did not change the PTN balance (chi-square 0.1, p = 0.7).

The magnitude of torque responses did not differ before and after MPTP, for M1 cells or for PTNs, by any of three measures (mean change, maximum change, area; Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Mann-Whitney, all p > 0.15).

In monkey V, the mean response magnitudes were 42.4 and 37.9 spikes/s for M1 flexion responses, 50.9 and 42.6 for M1 extension responses, 33.4 and 26.1 for PTN flexion and 38.8 and 29.3 for PTN extension responses, before and after MPTP.

Response latencies were shorter after MPTP for M1 cells and for PTNs, for flexion and extension (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, all p < 0.05). In monkey V the means were 39.2 and 34.6 ms (M1 flexion), 40.4 and 33.4 ms (M1 extension), 43.9 and 35.5 ms (PTN flexion) and 44.4 and 36.7 ms (PTN extension), before and after MPTP.
The latency shortening was not a history effect; latencies did not correlate with the days of training (monkey V Spearman |rho| = 0.02, p = 0.85).

Torque-evoked increases in PTN firing were briefer after MPTP; the FWHM fell from 73 to 50 ms over both monkeys (Mann-Whitney, p < 0.05 for each direction). In monkey V the PTN FWHM was 97 and 52 ms for flexion and 57 and 41 ms for extension, before and after MPTP.

Directional selectivity fell after MPTP; reciprocal and unidirectional responses became less common and bidirectional and non-directional ones more common (by about 10% of torque-related M1 cells; chi-square 22.2, p < 0.001).
In monkey V the mean DSI of torque-related cells was 0.72 and 0.66 for M1, 0.73 and 0.75 for PTNs and 0.81 and 0.83 for CSNs, before and after MPTP.
The loss of selectivity was not due to resting rates, as pre-torque rates did not differ between directional categories (one-way ANOVA, F = 0.77, p = 0.46).
After MPTP, torque-induced displacements were slower and smaller; mean peak velocity fell by 16.2% and amplitude by 6.6% (ANOVA, F > 515 and F > 49).
The latency of torque-induced displacements did not change after MPTP (F < 0.2, p > 0.05).
The long-latency (m2, 41 to 80 ms) EMG response of the stretched triceps was larger after MPTP (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, p < 0.05).
The total duration of EMG responses to torque increased after MPTP, from 57 +/- 6 to 79 +/- 3 ms (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, p < 0.001).
The latency of the earliest EMG responses did not change after MPTP (p > 0.05).
The short-latency m1 component (15 to 40 ms) was poorly formed and generally much smaller than the m2 component.

In sessions with equivalent torque-induced velocities (130 to 200 deg/s), MPTP did not change the magnitude of responses (Mann-Whitney, p = 0.19 for flexion and 0.46 for extension, with 24 and 33 flexion and 22 and 31 extension responses).

Across sessions, the mean PTN response latency did not correlate with the peak velocity of the torque-induced movement (|rho| < 0.18) or with the m2 EMG response (|rho| < 0.26; Spearman, p > 0.05 with threshold 0.05/4).
Trial by trial, PTN response latencies did not correlate with the peak velocity or the m2 EMG response (Spearman |rho| < 0.34, p > 0.05).
About 99% of Anxa1+ DANs co-express Aldh1a1, while about 40% of Aldh1a1+ DANs express Anxa1.
Anxa1+ DANs lie in the ventral SNc, with a small fraction in the VTA; they are lateral in anterior SNc and progressively more medial in posterior planes.
In MP-early mice the number of Anxa1+ DANs in the ventral tier of the SNc and the fraction of Anxa1+ DANs among Th+ SNc cells are significantly reduced, while the VTA Anxa1+ DANs are not reduced.
In iPSC-derived DANs from PD patients with SNCA triplication, ANXA1 mRNA is significantly reduced against healthy donors, while ALDH1A1 is not significantly altered.
After a mild unilateral 6-OHDA lesion, the Anxa1+ fraction of SNc DANs is significantly lower on the lesioned side than on the intact side.
The low-dose 6-OHDA model gives a partial loss of about 50% of Th+ DANs.
In 24-week-old cAtg7KO mice with Lewy body-like inclusions the SNc shows a specific, significant reduction of Anxa1+ DANs.
In the 6-OHDA and cAtg7KO models the Anxa1+ fraction in the VTA is not significantly changed.
Anxa1+ DANs extend long dendrites deep into the anterior and medial SNr, with a dendron-like structure in anterior SNr.
Anxa1+ DANs project densely to the most dorsal domain of the CP, with a density gradient enriched anteromedially, and sparsely to the core and medial shell of the ACB.
Optogenetic activation of Anxa1+ DANs evokes DA release in the dCP at varying intensities, and the evoked release in the cCP has a lower amplitude.
Anxa1+ DAN axons in dorsolateral CP are enriched in MOR+ striosomes and the subcallosal streak, suggesting a nigro-striato-nigral loop.
After low-dose 6-OHDA, degeneration of eYFP+ Anxa1+ SNc neurons is accompanied by near-complete loss of their eYFP+ axons in the dCP across the anteroposterior axis.
Anxa1+ and DAT+ axons in dCP ramp up before a water drop, peak at contact with it, and return quickly to baseline during water consumption.

DA release in dCP follows the same ramp-and-drop dynamics as Anxa1+ axons, while in cCP it shows a classical reward-related profile, ramping before contact and peaking during consumption before returning to baseline.

Against the baseline window, the legend lists three AUC changes, the second window of DAT GCaMP-dCP (p = 0.0308) and of dLight-cCP (p = 0.0028) and the third window of dLight-cCP (p = 0.0148), with only the dLight-cCP second window marked significant; the other groups and windows are not listed.
Optogenetic activation of DAT+ neurons strongly reinforces self-stimulation in the first two days, while activation of Anxa1+ DANs does not.

When the active port is reversed, DAT-ChRmine mice quickly switch to the newly active left port, while Anxa1-ChRmine mice develop no significant preference for the active port in the last reversal days.
Mice with silenced Anxa1+ DANs show no significant change in total nosepokes in the FR5 or PR stages.
Anxa1+ axonal activity in the dCP correlates positively with linear speed during open field exploration, above a shuffled control, and DA release in dCP shows a similar correlation.
DA release in the cCP correlates negatively with locomotion speed.
Unsupervised VAME analysis of open field pose identifies 37 kinematic motifs, grouped into action categories.
Anxa1+ axon activity is associated with the onset of high-speed motifs regardless of action type, as is DA in dCP, while DA in cCP rises strongly after the onset of low-speed motifs.
Across motifs, the onset AUC of Anxa1+ terminal activity correlates positively with that of dLight in dCP (R = 0.70) and negatively with that of dLight in cCP (R = -0.52).
The onset AUC of Anxa1+ terminal activity is highly correlated with mean motif linear speed across motifs (R = 0.83).
Anxa1-TeTx mice show moderate reductions in linear and angular speed in the open field, with a slight increase in immobility time.

The mild locomotor phenotype and acceleration distribution of Anxa1-silenced mice resemble the early-stage PD models (mild 6-OHDA, MP-early), consistent with a bradykinetic and not an akinetic/rigid profile.
In a PCA of motif usage, PC1 separates the groups by PD stage, with Anxa1-TeTx mice between the early and middle PD models, and PC2 separates middle-stage MitoPark mice from the others.
Walk and stationary motifs lie at opposite extremes of PC1 in the loading plot.
Motif PC1 values correlate negatively with mean motif speed (R = -0.762), while PC2 shows no significant correlation (R = -0.1494, p = 0.3772), nor do PC3 and PC4.
Anxa1-silenced mice show significant downregulation of five high-speed motifs (42, 34, 16, 0 and 25), not of all vigorous high-speed motifs.

Motifs 42 and 34 are reduced in all PD models; motifs 0 and 25 are reduced among the models only in middle-stage MitoPark mice; stationary motifs 3, 39, 27 and 28 are increased only in middle-stage MitoPark mice.

Anxa1+ DAN silencing has no major effect on the overall structure of motif sequences, but the reduced high-speed walk motifs form a small network of high-probability transitions (motif 0 to 16 to 34).
In the arrow maze, Anxa1-silenced mice show only a small decrease in linear speed on the fourth day and no change in immobility time.
Control mice learn to prefer the rewarded arm over four days, while Anxa1-silenced mice show no increase in preference for the rewarded arm.
Control mice improve task efficiency (reward relative to distance traveled) over the four days, while Anxa1-silenced mice do not.

Control mice improve reaching accuracy over four sessions; Anxa1-TeTx mice have normal accuracy in the first session but fail to improve, and Anxa1-Arch mice show reduced accuracy during the last three sessions with optogenetic inhibition.

On the real Neuropixels recording the six sorters return very different numbers of units: Tridesclous the fewest (187) and SpyKING Circus the most (628); HerdingSpikes2 210, Kilosort2 446, IronClust 233 and HDSort 317.
Of the 2031 units detected on the real recording, all six sorters agree on only 33, and two or more sorters agree on only 263.
For most sorters more than half of their units match no other sorter; IronClust and Tridesclous are the exceptions.
Matched units mostly agree closely: around 80% of the agreement scores of agreed-upon units are 0.8 or higher.

On a rat cortex Neuropixels recording (six sorters) and a mouse retina Biocam recording (the four sorters able to process it, HerdingSpikes2, Kilosort2, IronClust and HDSort) the sorters disagree as much as on the first recording.

On the simulated recording with 250 ground-truth units the sorters again return very different numbers of units: Tridesclous 189, HDSort 458, HerdingSpikes2 233, Kilosort2 415, IronClust 283 and SpyKING Circus 343.
Sorters trade precision against recall differently: HerdingSpikes2, SpyKING Circus and HDSort favour precision, IronClust recall, Kilosort2 scores well on both, and Tridesclous shows no bias.
Accuracy depends on the SNR of the ground-truth units for every sorter except Kilosort2, which reaches almost perfect accuracy on low-SNR units.
Kilosort2 scores higher than the other sorters for most ground-truth units.
Kilosort2 has the most well-detected units (245) but also many false positive (147) and redundant (21) units, and two overmerged units.

With Kilosort2's own curation, which removes units with an estimated contamination above 20%, false positive and redundant units are fewer but persist: 241 well detected, 93 false positive, 18 redundant and 2 overmerged.
Tridesclous detects very few false positive or redundant units while finding many well-detected units, and HDSort finds many more false positive units than any other sorter.
On the simulated recording only 139 of the 1921 detected units (7.24%) are agreed upon by all six sorters.
HDSort, SpyKING Circus and Kilosort2 are more prone to finding low-agreement units than HerdingSpikes2, IronClust and Tridesclous.

Almost all false positive units are found by a single sorter, while most real units are matched by more than one sorter; false positives found by two or more sorters number 4 for HerdingSpikes2, Kilosort2 and IronClust, 2 for SpyKING Circus and HDSort and 1 for Tridesclous.
With two sorters, combining Kilosort2 and IronClust identified true positives most reliably, with false positive and true positive detection rates of 96% and 95%.

A pair of sorters suffices to isolate almost all false positive units, but with fewer than four sorters a significant fraction of true positive units, found by only one sorter, are wrongly classed as false positives; four or more sorters reliably identify most true positives.
Ground-truth units with higher SNR are found by more sorters.
For Kilosort2, SNR is not a good predictor of false positives: many of its false positive units have an SNR above the mode of the ground-truth SNR.
The two experts' manual curations of the Kilosort2 output agree on most curated units (226 of 351, 64.2%), and 174 Kilosort2 units are discarded by both.
Only a small percentage of each sorter's units match the curated units; IronClust matches best (59.83% and 61.1%), above Kilosort2 (50.67% and 56.25%), from whose output the curations were made.
Consensus units (found by at least two sorters) match the curated units at above 70% for every sorter; Kilosort2 is highest (84.55% and 89.55%), slightly above IronClust (82.63% and 83.83%).
Units found by only one sorter rarely match the curated units; the only notable overlap is Kilosort2's (18.58% with C1 and 24.34% with C2).

Data come from 45 two-photon sessions in nine mice (three per Cre line for L2/3, L4 and L5), 15 sessions per line and 9 per area over V1, LM, AL, PM and AM, with one L5 AL session excluded for recording problems.
4018 cells were recorded over the 44 analysed sessions, 1683 in L2/3, 1781 in L4 and 554 in L5, with per layer and area totals from 62 (L4 AM) to 649 (L4 V1).
Calcium indicator kinetics, measured as the half-life of an exponential fit to each cell's mean isolated-event-locked dF/F, do not differ across layers, areas or their interaction.
Unscrambled stimuli evoke higher ND than their phase-scrambled versions in L2/3 but not in L4 or L5, with a significant layer by stimulus category interaction.
The higher ND for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli is specific to areas AL and AM, with a significant area by stimulus category interaction.
Over all 12 stimuli, naturalistic stimuli evoke higher ND than artificial ones in L2/3 and L5 (not L4) and in AL and AM (not V1, LM or PM), with significant interactions with layer and with area.
The L2/3, AL and AM specificity of the unscrambled against scrambled ND difference holds for nearly all choices of distance metric, state length, frequency spacing and spectral window.
Spectral ND of L0 calcium events gives results similar to dF/F, with greater ND for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in L2/3 and in AL, while AM is at the threshold (p = 0.050).
With the 200 ms after each L0 event removed from dF/F, ND remains greater for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in L2/3 and in AL, with significant interactions; AM is not significant (p = 0.0958).
Per-session permutation tests find ND greater for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in all 6 sessions of L2/3 AL and AM, in 8 of 15 L2/3 sessions, 1 of 15 L4 and 0 of 14 L5 sessions.
Within single L2/3 AL and AM sessions effect sizes are medium to very large (Cohen's d 0.57 to 1.25), while the effect over these sessions pooled is 0.34.
Multivariate ND (mean distance to the centroid in an 8-dimensional UMAP embedding) is higher for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli specifically in L2/3.
Multivariate ND is higher for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli specifically in AL and AM.
Multivariate ND of L0 events is also higher for unscrambled than scrambled stimuli in L2/3 and in AL and AM, and in V1 as well.
Stimulus category (unscrambled or scrambled) can be decoded accurately from most layers and areas, well above chance, without the layer and area specificity of ND.
Stimulus identity among all 12 stimuli can be decoded accurately from most layers and areas (chance 1/12).
ND differs among the five continuous naturalistic clips, over all layers and areas.
The snake (predator) clip evokes higher ND than the conspecifics, crickets and man writing clips, and the mousecam clip higher ND than man writing.
Within L2/3 of AL and AM, mean ND per stimulus is positively correlated with stimulus differentiation across the 12 stimuli, but the noise stimulus is highly influential (Cook's D 2.318).

Without the noise stimulus the ND and SD correlation is weak and not significant (r = 0.258), and among the scrambled stimuli and their unscrambled counterparts there is no evidence of a relation (r = -0.378); so ND is not inherited from SD.
ND in L2/3 of AL and AM is not explained by stimulus luminance, contrast or spectral energy.
The dataset holds 13 mice whose subject ids, sex, date of birth, imaged cell type (L2/3 or L5 pyramidal) and imaging plane (somata or distal apical dendrites) are as listed in Table 1.
Thirteen mice were imaged, three L2/3 dendritic, three L2/3 somatic, four L5 dendritic and three L5 somatic, each with at least three imaging sessions.
Seven of the mice are male and six female, and only one L2/3 dendritic mouse is female.
The dataset holds 50 imaging sessions from 13 animals, each session in its own files grouped by subject.
The 50 sessions have the subject ids, session ids, imaging dates, imaging depths, ROI counts, tracked ROI counts, QC results and stimulus seeds listed in Table 2.
Two animals had at least one session that failed the Allen Institute's QC thresholds, and some animals had more than three sessions, for example when an early session failed QC.
Each mouse had three 70-minute imaging sessions within three to six days, with at most one session per day.
Somata were imaged at 175 um (L2/3) and 375 um (L5) depth, and distal apical dendrites at 50 to 75 um (L2/3) and 20 um (L5).
Calcium movies were recorded at 30 Hz over a 400 um field of view at 512 x 512 pixels, and running was recorded at 60 Hz in cm/s.
ROIs that were too noisy, with a mean dF/F below 0 or a median dF/F above the midpoint between the trace's minimum and maximum, were rejected, so no retained ROI has either property.
Somatic planes yielded 15 to 224 ROIs per mouse per session and dendritic planes 159 to 1636.

Matching produced 254 tracked ROIs in L2/3 dendritic planes, 261 in L2/3 somatic, 516 in L5 dendritic and 129 in L5 somatic, about 100 to 500 per plane and about 32 to 75% of the theoretical maximum number of trackable ROIs.

The same imaging planes were recorded over three days and many ROIs could be identified in each day's recording, so that individual dendritic segments and somata can be followed over the three sessions.
In the example L2/3 dendritic mouse of Fig. 8a, removing four conflicting pairwise matches from the union over session orderings left 136 final matches.
In the example L5 somatic mouse of Fig. 8b, removing two conflicting pairwise matches left 47 final matches.

Gabor sequences are repeating 1.5-s sequences of five 300-ms images (A-B-C-D-G), each non-grey image holding 30 Gabor patches, with inconsistent sequences replacing D by U, whose mean orientation is shifted by 90 degrees (drawn from 90, 135, 180 and 225 degrees, against 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees for the other images).

Visual flow is 105 white squares of 8 by 8 degrees moving at 50 degrees per second, in two consecutive periods (rightward and leftward) in random order, with 25% of squares reversed for 2 to 4 s during inconsistent flow.
Each imaging session lasted 70 min, with 34 min of Gabor sequences and 17 min of visual flow in each direction, each stimulus period flanked by 30 s of grey screen.
Inconsistent sequences make up about 7% of Gabor sequences and 5% of visual flow time.

Each session is divided into about 30 blocks, each of 30 to 90 s of consistent stimulus followed by 3 to 6 s (Gabor) or 2 to 4 s (visual flow) of inconsistent stimulus, in multiples of 1.5 s (Gabor) and 1 s (visual flow).
Both somatic and dendritic ROIs responded clearly to the Gabor and visual flow stimuli, many with increased fluorescence at stimulus onset.
Responses to consistent and inconsistent stimuli differed clearly in the example ROIs.
Running velocity and pupil diameter were recorded in sessions 1 to 3 of all 11 mice, so their distributions can be shown per session across mice.
ROI dF/F traces have a relatively high SNR, above 1.
ROI SNR is stable over the three days.
The mean dF/F signal of ROIs is stable over days.
The distributions of pairwise ROI correlations are very similar for apical dendrite ROIs and somatic ROIs, which suggests the dendrites are not heavily over-segmented.
About 0.01% of possible pairs of L2/3 dendritic ROIs have correlations above 0.8.

Mean dF/F responses across ROIs show distinct transients aligned to stimulus onsets (grey screen to stimulus) and offsets (stimulus to grey screen), which validates the temporal alignment of stimuli and recordings.
Each session has three file versions; basic files are about 130 MB to 1.7 GB, the stimulus images add about 1.5 GB, and the motion-corrected stack adds about 45 GB.
The basic files of the sessions 1 to 3 that passed QC are 33 files totalling about 15 GB.
Of 206 mice that started training, 140 reached proficiency in the basic task and 98 in the full task.
Basic task training took 18.4 +- 13.0 days (s.d., n = 140 mice), from 3 days for the fastest mouse to 59 days for the slowest.
The number of days to basic task proficiency differed across laboratories; within-lab interquartile ranges ranged from 8 days (Lab 2) to 22 days (Lab 6).

Measured in trials, basic task training took 10.8 +- 8.6 thousand trials (s.d., n = 140), from one thousand for the fastest mouse to 43 thousand for the slowest; reaching 80% correct on easy trials took on average about 7.4 thousand trials.
About 80% of mice that started training would learn the basic task within the 40 days usually allotted (Kaplan-Meier estimate over all 206 mice).

Contrast threshold and bias varied little during training; the threshold interquartile range slightly decreased from 12-29% in the first 10 training days to 11-23% thereafter, and the bias interquartile range went from -5.2 to 7.1% to -5.6 to 6.5%.
During training mice were not systematically biased to one side; absolute bias averaged 9.8 +- 12.1 (s.d.), and contrast threshold, which stabilized after about 10 sessions, averaged 17.8 +- 11.7%.

Variability in performance across mice decreased with training but did not disappear; between training days 15 and 40, mean easy-trial performance rose from 80.7% to 91.1% while its s.d. across mice fell from 19.1% to 10.1%.

A Random Forests decoder applied to the change in easy-trial performance over the first five sessions predicted whether a mouse would be in the bottom quartile of learning speed with 53% accuracy (chance 25%), and misclassified a top-quartile mouse as bottom-quartile only 7% of the time.
At basic task proficiency, errors on easy (50% and 100%) contrasts were low, 9.5 +- 3.6%, with no significant difference across laboratories.
At basic task proficiency the contrast threshold was similar across laboratories at 14.3 +- 3.8 (s.d., n = 7 laboratories) and the response bias was small at 0.3 +- 8.4.
At basic task proficiency, easy-trial performance, contrast threshold and bias did not differ in median across laboratories.
At basic task proficiency, easy-trial performance, contrast threshold and bias did not differ in variance across laboratories.
At basic task proficiency the median trial duration (stimulus onset to feedback) was 468 +- 221 ms, with some differences across laboratories.
At basic task proficiency mice performed 719 +- 223 trials per session; the difference across laboratories was significant but only in one laboratory relative to the rest.

A Naive Bayes classifier could not identify a mouse's laboratory from its basic-task performance, threshold and bias; its accuracy was 0.12 +- 0.051 against a chance level of 0.11, and the 95% range of its distribution included chance.
With the laboratory's time zone added as a feature, the classifier performed above chance and confused labs in the same time zone.
Random Forest and Logistic Regression classifiers also failed to predict laboratory membership from basic-task behavior.
In the basic task, mouse choices were no more consistent within laboratories than across laboratories.
In the full task, neither choice fractions nor the bias shift between blocks were more consistent within laboratories than expected by chance.

With a looser proficiency criterion (80% correct on easy trials over three sessions, n = 150 mice), behavior was again consistent across laboratories; only the number of trials per session differed slightly, and a classifier failed to identify a mouse's laboratory.

In the first three sessions of the full task, bias in each block, contrast threshold in each block and performance on 100% contrast trials did not vary significantly across laboratories, and a classifier could not predict lab membership.
Mice incorporated the block priors into their choices from the first sessions of the full task.

Mice that reached full task proficiency took 31.5 +- 16.1 days, or 20,494 +- 10,980 trials (s.d., n = 98), from the start of training; the fastest took 8 days (4691 trials), the slowest 81 days (61,316 trials).

Block structure had the greatest effect on choices when sensory evidence was absent; the shift in rightward choices between 20:80 and 80:20 blocks was highest at 0% contrast in every laboratory, averaging 28.5%.
The bias shift at 0% contrast did not differ across laboratories more than within them.
Block type did not significantly affect the contrast threshold.
Block type changed lapse rates, which were higher on the left in 20:80 blocks and higher on the right in 80:20 blocks.
Block type changed the overall bias consistently, with curves shifting left in 20:80 blocks and right in 80:20 blocks.
Threshold, lapses and bias in each block type showed no significant differences across laboratories.
A classifier trained on the full-task psychometric parameters could not predict the laboratory of individual mice above chance.

In a logistic choice model fitted to each mouse, visual weights grew with contrast to above 3 at 100% contrast, while weights for past choices were much smaller and positive after both rewarded (basic 0.19, full 0.42) and unrewarded (basic 0.33, full 0.46) trials, indicating perseverance.
Previous choices influenced behavior more strongly in the full task than in the basic task, after both rewarded and unrewarded trials.

The model predicted individual mouse choices well, with cross-validated accuracy of 81.03 +- 5.1% in the basic task and 82.1 +- 5.8% in the full task, similar across laboratories; mean condition numbers were 2.4 and 3.2.
Fitted model weights and predictive accuracy were similar across laboratories.
After correcting for slow fluctuations in decision bound, most mice used a win-stay lose-switch strategy, in both the basic and full tasks.
After rewarded trials, choice updating was largest when the previous stimulus had low contrast and much smaller after high-contrast rewarded trials.
The session-ending criterion was not mandatory; 5,316 of 10,903 sessions ended earlier and 5,587 later, the latter continuing for a median of 19 +- 16 extra trials (m.a.d.).
The J-array dataset holds 146 single- and multi-unit isolations from two 96-electrode arrays, recorded on the maze task with 108 conditions, with a mean of 2166 trials per neuron.
The single-electrode datasets hold 64, 74 and 172 single units for monkeys A, B and J, with means of 311, 492 and 388 trials per neuron.
In the speed task one example neuron keeps its preparatory preference (reaches up and left) into the peri-movement epoch, with a preparatory to peri-movement tuning correlation of 0.72.

Three other speed-task neurons with clear preparatory tuning do not keep their preferences into the peri-movement epoch; their preparatory and peri-movement tuning are negatively correlated, even for straight reaches at one distance and speed.
In the maze task some neurons keep similar tuning between the preparatory and peri-movement epochs, but most do not.
In the J-array dataset the correlation between a neuron's preparatory and peri-movement tuning is positive on average but small (mean r = 0.13, p = 0.03; mean Spearman r = 0.11).
In the single-electrode datasets (monkeys A, B and J) the mean tuning correlation is 0.21, 0.19 and 0.06 (p = 0.01, 0.01 and 0.12), with mean Spearman correlations of 0.20, 0.20 and 0.06.

The distributions of tuning correlations give little evidence (except perhaps weakly for monkey B) of one population with concordant tuning (r near 1) and another with opposing tuning (r near -1); most neurons have weakly correlated tuning, with a broad range of correlations centred near zero.
The correlation between preparatory tuning and peri-movement tuning measured at single time points begins to decline about 200 ms before movement onset and is near zero by movement onset.

In population averages sorted by each neuron's preparatory preference, the weak agreement between preparatory and peri-movement tuning dominates early, but the separation shrinks with time and shows little relation to preparatory tuning by movement onset.

For every dataset the highest cross-validated PD performance in accounting for preparatory tuning is reached when the PD is expressed in the space built by PCA from the population peri-movement response, compared with task spaces and PCA-based kinematic and EMG spaces.

Considering each dimensionality separately, PD performance is almost always higher in the peri-movement space than in other spaces of the same dimensionality; for the maze task the 3-D endpoints and peak speed space does not perform well.
PD performance in PCA-based spaces generally improves with dimensionality, peaks in a middle range, and declines beyond about 10 dimensions through over-fitting.
Preparatory activity is moderately high-dimensional; depending on the dataset, 7 to 10 dimensions capture 90% of its variance across conditions.

Averaged over monkeys A, B and J (J-array excluded, no EMG), PD performance is highest in the peri-movement space at every dimensionality limit, the advantage grows with dimensionality, and task spaces are largely outperformed by the kinematic and EMG spaces, which are in turn outperformed by the peri-movement space.

A control space built from peri-movement responses in which each neuron's peri-movement pattern was inverted on a random half of the conditions performs poorly, so the trailing end of preparatory activity does not explain the peri-movement space's success.

Moving the start of the peri-movement window from 150 ms before movement onset to movement onset costs little PD performance; at movement onset performance is 97% (monkey J) and 94% (monkeys A, B) of its original value.

The weak correlation between preparatory and peri-movement tuning does not depend on anterior-posterior recording location; regressing tuning correlation on AP location gives r = 0.20, p = 0.27 for J-array and no significant effect in any dataset.
The peri-movement space captures preparatory tuning at both anterior and posterior sites, with performance slightly better at anterior sites.
When the PD is measured on two random sets of 25 conditions, it is most stable in the peri-movement space, for every comparison space and all four datasets.

In a simulated linear dynamical system (a harmonic oscillator held at 25 random initial states, then released), the preparatory to peri-movement tuning correlation of a unit is low (0.08), and a given preparatory rate can lead to opposing peri-movement patterns.
In the same simulated system, preparatory tuning is captured perfectly by a PD in the two-dimensional space found by PCA of the peri-movement activity.
